A notice dated 01/01/2026 credits a $5.00 preservation surcharge from Senate Bill 94 for the present level. Its sample chart shows three pages at $47.00, five at $63.00 and ten at $103.00.

What happens at the Lorain County Auditor before recording?

The Auditor endorses the deed first. Section 319.202 of the Revised Code has the buyer file a value statement, then the Auditor marks the fee on the deed. The seller pays it.

The Auditor's transfer page lays down rules that trip up late arrivals:

  • Transfers happen Monday through Thursday, 8 AM to 4 PM, so Friday closings need planning.
  • E-filed packets are cut off at 3 PM, and walk-ins at 4 PM.
  • Since November 1, 2012 the office has refused anything sent through the U.S. Postal Service.
  • Handwritten forms go back to the sender. Typed, fully completed forms only.
  • A packet with a missing form or the wrong payment is returned, never held.

Staff may not fill out the conveyance or exempt form or give advice about it, citing section 4705.01. Your closing agent or attorney should assemble the packet and confirm the amounts with the Auditor's office in advance.

How is the conveyance fee set in Lorain County?

Ohio law fixes the base at a one dollar minimum, or ten cents for each $100 or fraction of $100 of value, whichever is more, in section 319.54(G)(3). A county commission may add a transfer tax of as much as thirty cents per $100 under section 322.02. Phone the Auditor for the combined Lorain County rate before you estimate your net proceeds.

Many transfers owe no conveyance fee, though the form must say why. Common cases for families include gifts between spouses or from parents to children, deeds among heirs of one estate where no money is paid, and moves into or out of a revocable trust. Every transfer, exempt or not, also pays fifty cents for each parcel.

What formatting rule can add $20 to a Lorain County filing?

Documents prepared after June 30, 2009 must meet the standardization rules of section 317.114, and the Recorder adds $20.00 when they miss. Its fee page spells out font size, ink color, paper size, a three inch blank band on page one and margins on every side, and offers a downloadable template. Court papers, plats, DD-214 discharges and state or federal documents are exempt.

Have the preparer check the template before signing, since a rejected deed costs a second trip to Elyria. The Recorder does not help complete forms, so the preparer is your only safeguard here.

What does Lorain County look like for a seller?

Lorain County stretches along Lake Erie west of Cuyahoga County. Of its 923 square miles, 432 are water, or 47 percent, according to Wikipedia. Elyria holds the courthouse, while the city of Lorain has the most residents. Amherst, Avon, Avon Lake, North Ridgeville, Oberlin, Sheffield Lake and Vermilion complete the list of cities.

On its QuickFacts page, the Census Bureau estimates 323,219 residents in July 2025 and 139,777 housing units. Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows a typical owned home worth $223,200 and a typical household income of $73,347. Owners live in 74.0 percent of homes. Median gross rent was $966, and the mean commute was 25.4 minutes. Most Lorain County sales therefore involve an owner-occupied house with a deed and mortgage already on file.

How can a Lorain County owner guard against deed fraud?

Sign up for the free property alert service offered on the Recorder's website. The FAQ describes deed fraud as criminals transferring a property without the owner's knowledge and advises owners to check their records and be wary of unsolicited deed offers.

Before you list a house, search your own parcel online and confirm the last recorded deed carries the name of the person who will sign. If an old mortgage was paid off but its release never reached the record, have it recorded, at the $4.00 marginal notation charge.

Does the Lorain County Recorder keep veterans' discharge papers?

Yes. According to the FAQ, a veteran can record a DD-214 or NGB-22 so a safe copy exists if the original is lost. The records are protected, and only the veteran or an authorized person can see them. The fee page lists one certified copy of a veterans service discharge at no charge.

How has Lorain County grown, and why does page count matter?

Wikipedia shows 5,696 residents in 1830, 217,500 in 1960 and 312,964 in 2020. The county was set up in 1822, became judicially independent in 1824, and is home to Oberlin College.

Since each extra page adds $8.00, ask your preparer to keep the deed brief. A reference to an older recorded document also triggers the $4.00 notation charge.

What goes in the Lorain County closing packet?

Assemble these items so neither office sends you back:

  • The signed, notarized deed, typed, with the legal description and every parcel number.
  • The right conveyance form, or the exempt form with its reason written out.
  • Payment to the Auditor for the conveyance fee and the per-parcel charge.
  • A check to the Recorder sized to the page count.
  • A check that each page is in black or blue ink and has the margins the template calls for.

Because the Auditor cuts off e-files at 3 PM on transfer days, line up the vendor early on the day you close.

More questions about Lorain County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What does Lorain County charge to record a deed?

The 2026 fee page prints $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 per page after that. A $4.00 notation applies to each release or assignment, and a layout violation adds $20.00. The Auditor's conveyance fee is paid separately.

Will the Lorain County Auditor take a deed by mail?

No. Mailed transfers have been refused since November 1, 2012. Deliver the packet in person Monday through Thursday or send it through an approved e-file vendor before 3 PM.

Can the Lorain County Recorder fix a mistake on my deed?

No. The Recorder says it cannot alter a deed and is not trained to search for liens for you. An attorney can prepare a corrective deed, which the Recorder then files.

Who bills property tax in Lorain County?

The County Treasurer and County Auditor, according to the Recorder's FAQ. The Recorder only keeps the documents that show who owns the land.

Where can I see an old Lorain County deed?

Use the online property search on the Recorder's website to view and download a free copy. Records reach back to 1824, and certified copies are available in person.

Where is the Lucas County Recorder, and how do I submit a deed?

The office says it strongly encourages electronic recording or mailing, and it names CSC, ePN and Simplifile as the e-recording partners. If you mail a deed, include a self addressed stamped envelope or add return postage to the payment. The fee page accepts cash or a check payable to the Lucas County Recorder.

What does recording a deed cost in Lucas County?

The Lucas County recording fee schedule sets the basic fee at $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed or mortgage, and $8.00 for every extra page. The Recorder's news item says the $5.00 increase behind that figure took effect April 1, 2026 under Senate Bill 94, and the schedule lists $39.00 as a minimum.

ItemAmount shown
Deed or mortgage, first two pages$39.00 minimum

There is no reference fee on a master mortgage reference. Plats are priced by size, at ten cents per square inch with a $40.00 minimum per page, and the schedule lists three common sheet sizes with their totals.

What does the Lucas County Auditor charge before the deed is recorded?

Lucas County's Auditor publishes a real estate transfers fact sheet with two charges. The transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. The conveyance fee is $4.00 for every $1,000 of the sale price, and some transfers outlined in law are exempt from it.

The sheet adds that transfers caused by a death, adding survivorship, or placing the property into your own trust are generally exempt and cost only the $0.50 per parcel. The Auditor cannot prepare a deed, and the sheet recommends hiring an attorney because a wrong detail can get the document rejected or cause trouble years later. The Auditor's main line is 419-213-4406.

The statewide rules behind these steps are in section 319.202, which requires the buyer's value statement before the Auditor endorses a deed, and section 319.54, which lists the exempt transfers.

How can I check a Lucas County deed online?

The Recorder's page says recorded documents after 1985 can be viewed through its Online Recordings tool, which is run by a document technology vendor. The Auditor's fact sheet points to the AREIS property system, where deeds and transfers are public.

AREIS shows how title is held, which helps when you are sorting out a sale after a death:

  • Property held in survivorship carries the code ORSURVTC after the owners' names.
  • Property held by a trustee shows the word Trustee after the name.
  • A transfer on death confirmation appears as document type OD on the Transfers page.

For records from before 1985, call the counter on 419-213-4400 and ask how to request a copy.

Why should I avoid paid deed retrieval companies in Lucas County?

Because the county sells the same copy for far less. The Recorder's news section warns residents about solicitations from document retrieval companies that quote $49.50 to $87.00 for a certified copy of a deed. It adds that copies of all land records are available from the office, often for as little as $2.00.

The fee schedule backs that up: assisted copies are $2.00 per page and a certification is $1.00 per document. A copy order form can be emailed to the Recorder or faxed to 419-213-4284 if you have an escrow account with the office. Copies are paid by cash, check or escrow account only.

What does Lucas County look like for a house seller?

Lucas County covers 596 square miles of northwest Ohio, of which 255 square miles is water, along Lake Erie and the Maumee River, based on Wikipedia's county entry. Toledo is the county seat and largest city. The other cities are Maumee, Oregon, Sylvania and Waterville, and the villages include Holland, Ottawa Hills, Whitehouse and Swanton. Much of the land lay within the Great Black Swamp before settlement. I-75, I-475, I-280 and the Ohio Turnpike cross the county.

The Census Bureau reports 423,347 residents in July 2025, down 1.8 percent from the 2020 base, and 201,974 housing units. For 2020 to 2024 it shows a median owner-occupied value of $163,900, median household income of $62,224, owner occupancy of 62.0 percent and median gross rent of $934. With nearly four homes in ten rented, many Lucas County sales involve a tenant-occupied house.

Which documents does the Lucas County Recorder file besides deeds?

The office's overview lists the full range of paperwork it accepts for the permanent land record:

  • Certificates of transfer, deeds and land contracts.
  • Mortgages, liens and real estate financing statements.
  • Plats and powers of attorney.
  • Military service discharges, and any other document made recordable by the Revised Code.

For lien paperwork the schedule gives $5.00 for a federal tax lien, $3.00 for its release and $4.00 for a personal tax release. Bureau of Workers' Compensation liens and releases carry no fee. The e-recording partners also list direct lines: CSC at 866-652-0111, ePN at 888-325-3365 extension 11234, and Simplifile at 800-460-5657 extension 1031.

How did Lucas County's recording fee reach its present level?

The Recorder's news section tracks two jumps. On October 17, 2019, the state budget raised the fee for most documents by $6.00, to $34.00 for the first two pages, with half of all recording fees going to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. The later $5.00 increase came from Senate Bill 94 and brought the figure to $39.00, under section 317.32.

The office also posted a postage change for mailed recordings. From August 17, 2026, the postage for a standard one ounce first class letter rose from $.80 to $1.00, and that amount should be included whenever no self addressed stamped envelope is enclosed. Counting a mailed deed's return postage in the payment avoids a delay at intake.

How did Lucas County come to exist, and why does it matter for a title search?

Lucas County was organized in 1835 and named for the governor of Ohio at the time. Its creation was tied to the Toledo War, because both Ohio and Michigan Territory claimed a strip of land along the border. Earlier, the Battle of Fallen Timbers took place near present day Maumee in 1794.

For a seller, the practical point is that a title company orders the ownership search. The Recorder's online system covers documents recorded after 1985, so ask the title company how it will pull anything older.

More questions about Lucas County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How much is the basic recording fee in Lucas County?

The schedule lists $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed or mortgage, with $8.00 for each additional page. A document that breaks the state layout rules draws a $20.00 non-compliance fee, and each reference for a marginal notation costs $4.00.

What are the Lucas County transfer and conveyance fees?

The Auditor's fact sheet shows $0.50 per parcel as the transfer fee and $4.00 for every $1,000 of the sale price as the conveyance fee. Transfers due to death, survivorship or moving the property into your own trust are generally exempt from the conveyance fee.

Does the Lucas County Recorder accept mailed deeds?

Yes. The Recorder encourages mailing and e-recording. Include a self addressed stamped envelope or add return postage to the payment, and make the check payable to the Lucas County Recorder.

Is there a fee to record a veteran's discharge in Lucas County?

No. The fee schedule lists no fee to record a DD-214 or to get certified copies of it from the Recorder.

Can the Lucas County Auditor prepare my deed?

No. The Auditor's fact sheet says the office cannot prepare transfer documents, including deeds, and recommends hiring an attorney. Staff can answer questions about the transfer process at 419-213-4406.

  • E-recording via CSC eRecording (866-652-0111), Simplifile, ePN, Hopdox.

Madison County by the numbers

Where does a Madison County deed get recorded?

In London, at the courthouse. The Madison County Recorder sits at 1 N Main St, Room 40, London, OH 43140, and takes calls at 740-852-1854. The counter opens at 8 AM and closes at 4 PM on weekdays, though recording ends at 3:30 PM, so a deed handed over at 3:45 waits until the next business day.

Electronic recording is available through four named platforms: CSC eRecording (866-652-0111), Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox. Ask your title company or attorney which platform they use, since the deed can then be recorded without a trip to the courthouse.

What is the recording fee in Madison County?

A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00, a schedule in effect since January 1, 2025 per the Recorder. Senate Bill 94 added a $5.00 surcharge to most documents, the page explains, to fund the preservation and digitizing of records and the office's running costs, and it points to section 317.32.

That statute shows how the amount is built: half base fee, half housing trust fund fee, plus an optional county surcharge. Copies, certified copies, references to older documents and zoning filings carry their own listed amounts. Phone 740-852-1854 to price any unusual document before you mail payment.

How far back do Madison County's online land records reach?

Different record types start at different dates, according to the Recorder's own note. Checking the right category saves a trip to the courthouse:

Online coverage listed on the Madison County Recorder's page
Record typeCoverage stated
DeedsScanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 to present
Mortgages, indexingIndexed from July 17, 1964
Mortgages, imagesScanned and indexed from September 25, 1968
Miscellaneous, lease, lien, federal tax lien, mechanics lien, unemployment compensation lien, mortgage releaseHistorical Archive online, dating to at least 1980, some older

All the original books remain in the office. If a search turns up a gap, call the counter and ask staff to follow up in the books.

What does the Madison County Auditor do with a deed first?

Ohio makes the Auditor endorse the deed before the Recorder files it. Under section 319.202, the buyer's representative submits a statement of value, or a statement of the exemption reason, and the Auditor notes the conveyance fee on the deed itself.

The Madison County Auditor is at 1 N Main St, PO Box 47, London, OH 43140-0047, phone 740-852-9717, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM. Its property transfer forms page lists the packet pieces a closer may need:

  • DTE 100, the conveyance fee statement of value and receipt.
  • DTE 100EX, the statement of the reason for an exemption.
  • DTE 101, a statement of conveyance of homestead property.
  • DTE 102, a statement of conveyance of current agricultural use valuation property.
  • DTE 100M and DTE 41 for manufactured or mobile homes.
  • Affidavits of trustee and successor trustee under sections 317.22 and 5302.171.

The Auditor's site also carries a conveyance fee calculator under its Tools menu. Run your sale through it, or phone the office, rather than guessing at the county's rate.

How does the Auditor treat sale price and gifts?

For an arm's length sale, the Auditor's measure under section 319.202 is everything paid or promised, including any mortgage balance the buyer takes over. For a gift, the measure shifts to what the house would sell for on the open market. Misstating either figure on purpose is unlawful.

The buyer's statement also answers two questions. Was the seller asked whether tax reductions for owner occupancy or homestead apply? Was the land under the agricultural use valuation? A yes to either needs a sworn instrument attached. If the house is a rental, the endorsement points the buyer to a landlord filing under section 5323.02.

Which free tools does the Madison County Auditor's website offer sellers?

The Auditor's home page invites visitors to search any parcel by owner, address or parcel number to see its appraisal and payment history. A menu of tools sits beside the search box, and several help a seller price and plan:

  • A sales report and a sales list of recent transfers.
  • A delinquency report.
  • A conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator.
  • A levy estimator, plus a GIS parcel viewer reached from the map link.

Office hours are 8 AM to 4 PM on weekdays, and the number to call is 740-852-9717.

Which rules govern conveyance fee amounts in Madison County?

Two statutes work together. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the state charge at a dollar or a dime per hundred, whichever is bigger. Section 322.02 lets commissioners layer on a local tax up to thirty cents per hundred, owed by the grantor.

Exemptions cover several family and estate situations:

  • Gifts within a marriage, or handed down to a son or daughter.
  • Transfers among the heirs of one decedent when nobody pays money.
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust.
  • A corrective deed that fixes an earlier recorded deed.

The exemption reason belongs on the form.

What is Madison County like around London?

Madison County lies in central Ohio west of Franklin County, with London as the seat and largest city. Wikipedia gives the area as 467 square miles with almost no water, and places the county in the Columbus metro area. Interstates 70 and 71 cross it on the way to Columbus, and a sliver of Dublin lies inside the county line.

QuickFacts puts Madison County at 46,985 residents in mid-2025, up 7.1 percent since the 2020 base, with 17,383 housing units. Over 2020 to 2024, a typical owned home was valued at $250,100 and a typical household earned $87,045. Owners occupy 77.5 percent of homes, rent runs a median $943, and the mean commute runs 24.9 minutes. The Auditor has also finished a countywide reappraisal for tax year 2026, with tentative values shown for each parcel on its website, so sellers should look up their own parcel before setting a price.

Who else works in Madison County, and what borders it?

London is the seat and the largest city. Madison County was established in 1810 and named for James Madison. In 1850 it counted 10,015 residents, mostly in farming, and in 2020 it counted 43,824. Wikipedia also lists the Ohio Peace Officer Training Academy and the state Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation among its institutions.

Neighbors include Union and Champaign counties to the north and northwest, Franklin County to the east, Pickaway to the southeast, Fayette to the south, and Greene and Clark to the west. An owner with land across a county line needs a separate recorder and auditor filing in each county.

More questions about Madison County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When does Madison County stop recording each day?

3:30 PM. The office is open until 4 PM on weekdays but stops recording at 3:30, so deliver deeds earlier in the afternoon or use an e-recording service.

What is Madison County's price for recording a deed?

A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00, a schedule in effect since January 1, 2025 per the Recorder. Check with the office for extra charges that apply to references, copies or special filings.

Can I e-record a deed in Madison County?

Yes. The Recorder names CSC eRecording, Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox as the electronic routes. Ask your title company or attorney which one they use.

Does the Madison County Auditor have a form for a trust or estate transfer?

Its forms page lists DTE 100EX for exemption reasons and affidavits for a trustee or successor trustee under Revised Code sections 317.22 and 5302.171. An attorney should pick the right ones for your situation.

How old are Madison County's scanned deeds?

Deeds are scanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 forward, according to the Recorder. Mortgages are scanned and indexed from September 25, 1968, and the original books stay in the office.

Mahoning County by the numbers

How do I reach the Mahoning County Recorder?

Walk in at 120 Market Street, Youngstown, OH 44503, on the building's first floor. Counter service runs weekdays from eight in the morning until half past four, while the basement self-serve room closes at four. Dial 330-740-2345 for the office or send a fax to 330-740-2347.

Employees will pull a copy when you can name the recording details, yet they do not run searches for the public. Anyone who must look something up can sit at one of thirteen public terminals or use the online index. Legal advice is not offered by phone or at the desk.

Online searching runs on a system the recorder calls Laredo Anywhere, with a basic search link and a professional one. The page says the web version will eventually replace the older desktop program on the office terminals. An owner tracing an old deed, or checking that a mortgage release was ever filed, can begin there and then ask for a copy using the recording reference the search returns.

At the counter you pay with a check or cash, because the fee schedule rules out credit cards. Documents sent by mail are returned when the check exceeds the exact recording charge, so verify the amount first.

What does recording a deed cost in Mahoning County?

The recorder explains that every charge is set by state law. A posted notice says Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to most recording charges beginning January 1, 2026. Figures in the table come straight from the county's schedule and assume the paper meets the state layout rule.

Recorder charges quoted from the county's published fee schedule
ServiceCharge listed
Deed, mortgage, lease and similar records$39.00 covers pages one and two, then $8.00 per further page or side
Marginal notation (release, assignment, re-recording)Standard fee and another $4.00 per notation
PlatTen cents a square inch, with a $40.00 floor
Certified copy$2.00 a page and $1.00 to certify
Uncertified copy$2.00 a page
Military discharge (DD214)No charge
Paper that breaks the layout ruleAdditional $20

A short two-page warranty deed falls under the first line. A long legal description or attached exhibit adds pages, and each one adds cost. Smaller lines in the same schedule include $5.00 to file a federal tax lien, $3.00 to release one, $4.00 to release a personal property tax lien, and $50.00 for a zoning resolution. A seller whose title search turns up an old lien should ask the recorder whether a release is on file, because a missing release can hold up a closing.

What must the Auditor approve before a Mahoning County deed can be recorded?

Start at the auditor's counter. The published checklist says an incomplete deed comes back with all its attachments for correction. What the auditor looks for:

  • Whether the grantor is married, single or signing with a spouse
  • Where the buyer wants tax bills mailed
  • The legal description, tied back to the previous deed
  • Seller and spouse signatures, plus a notary clause and stamp
  • Who drafted the deed, with contact information
  • A finished state form: DTE 100 for a sale, or DTE 100 EX for a transfer with no payment

Leave a contact name and phone number with the drop-off. The auditor wants a separate check for each transaction, payable to the Mahoning County Treasurer, and will not take a blank one. On a sale the checklist charges $1.00 per $1,000 of price as the conveyance fee, adds $3.00 per $1,000 as a permissive fee, and tacks on 50 cents for each parcel. An exempt transfer owes just the parcel charge. For questions call 330-740-2010 and press 0.

Land measured in acres, a slice of a platted lot or an outlot needs one extra visit first. The GIS and Tax Map desk, in the lobby at 21 West Boardman Street, signs off before the auditor moves the parcel. The recorder sees the deed only once the auditor has stamped it.

Which layout rules can add $20 to a deed?

A state standardization law has applied since mid-2009, and the recorder enforces it on ordinary deeds. A page that ignores it is still taken, but with a $20 surcharge. The recorder's rules:

  • Print no smaller than a 10 point font
  • Sheets from letter size up to legal length
  • Dark ink only, in black or blue, and no highlighter
  • A margin of one inch down both sides and along the bottom
  • Three blank inches above the text on page one, reserved for office stamps
  • Inch-and-a-half headroom on every page after the first

Court and tax authority papers, plats, DD214 forms, state or federal documents, and anything signed before the law began are exempt. The recorder's home page also carries a notary fraud alert. A title company that prepares the package normally takes care of all of this.

Can I file a deed online in Mahoning County?

Yes, for deeds, mortgages and related papers. The recorder names three vendors:

  • ePN, 888-325-3365
  • Simplifile, 800-460-5657
  • CSC eRecording Solutions, 866-652-0111

Title companies and lenders tend to use these services, which skips the drive downtown and the no-card rule at the counter. A family member handling a quitclaim is more likely to bring paper. Both routes still require the auditor's stamp before recording.

What does the Mahoning County market look like?

The county measures 425 square miles, about 14 of them water, and touches Trumbull, Portage, Stark and Columbiana counties as well as two in Pennsylvania. Named for the Mahoning River, it was formed in 1846. Youngstown, the seat, grew as a center of American steelmaking. Mercy Health, the Youngstown school system and the county government led the list of employers in the county's 2019 financial report.

In QuickFacts, owned homes carry a midpoint value of $154,700 for 2020 to 2024, owners live in 70.3 percent of the housing, and household income at the midpoint is $56,942. Builders took out 174 permits in 2025. Headcount dropped from 238,823 in 2010 to 228,614 a decade later. The 2020 census counted 107,989 housing units, 9.3 percent of them vacant, and found 84.4 percent of residents living in urban areas. Twenty school districts cover the county, including Austintown, Boardman, Canfield, Poland, Springfield and Struthers, so a deed for a house in any of them is filed in this one Youngstown office. Cities such as Youngstown, Struthers, Campbell and Canfield and villages such as Sebring, Poland and Lowellville all record in the same office.

What should a seller settle before filing?

Each item below is a call to a different office:

  • Ask the treasurer, at 330-740-2460, for the unpaid balance on the parcel
  • Get a recorded release from any lender whose loan was paid off
  • Look for liens at the recorder, since mortgages, judgments and mechanic's liens never show on a tax bill
  • Ask the probate court who has authority to sign after an owner's death
  • Compare the legal description in your old deed with the auditor's parcel record

A cash sale follows the same path: the auditor first, then the recorder.

More questions about Mahoning County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What number reaches the Mahoning County Recorder?

330-740-2345. Faxes go to 330-740-2347, and the counter is staffed on weekdays.

Does the recorder accept credit cards?

No. The fee schedule lists check or cash only. People who file electronically pay through their vendor.

Did recording fees change in 2026?

Yes. A county notice says Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to most fees from January 1, 2026, and the schedule now shows $39.00 for a deed's first two pages and $8.00 for every page after.

Does the auditor see the deed before the recorder?

Yes. The auditor reviews the deed and collects the transfer charges, and then the deed goes to the recorder. A deed lacking a required item is sent back.

Is a military discharge copy free?

Yes. The schedule lists military records, including the DD214, at no charge and cites Ohio Revised Code section 317.24(A).

Marion County by the numbers

Which offices touch a deed in Marion County, Ohio?

Three county offices handle every Marion County deed, always in the same sequence: engineer, auditor, recorder. The recorder comes last and is the one that places the deed in the permanent public record. You can reach the recorder at 740-223-4100, the auditor at 740-223-4020 and the engineer at 740-223-4110.

Beyond deeds, the recorder files mortgages, easements and related land papers. An online records system lets anyone look up property documents. Paper copies and certified copies are another matter, since the recorder says they require a visit in person or a written request with payment enclosed. The system's own disclaimer tells users to read the actual document, because database entries can be changed without notice.

What does each office do with the deed?

The county's published instructions give the order, which differs from counties that send the deed to the auditor first.

  • Engineer. Staff compare the deed's legal description with the engineer's records and stamp it approved. That stamp expires after 60 days, so a deed left sitting must be stamped again.
  • Auditor. The seller completes and signs a conveyance form. Payment has to arrive before processing begins, and the auditor then stamps the deed as transferred.
  • Recorder. The office confirms the deed was signed and acknowledged correctly and carries both earlier stamps. After recording, the original is kept for imaging and data entry and then mailed back or picked up.

Several other papers follow the same route: a certificate of transfer, an affidavit of survivor, a life estate, a transfer on death designation and a land contract. Putting the engineer first means a faulty description is caught before any money is paid to the auditor.

How much do the engineer, auditor and recorder charge?

Fees come from two places. The auditor's conveyance charge is a local rate, and the recorder's charge follows state law. A notice on the recorder's home page says Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to recording fees for most documents starting January 1, 2025.

Marion County deed steps and rates, quoted from the county's pages
OfficeWhat the county states
EngineerApproval stamp on the legal description, valid 60 days
Auditor, conveyance$4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price
Auditor, line fee50 cents per parcel in the transfer
Auditor, very small sale$4.00 minimum conveyance fee plus line fees under a $1,000 price
Recorder$34.00 covers two pages, $8.00 each later page (rate dated October 17, 2019)

The auditor's online fee calculator asks for the total price, rounded up to the next dollar, and the parcel count. A box marks transfers that qualify as exempt on state form DTE 100 EX. Let the auditor confirm the final total before you write a check.

Can I send a Marion County deed through the mail?

You can, provided the stamps come first. The recorder's page states that, since September 1, 2005, no deed is accepted by mail unless it already bears current engineer and auditor stamps. The county describes three mailings:

  • The deed alone goes to the engineer, with a stamped, self-addressed return envelope
  • The approved deed then goes to the auditor with a signed conveyance form, a check and another return envelope
  • The twice-stamped deed finishes at the recorder with the recording fee

Expect the recorder to take about five days. That window covers proofing, imaging, and a side-by-side comparison of the image against the original before the deed goes back in the envelope you provided. Electronic filing skips the mail altogether. The recorder lists four companies: CSC at 855-200-1150, ePN at 888-325-3365, Simplifile at 800-460-5657 and Indecomm at 651-765-6400.

Can the recorder's closed days change a closing date?

They can. The recorder publishes a closure list that goes beyond the usual holidays. The 2026 version named Good Friday, Juneteenth, part of July 2 and all of July 3, and the afternoon of September 10 plus all of September 11, when the office closed for the Popcorn Festival because of parking. It also showed closings for Veterans Day, most of Thanksgiving week, the afternoon of December 11, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, and New Year's Day 2027.

A deed cannot be recorded on a closed day. A buyer's lender sometimes wants proof of recording before releasing funds, so ask the title company which date it plans to file, and plan around the office calendar when the target falls near a holiday.

What does Marion County look like for homeowners?

Marion County lies in the middle of Ohio, bordered by Crawford, Morrow, Delaware, Union, Hardin and Wyandot counties. It was erected on February 20, 1820, reorganized in 1824, and named for Francis Marion, a South Carolina officer in the Revolutionary War. At 404 square miles it ranks fifth-smallest in the state. The city of Marion holds the seat and the largest population, and U.S. 23 joins state routes 4, 37, 95 and 309 among its main roads.

QuickFacts from the Census Bureau paint a modest market:

  • 2020 headcount of 65,359, with an estimate of 65,115 for 2025
  • Owners live in 67.5 percent of occupied homes
  • Typical owned-home value for 2020 to 2024: $156,800
  • Typical monthly gross rent: $864
  • Typical household income: $59,371
  • Adults with a bachelor's degree: 14.7 percent

Of 27,348 housing units in 2020, 8.8 percent stood empty, and about two of every three residents lived in an urban area. Only 60 building permits were issued in 2025, so existing houses make up most of the sales.

What else does the recorder publish for property owners?

The home page carries two warnings, a property fraud alert and a notary fraud alert, each linking to details. The Documents and Forms page holds three items: a public records policy, security procedures for electronic recording, and a notice to Medicaid Estate Recovery of a pending transfer of property by transfer on death deed.

That last notice concerns transfer on death deeds. Ask the office whether it applies before you plan a transfer of that kind. Staff cannot give legal advice and say some questions may need an in-person visit, so bring the deed and any prior recording references.

How do property taxes fit into a Marion County sale?

Call the County Treasurer at 740-223-4030, the office that takes every property tax payment. According to the auditor, the rate on a bill is the sum of voted levies and bond issues, and Ohio limits unvoted taxation to 10 mills, which works out to $10 per $1,000 of assessed value. Whatever exceeds that was approved by county voters.

The auditor's property search site accepts payments: look up the parcel by number, owner or address, open the tax tab on the property record, and add the amount due to your online cart, where you can adjust it before checkout. Debit and credit cards incur a 2.5 percent fee with a $1.50 floor, e-checks cost a flat $1.50 up to $10,000, and the page shows the amount before you submit. For a seller, the practical step is to request a balance from the treasurer ahead of closing, so the title company can pay anything owed out of the proceeds and the buyer receives a clean record.

More questions about Marion County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What number reaches the Marion County Recorder?

740-223-4100. The engineer's line is 740-223-4110 and the auditor's is 740-223-4020.

How many days does the engineer's stamp last?

Sixty. A deed that waits longer needs a fresh stamp before the auditor and recorder will take it.

What does the Marion County auditor charge on a sale?

The county prints $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price plus 50 cents per parcel. A non-exempt sale under $1,000 pays a $4.00 minimum plus the line fee.

How quickly does the recorder send a deed back?

That time covers proofing and imaging.

Is electronic recording available in Marion County?

Yes. The recorder names CSC, ePN, Simplifile and Indecomm as e-filing companies you can contact.

What does the Medina County Recorder do?

The Medina County Recorder keeps the permanent land records for the county: every deed, mortgage, easement and similar paper that conveys or encumbers land. The office is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, in the city of Medina, and the main number is 330-725-9782. A document search page on the recorder's website lets you look up recorded deeds and mortgages from home.

Staff accept documents, index them and store them in archival form. They do not decide who owns a house. For a seller, the recorder's index is where a title company confirms the chain of owners and finds any open mortgage that must be released at closing.

What will the Medina County Recorder charge to file a deed?

The recorder's fee page lists $34 for the first two pages of a deed, $8 for each added page and $4 for each marginal notation. The office says half of that goes to the basic recording fee and half to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, which matches section 317.32 of the Ohio Revised Code.

State law lets a county add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars. The fee page does not mention one, so call the office before you mail a check and ask for the exact total for your page count.

Who collects the transfer charge on a Medina County sale?

The county auditor does, before the deed ever reaches the recorder. The auditor's page sets the real property conveyance fee at $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price, rounding up to the next $100 when the price ends in a fraction of a hundred. A conveyance fee calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

A regular sale goes in with DTE Form 100. A transfer that qualifies for an exemption goes in with DTE Form 100EX. The auditor's list of exemptions includes:

  • a gift between spouses, or between a parent and child;
  • a transfer to an heir or devisee, or to a surviving spouse;
  • a deed that corrects or confirms one already recorded;
  • a transfer under a court order that is not itself a sale;
  • a deed to the trustee of a trust the grantor can revoke.

Manufactured homes carry their own rate of $1.00 per $1,000. Ask the auditor which form fits your deed before the signing.

Which county offices does a Medina County house sale touch?

A sale usually moves through three counters in the county seat, and the order matters. Getting it backward costs a few days.

  • Auditor: receives the statement of value and collects the conveyance fee.
  • Recorder: records the endorsed deed, any mortgage release and any affidavit.
  • Treasurer: holds the real estate tax payoff. Your title company will want the tax payoff figure, which comes from the county treasurer.

Title companies, lenders and attorneys can skip the trip by e-recording. The recorder lists three approved vendors, Simplifile, ePN and CSC eRecording Solutions, plus File and Go for notices of commencement. Each filer makes one ACH payment per day no matter how many documents go in, so there is no check written for the wrong amount.

What kind of county is Medina County?

Medina County covers 423 square miles in northeast Ohio and borders Cuyahoga, Summit, Wayne, Ashland and Lorain counties. According to Wikipedia, it was created in 1812, organized in 1818 and sits in the old Connecticut Western Reserve. It belongs to the Cleveland metropolitan area, although its southeastern corner is part of the Akron urban area.

Medina is the seat of government and Brunswick is the biggest city. Wadsworth is a city too, and Rittman reaches in from the south. Sharon Center and Valley City are census-designated places. The Medina County Park District, started in 1965, manages 6,353 acres across 18 parks and trails.

Westfield Insurance led the county's list of employers in 2020 with 2,040 workers, followed by the Cleveland Clinic Medina Hospital at 1,431 and county government at 1,365.

Which papers from a Medina County sale go through the recorder?

The fee page names the documents the office handles at the standard rate, and the list shows how varied a house transfer can be. Most Medina County sellers will meet only a few of them.

  • Warranty deeds, quit claim deeds and survivorship deeds.
  • Sheriff's deeds, which close out a foreclosure sale.
  • Mortgages, mortgage releases, assignments and subordinations.
  • Affidavits, powers of attorney and various trust documents.
  • Land contracts, leases and easements.

An inherited house often needs an affidavit or certificate alongside the deed. A house with a lender needs a release recorded after payoff, which carries the $4 release fee. Each paper is priced separately by page count, so a closing with a deed, a release and an affidavit produces three charges.

What makes a Medina County deed easy to record?

Ohio's standardization law, ORC 317.114, took effect July 1, 2009, and the recorder's fee page repeats it: a document that does not meet the requirements can be charged an extra $20. A clean deed avoids that charge and avoids a call back from the office.

Have the deed prepared by someone who knows Ohio's format and legal description rules, and confirm the page total before you pay. The county's website directs questions to the office at 330-725-9782. The Medina County Auditor also posts conveyance forms and a sales report, which show what nearby parcels sold for and help a seller check the figure going on the statement of value.

How big is the Medina County housing market?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table credits Medina County with 185,025 people as of July 2025. Its housing rows paint a prosperous, owner-heavy county.

  • Eight in ten homes (80.3 percent) are lived in by their owners, across 73,086 households.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $287,000.
  • Homeowners with a mortgage report $1,726 a month in costs; those without report $650.
  • Renters pay a median $1,143 in gross rent.
  • Household income reaches $94,968 at the median.
  • The county counted 77,727 housing units and issued 430 building permits during 2025.

Because so many households own, most recorded deeds here are ordinary owner-to-owner sales. Rental and inherited houses make up the rest.

How can a Medina County owner guard against deed fraud?

A free Property Fraud Alert comes with the office. Sign up through the recorder's website, and the automated system sends an email or phone alert whenever a transaction involving your property is recorded. The idea is to catch a forged deed early. The office at 330-725-9782 can help with the sign-up.

Veterans can record a DD214 at no cost, and the office issues a free Veteran's Identification Card once the discharge is on file. Recording the paper creates a certified source if the original is ever lost.

Where is the Medina County Recorder's office?

It is at 144 N. Broadway Street, Room 117, Medina, Ohio 44256. The office phone is 330-725-9782. Call before you go to confirm hours and the total fee for your document.

What are the recording fees in Medina County?

The fee page prints $34 up to two pages and $8 per page beyond. A document that fails the state formatting rules draws an extra $20. Ask the office whether the optional preservation surcharge applies to your filing.

Does the recorder charge the real estate transfer tax?

No. The county auditor collects the conveyance fee, which the auditor's page sets at $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price. Exempt transfers use DTE Form 100EX and pay no conveyance fee.

Can lenders and title agents e-record Medina County deeds?

Yes, through Simplifile, ePN or CSC eRecording Solutions, all under contract with the office. Homeowners generally do not e-record on their own, so ask your closing agent.

Can Medina County owners get an alert when a document hits their property record?

Yes. The recorder runs a free Property Fraud Alert program that sends an email or phone notice when a transaction involving your property is recorded.

Where do you file a deed in Meigs County, and when can you walk in?

Deeds for Meigs County land are filed at the recorder's office, 100 E. Second Street, Pomeroy, Ohio 45769. The Ohio Legal Help directory shows weekday hours of eight in the morning to four in the afternoon. Whatever conveys, mortgages or otherwise burdens a parcel gets a permanent entry in that office's records.

Sellers care about the entry because a title company reads it before closing. An old mortgage, a lien or a missing link in the chain of owners must be cleared first, or the buyer cannot take clean title.

What are the Meigs County recording charges?

Ohio law fixes recording charges, and the Ohio Recorders' Association publishes the schedule. Each fee splits evenly between the recorder's own fee and the state's Housing Trust Fund. Counties also have the option of a preservation surcharge capped at five dollars, so ask the Meigs office whether it adds one before you write a check.

Copy charges differ from one county to the next. Ask the Meigs office what it asks for plain and certified copies.

What is the transfer charge on a Meigs County sale?

Meigs County's conveyance fee, often called the transfer tax, is collected by the auditor rather than the recorder. The auditor's page prints a rate of $4.00 for each thousand dollars of price, and it applies to houses and manufactured homes alike.

Paperwork for the auditor includes DTE Form 100 (statement of value and receipt) and DTE Form 100EX (exemption). Form 101 covers the conveyance of homestead property. The auditor's site also lists conveyance standards dated July 1, 2025, which a surveyor or attorney should read before drafting a legal description.

A used manufactured home sold after January 1, 2000 must be transferred through the auditor, who adds a 50-cent transfer fee. Once the conveyance is paid, the clerk of courts can move the title with no sales tax.

How are values set and contested in Meigs County?

The auditor values real property at the price it would fetch in an arm's-length sale. Staff review permits, land splits and boundary surveys and inspect new construction.

Disputes go to the Board of Revision, with the auditor as permanent secretary alongside the county treasurer and the president of the commissioners. The complaint form comes from the auditor's office (DTE Form 1) and must arrive by March 31 each year.

Owners who live in their house can also seek the 2.5 percent tax reduction. The auditor sets three tests:

  • the applicant owns the home;
  • it is the applicant's main residence;
  • the application is filed between January 1 and the first Monday in June.

Rentals, corporate or partnership owners and acreage past the first acre do not qualify.

What shaped Meigs County land and houses?

Meigs County was cut from Gallia and Athens counties in 1819 and named for an early Ohio governor. Wikipedia lists 433 square miles. The Ohio River runs along the east and south sides, facing West Virginia, while Vinton, Athens and Gallia counties adjoin it inside Ohio. Pomeroy houses the government, Middleport is the largest village, and Racine, Rutland and Syracuse make up the rest.

Rolling to rugged Appalachian Plateau terrain covers the county, drained largely by Shade River and Leading Creek. Coal mining, strip and underground, left its mark from the late nineteenth century onward. The Yellowbush mine near Racine opened in 2009 and closed by 2015. Anyone selling land over old workings should read the auditor's posted guide, Developing on Abandoned Mine Land.

How many people and homes does Meigs County have?

QuickFacts, the Census Bureau's county table, puts Meigs County at 21,587 people in July 2025, a drop of 2.8 percent since the 2020 count. Housing rows from the 2020 to 2024 survey period read as follows.

  • About three of every four households (75.4 percent) own their home, out of 9,102 households.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $119,300.
  • Owners with a mortgage report $1,130 a month in costs, and those without one report $473.
  • Renters pay $722 at the median.
  • Household income is $46,873 at the median.
  • No building permits were recorded for the county in 2025.

The 2020 census found 10,649 housing units and a 13.6 percent vacancy rate, so roughly one home in seven stood empty when the census was taken.

What should Meigs County owners of manufactured homes know?

The Meigs County Auditor keeps a separate page on manufactured homes. Homes bought after January 1, 2000 are taxed like real property under the appraisal method, with values reset every three years at 35 percent of estimated market value. Older homes may stay on the depreciation method or make a one-time switch to the appraisal method after all taxes are paid.

  • Owners must register a home with the auditor within 30 days of locating it in the county, and a failure to register can bring a $100 fine.
  • A relocation notice, required to move a home on a public road, costs $5 at the auditor's office and requires that taxes be paid.
  • A home on a permanent foundation on land the owner also owns may qualify to be taxed as real estate after the title is inactivated and surrendered.

If you plan to sell a manufactured home that has moved or changed tax methods, call the auditor first so the transfer paperwork matches the home's status.

Where do Meigs County parcel maps and boundary questions go?

The auditor's site says the county tax map office now runs its own website at meigscountytaxmap.com. Land splits and boundary surveys go through the tax map department before the auditor reviews them for new values, so a seller who is dividing a parcel should start there. Ask that office for the current requirements before you order a survey.

What documents show up when a Meigs County house changes hands?

Most sales involve a deed and, if the seller owed money, a mortgage release. Each one is recorded on its own and priced by page. A release or assignment also carries the per-reference charge shown in the table above.

  • Warranty or fiduciary deed from seller to buyer.
  • Mortgage release recorded after payoff.
  • Affidavit or court certificate when an estate is the seller.

If the lender has started a foreclosure, the auditor's page points owners to the county sheriff's website at meigssheriff.org for the list of upcoming sheriff's sales.

More questions about Meigs County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the address and phone number for the Meigs County Recorder?

The office is at 100 E. Second Street, Pomeroy, Ohio 45769. Ohio Legal Help lists weekday hours of eight to four.

How much does Meigs County charge for filing a deed?

The Ohio Recorders' Association lists $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each added page. A county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. Call the recorder to get the exact total for your page count.

How much is the conveyance fee on a Meigs County sale?

The county auditor lists $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price for both real estate and manufactured homes. A 50-cent transfer fee also applies to manufactured homes. Ask the auditor which form your deed needs.

When must a Meigs County valuation complaint be filed?

By March 31 of the year you are contesting. File it with the county auditor, who is secretary of the Board of Revision. Forms are available from the auditor's office.

Does recording a military discharge cost anything in Meigs County?

No. Ohio sets no fee for recording a military discharge, and the Ohio Recorders' Association fee list shows it as free.

Where is the Mercer County Recorder, and how do you pay?

The recorder works from Room 203 of the Celina courthouse, 101 N. Main Street, Celina, Ohio 45822. Call (419) 586-4232 to reach staff. Doors open at half past eight each weekday. Mondays run later, to five, while Tuesday through Friday end at four. Federal holidays are closed days.

Anything that deals with land can be recorded there and read by the public. Recording is paid in cash or by check payable to the Mercer County Recorder, and cards are not accepted for it. Requests for copies are the exception, since the office offers an online payment link for card or eCheck.

What are Mercer County deed recording charges?

An increase of $5.00 per document began January 1, 2025, following Ohio Senate Bill 94 (effective October 24, 2024), which lets a recorder add a preservation surcharge up to that amount. The county's notice sets the base at $39.00 through page two and $8.00 for each page past that. Its own chart reads as follows.

References add $4.00 each, and the formatting rules below still apply. Papers that carry their own fee under the Revised Code, among them federal tax liens, plats, township zoning and UCC filings, skip the new $5.00 charge.

Which formatting mistakes cost extra in Mercer County?

The state's standardization law, ORC 317.114, covers documents prepared after June 30, 2009. A paper that misses the mark draws a $20.00 charge. The recorder lists the standard this way:

  • Print in a font of at least ten points.
  • Use paper no smaller than letter size and no longer than 14 inches.
  • Use black or blue ink with no highlighter.
  • Keep a one-inch border at the sides and bottom.
  • Leave three inches clear at the head of the first page, where the recorder, auditor and engineer stamp, and an inch and a half at the top of later pages.

The rules skip court and taxing authority papers, plats, DD214 forms, state or federal documents and anything signed before the law took effect. The office also wants an original rather than a photocopy, a legal description, the preparer's name, a notary and English text. A deed that conveys land has to clear the Tax Map office and the auditor before it gets to the recorder.

Can a Mercer County deed go in by mail or e-recording?

Both routes are open. Mail-in conveyances have been accepted since November 1, 2024 by the auditor, tax map and recorder offices together, with firm conditions. The Tax Map office must approve the legal description first, and the packet needs the email showing it did.

  • Complete the auditor's forms.
  • Send separate checks to the auditor, the recorder and the treasurer. A combined check gets the packet rejected.
  • Add any recording instructions and a return envelope with postage.

The recorder quotes a one-day turnaround by mail and an immediate one at the counter. Electronic filing has been taking documents since 2010, and from November 5, 2025 conveyances can be sent through all three vendors (Simplifile, CSC and ePN). Title companies and lenders usually handle that.

Where do I find a copy of a recorded Mercer County deed, or track a sheriff's sale?

Prints made by the office cost $2.00 a page. Deeds recorded since 1946 can be viewed and printed free from the recorder's records search website. For a mailed copy, send the owner name or property address and the exact fee, plus an envelope addressed to yourself with postage, to the Room 203 address, or email the office. Staff are not permitted to do title searches.

The recorder is the last office to see paperwork from a sheriff's sale. After a foreclosure ends, the Mercer County Sheriff's Office sends the sheriff's deed to the recorder. The sheriff keeps a searchable list of properties going up for sale, and the foreclosure case itself can be read on the Clerk of Courts website once you have the case number.

What should Mercer County sellers ask the treasurer?

The treasurer's office is Room 201 in the courthouse, reachable at (419) 586-2259. Its FAQ says Ohio bills real estate tax one year behind. Who owes what at a sale therefore comes down to the closing agreement, and tax that falls due after the purchase date belongs to the buyer.

Bills are mailed in January and June, usually with payment due on the 20th of February and July. Pay within ten days of the deadline and the penalty is 5 percent. Pay later and it is 10 percent. A remission application goes before the Board of Revision (treasurer, auditor and a commissioner). Monthly ACH or coupon plans are available too.

A delinquency notice goes out in late September. The auditor's site says parcels still unpaid at noon on November 2, 2026, with no installment plan, were advertised November 4, 2026. Request a payoff figure well ahead of closing.

What is happening with Mercer County values and credits?

The auditor's 2026 triennial update reviews arm's-length sale prices from 2023, 2024 and 2025. It does not repeat the full exterior inspection of each parcel done for the 2023 reappraisal. New values will appear on the 2027 tax bills.

The auditor also explains the Inflation Cap Credit from House Bill 186. It reached second-half 2025 bills payable in 2026, and every parcel gets its own figure (a few get none). Any overpayment rolls into the first-half 2026 bill. The auditor's site includes a conveyance fee calculator, which is the place to get the county's rate for a sale.

What is Mercer County like?

Mercer County lies along Ohio's border with Indiana, next to Van Wert, Auglaize, Shelby and Darke counties. Wikipedia says it was formed in 1820 and fully organized on January 2, 1824. Celina took over as seat in 1839 from St. Marys. German immigrant farm families arrived in the mid to late 1800s.

The auditor calls Grand Lake St. Marys the largest inland lake in Ohio. The Wabash and St. Marys rivers cross the county, and a continental divide runs between their watersheds. Celina holds the courthouse and is the only city. Maria Stein is the one census-designated place, and townships including Black Creek, Dublin, Franklin and Liberty cover the rest. Manufacturing and health care anchor local work, with Celina Insurance Group, Celina Aluminum Precision Technology and J&M Manufacturing among the named employers.

How large is the Mercer County housing market?

The Census Bureau counts 42,737 people for July 2025, a small gain over the 2020 base. Housing rows describe a steady owner market.

  • Close to four in five households (79.6 percent) own their homes, out of 16,408 households.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $210,600.
  • Those paying a mortgage spend $1,340 a month on owner costs, and those without spend $553.
  • Renters pay $804 in median gross rent.
  • Household income is $76,782 at the median.
  • Builders pulled 83 permits in 2025 for a stock of 18,384 housing units.

More questions about Mercer County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When can you reach the Mercer County Recorder?

It opens at 8:30 a.m. on weekdays, closes at five on Mondays and at four Tuesday through Friday, and shuts on federal holidays. The office is in Room 203 of the courthouse at 101 N. Main Street in Celina.

What is the price to record a short Mercer County deed?

The county lists $39.00 for a deed of one or two pages. Each further page adds $8.00, and a $4.00 reference fee or a $20.00 non-standard charge may apply.

Can I pay recording fees with a card in Mercer County?

No. The recorder's page says recording is paid by check or cash, with checks payable to the Mercer County Recorder. Copy requests can be paid by card or eCheck online.

What does a veteran pay to record a DD214 in Mercer County?

Nothing. The office records a DD214 and issues copies free. Copies are limited to authorized people with identification, such as the veteran or an estate executor.

What approvals come before the Recorder in Miami County?

A deed must clear the County Engineer and the Auditor first. Miami County's conveyance standards, adopted August 12, 2025, say every instrument is approved for transfer by the Engineer's Office, with a signed DTE 100 value statement or a DTE 100EX exemption form turned in alongside it.

Three rules in those standards matter to sellers:

  • No transfer is approved when the grantor never appears as an earlier grantee, unless the deed or an affidavit under section 5301.252 explains the gap in the chain of title.
  • A deed that carves a piece off an existing parcel, or changes the legal description, needs a boundary survey plat that the Engineer reviews.

The Auditor's fee comes from section 319.54: $1, or ten cents per $100 of value if that is larger. Separately, section 322.02 lets county commissioners levy a transfer tax that tops out at 30 cents on each $100. Sellers pay both. Call the Miami County Auditor to learn which applies before you build a closing statement.

What else does the Miami County Recorder file, and at what price?

Deeds are one entry on a long list. The recorder's fee page names affidavits, easements, land contracts, leases, mechanic's liens, notices of commencement, powers of attorney, sheriff's deeds, survivorship deeds, trust documents and warranty deeds among the items it accepts. A few carry their own prices:

  • Federal tax lien: $5.00 to file and $3.00 to release.
  • Release of a personal property tax lien: $4.00.
  • Financing statement: $12, plus $4 for each name indexed.
  • Living will or durable power of attorney for health care: $28 minimum, $40 maximum.
  • Plats: ten cents a square inch, minimum $40.00.
  • Faxed pages: $2 local or toll-free, $4 long distance.

Sellers most often meet the mortgage release. If a lender never recorded one after an old payoff, the lien still shows on the record, so ask the title agent to check before the buyer's lender does.

What does the Miami County value statement ask the seller?

The buyer's statement under section 319.202 records whether the seller expects a reduced tax bill, such as the homestead or owner-occupancy credit, and whether the land was enrolled in the agricultural use valuation. A yes on either needs a sworn paper that both sides have accounted for the amount.

Farm ground is worth a question in a county that covers 410 square miles and has only five cities. If a seller's acreage was enrolled, leaving the program can trigger a recoupment charge, and the buyer and seller are expected to account for it before the Auditor endorses the deed.

For a rental, the Auditor's stamp also reminds the buyer to file landlord information with the Auditor under section 5323.02.

How can you look up or copy Miami County land records?

The county's records search page offers a free basic search by last and first name, or business name, in the AVA database. Images carry a watermark, and a watermarked copy is not accepted for recording.

  • Basic search: free to view and print, with a watermark.
  • Clean copies: email or call the Recorder's Office; since January 2026 copies cost $2.00 per page, paid in advance.
  • Credit cards: a service fee of $2.00 or 2.65% applies, whichever is greater. Cash and check are also taken.
  • Title searchers: Laredo Anywhere, run by Fidlar Technology, reaches deeds back to the county's start in 1807.

Deeds from 1807 through 1979 are scanned as whole books. Records for 1980 through 2008 are only partly indexed, and for anything before 1980 the county asks you to contact the office. A certified copy is $2.00 a page, and each seal adds $1.00.

Can a title company e-record a Miami County deed?

E-recording exists, but the county describes it as a tool for businesses that file regularly, not for one-time submissions. Its e-recording page lists five vendors: ePN, Simplifile, Hopdox, Indecomm and CSC. Each sets its own pricing, so a title agent signs up with a vendor directly.

A private seller closing without a title company can send the deed by mail or hand it over at the window. Ask the Recorder's Office at (937) 440-6040 whether your document type can go electronically before you plan around it.

What should a Troy-area owner know about Miami County itself?

Founded March 1, 1807 and named for the Miami people, the county seats its government in Troy. Per Wikipedia, it covers 410 square miles in the Dayton metro area and borders Shelby, Champaign, Clark, Montgomery and Darke counties. Its cities are Troy, Piqua and Tipp City, plus slices of Huber Heights and Union.

QuickFacts puts the 2025 headcount at 112,634, a 3.5% gain on the 2020 base, spread over 47,930 housing units. Roughly three in four homes are lived in by their owners (73.4%). Median home value stands at $229,100 and median household income at $76,817 in the 2020 to 2024 survey period. Commuters average 22.0 minutes to work, and the county issued 340 building permits in 2025.

A sale of any kind, from a tidy listing to a tenant-occupied fixer, follows one path here: Engineer, Auditor, Recorder.

More questions about Miami County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the address of the Miami County Recorder?

The office sits at 201 West Main Street in Troy, OH 45373. Call (937) 440-6040; it is open weekdays from 8 am until 4 pm.

What is the Miami County deed recording fee?

Two pages cost $39.00, which includes a $5.00 preservation fee, and every extra page adds $8.00. A $4.00 marginal notation fee applies to mortgage releases, assignments and modifications, and a $20.00 fee applies when a document misses the Ohio standardization rules.

Who covers the conveyance fee when a Miami County house sells?

The seller settles it with the Auditor before recording. State law sets the minimum at $1, rising to ten cents per $100 on larger values, and a local transfer tax may be added if the commissioners adopted one. The Auditor can tell you what applies to your parcel.

Does Miami County need a survey to split a parcel?

Yes. The county's conveyance standards require a boundary survey plat when a deed cuts up an existing parcel or changes its legal description, and the County Engineer reviews it before the Auditor accepts the deed.

Can I print my deed for free in Miami County?

Yes. Anyone can pull up and print a watermarked image through the basic records search without paying. A copy without the watermark must be requested from the Recorder's Office and costs $2.00 per page.

Montgomery County by the numbers

Where is the Montgomery County Recorder's Office in Dayton?

The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building, 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Per the county's Recorder FAQ, the full deed and index collection, 1805 to the present, is kept there on books and microfilm.

Older material sits at the County Records Center and Archives, 117 South Main Street, 6th floor, reached by the Main Street elevator, at 937-225-6366. The office records, scans and indexes paperwork on the day it arrives, whether it comes by mail, over the counter or from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department. Documents go back in the mail the next business day, and the office works from 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays.

The Recorder is one of Ohio's oldest county offices. Ohio's General Assembly made it a required county office in 1803, the year Montgomery County was founded. Judges appointed the first recorders, and voters began electing them in 1829. Today the term is four years.

What does recording a deed cost in Montgomery County?

The county's own pages show two figures, so confirm the current one with the office before you bring a check. The Recorder FAQ quotes $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each added page. The eRecording page quotes $39.00 and $8.00.

Montgomery County recording charges as printed on two county Recorder pages
ChargeRecorder FAQeRecording page
First two pages$34.00$39.00
Each added page$8.00$8.00
Mortgage release or assignment, marginal notationNot listed$4.00
No clear 3-inch top margin on page one$20.00 standardization feeStandardization laws apply

The gap matches the statute. Section 317.32 sets $17 plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for two pages, which is $34, and lets a county add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. Pay at the counter in cash, or by check or money order made out to Montgomery County Recorder.

What must a Montgomery County deed contain?

The county lists the elements a clerk checks at the window. A deed needs:

  • The names of the buyers and sellers.
  • A legal description, which you can get from the Copy Center.
  • The sellers' signatures.
  • A preparation statement, if the deed was notarized in Ohio.
  • A Transfer or No Transfer stamp from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department, plus the Engineer's approval where the property calls for it.

Notarization follows the law of the state where the signer stood. The notary block has to show a statement, a signature and an expiration date. A mortgage adds the loan amount and the lender and borrower names.

Changing a name on a deed means a new deed, a stop at the Auditor for a stamp and then the Recorder. No new deed is generated when a loan is paid off. The lender records a Release or Satisfaction of Mortgage instead.

Which Montgomery County transfers must visit the Auditor first?

Anything that conveys land passes through the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department before recording. Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement, and the grantor pays the fee set in section 319.54, plus any transfer tax the county commissioners have levied.

The county's eRecording rules draw the line clearly. Mortgages, assignments and releases with no transfer can go in electronically through Simplifile. Deeds and anything needing a No Transfer stamp, such as a transfer on death designation, an easement or an affidavit that references a deed, must be mailed or walked through the Auditor's department first.

The Auditor and Engineer also publish conveyance standards, adopted August 2, 2021, governing legal descriptions and splits. Copies are on the Auditor's third and fifth floors and the Engineer's eighth floor at 451 West Third Street.

How do you find or print a Montgomery County deed?

Print any document you find on the Recorder's online search at no charge. If you cannot print, the Copy Center charges $2.00 per page, and certification adds $1.00. The office does not run title searches, but the 5th floor Public Research Area has public computers for doing your own.

  • Deeds, releases and liens are searchable by name on the county's online system.
  • To trace an older house, build the chain of owners from the grantee-grantor or tract index, then check the Auditor's tax lists for a jump in value that suggests new construction.
  • Veterans who recorded a DD214 can request a copy at no charge, and the Recorder issues a free Veteran ID card to those who record one.

Searching by street address happens on the Auditor's site instead of the Recorder's.

How do Montgomery County records help trace an older house?

The county's FAQ lays out a research route for anyone curious when a house was built. Start with the chain of ownership in the Recorder's deed records, using either the alphabetical grantee-grantor index or the tract index, which is organized by legal description. Both index types run from 1805 to the present, with deed books and microfilm for 1935 on and microfilm for 1805 through 1934.

  • At the Records Center and Archives, the alphabetical indexes cover 1805 to the present, and tract index microfilm covers 1805 to 1934.
  • The Auditor's tax lists run 1803 to 1954 as indexes and 1955 to 1985 as original books.
  • A jump of more than 50% in one year's taxable value usually points to construction or improvements.

The FAQ adds that taxable values were recorded at 35% of market value since 1973, and at 40 to 45% before that. The county says the research is the individual's job, though the archives answer questions at 937-225-6366. The Recorder's computerized tract index, one of few in-house systems of its kind, earned a National Association of Counties achievement award, and new records are indexed the day they arrive.

What is Montgomery County like for a house seller?

Dayton is the county seat, and the county spans 464 square miles in southwest Ohio, according to Wikipedia. It touches Miami, Clark, Greene, Warren, Butler, Preble and Darke counties. Besides Dayton, the cities include Kettering, Huber Heights, Centerville, Miamisburg, Vandalia, Trotwood and Englewood, and the villages are Farmersville, New Lebanon, Phillipsburg and Verona.

The county reports roughly 230,000 parcels. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts lists 539,598 residents in 2025 and 254,375 housing units. Owners occupy 62.5% of homes, the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $180,900, and median gross rent is $1,026. Median household income is $66,139.

Because more than a third of homes are rented, many sellers here are landlords. The Auditor's deed endorsement for residential rental property reminds the buyer to file landlord information under section 5323.02, so a rental sale carries one more form than an owner-occupied home.

More questions about Montgomery County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the address of the Montgomery County Recorder?

The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Records Center and Archives material is at 117 South Main Street, 6th floor.

How much does Montgomery County charge to record a deed?

The Recorder FAQ prints $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per added page, while the eRecording page prints $39.00 and $8.00. Call the office to confirm which figure applies the day you file.

Do I need the Auditor before the Recorder in Montgomery County?

Yes, for any deed. The Auditor's Deed Transfer Department stamps it Transfer or No Transfer and collects the conveyance fee, then the deed goes to the Recorder. Only non-transfer papers such as mortgages and releases can be e-recorded directly.

Is there a fee for a poorly formatted document in Montgomery County?

Yes. The Recorder FAQ adds a $20 standardization fee when page one lacks a clear 3-inch top margin, and the eRecording page says all Ohio standardization laws apply.

Can I get a free copy of my Montgomery County deed?

Yes, if you print it yourself from the Recorder's online search. The Copy Center charges $2.00 per page if you cannot print, with certification costing $1.00 more.
