Which Morgan County office takes a deed for recording?

The Morgan County Recorder's Office is in the Riecker Building at 155 East Main Street, Room 160, McConnelsville, OH 43756. The county recorder page gives 740-962-4051 for calls and recorder@morgancountyohio.gov for email.

The Auditor works from the same building and answers at 740-962-4475. A Morgan County deed does not go straight to the Recorder, though. The Auditor's FAQ sends questions about prior deeds and recording fees to the Recorder's counter on the first floor, so call that number before you drive in.

In what order do Morgan County offices handle a deed?

A deed starts at the County Engineer, moves to the Auditor, and ends at the Recorder. The Auditor's real estate FAQ applies the same route to transfer on death designations, land contracts, easements and covenants, and says Auditor staff will take your papers to the other offices in the proper order.

The Engineer's number is 740-962-3171. The county's conveyance standards want these items in or attached to any document that transfers land:

  • The parcel number.
  • A full legal description.
  • The property address.
  • A reference to the prior instrument.
  • The tax-mailing address.

Signatures must be legible, and a printed name below an unclear signature is accepted. After the Auditor finishes, the county's property website refreshes within one to two business days.

What does the Morgan County Auditor collect on a sale?

The Auditor's transfer page lists the charges that precede recording. The office takes cash, or a check made out to the Morgan County Auditor.

Morgan County Auditor transfer charges as printed on the county's transfer page
ChargeAmount
Conveyance fee$3.00 per $1,000 (sale price x .003)
Transfer fee$0.50 per parcel
Split fee, for every split$100.00

Morgan quotes one conveyance figure of $3.00 per $1,000. State law behind the Auditor's fee (section 319.54) starts at $1 or ten cents on each $100, and section 322.02 allows commissioners to levy a local transfer tax with a ceiling of 30 cents per $100. Ask the Auditor how Morgan's single number is divided if your closing statement needs a line for each. For acreage splits, call the Engineer, since the survey and the split fee start there.

What fees apply when the Morgan County Recorder records a deed?

Morgan County's published pages send recording-fee questions to the Recorder, so ask for the current sheet when you call 740-962-4051. The ceiling comes from section 317.32. Two pages carry $17 for the recorder and $17 for the housing trust fund, and each page beyond them adds $4 and $4. On top, the county may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at $5 an instrument.

The same section prices a certified copy at $1 plus $1 per page, a counter photocopy likewise, and a marginal reference made by separate instrument at $2 plus $2. Page counts use legal-size sheets and include the caption page, which is why a third page raises the bill.

Is a Morgan County transfer taxable if no money changes hands?

It can be. According to the Auditor's FAQ, a sale is taxable, and so is a gift with no money involved unless an exemption fits. Only the relationships listed on the DTE 100EX form are exempt, and the filer reads each lettered choice to see whether one fits.

The statute lists many of those exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3), including transfers among heirs of one decedent when no money is paid and transfers to the grantor of a trust the grantor can revoke. If someone on the deed has died, the Auditor points families to Morgan County Probate Court at 740-962-2861 when there is a will, and to a title agent or real estate lawyer when a survivorship deed or transfer on death designation was recorded.

Section 319.202 (full text) also has the buyer certify what the seller said about reduced taxes and farm-use valuation. An owner who sells a home that carried the homestead reduction also files form DTE 101, the Statement of Conveyance of Homestead Property, which the Auditor's homestead page lists. Morgan's Auditor lists a $25 one-time filing fee for the farm program (CAUV), which requires crops, animals or timber on at least 10 acres.

What should a Morgan County seller expect on parcels and tax bills?

Parcel changes take effect at once, but the bills lag. After combining parcels, the owner keeps getting separate paper bills until the next tax year, and the owner of an original parcel receives the tax bill for the whole original parcel until the next year after a split. The Auditor advises raising that with a title company or real estate attorney before the sale closes.

Taxes are due in February and July, and the Treasurer at 740-962-3561 bills and collects them. Value complaints go to the Auditor between New Year's Day and the end of March. The standard Homestead Exemption exempts $25,000 of a home's market value for qualifying seniors and for owners who are permanently and totally disabled, with a $50,000 enhanced version for qualifying disabled veterans.

Why did the Morgan County Auditor change a property's value?

Value changes come from a short list of causes, per the Auditor's FAQ:

  • A full reappraisal, which Ohio law requires of every parcel once every six years.
  • A countywide update in the third year of that cycle, based on market trends.
  • New construction, as shown by local permits.
  • Corrections to square footage, bedroom or bathroom counts.
  • A Board of Revision decision, or damage to or destruction of the property.

The Board of Revision has three members: the Auditor, the Treasurer and the president of the county commissioners, or their designees. It adjusts values, not tax dollars. Ohio law generally allows one filing in a three-year period, and withdrawing a complaint still counts as that filing. Corporations should have an attorney file for them.

What does Morgan County look like on paper?

Morgan County was formed December 29, 1817, from parts of Guernsey, Muskingum and Washington counties and organized in 1819, per Wikipedia. It covers 422 square miles, and McConnelsville, Chesterhill, Malta and Stockport are its villages. The county is the third-least populous in Ohio, with 13,802 people in 2020. Neighbors are Muskingum, Noble, Washington, Athens and Perry counties.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts reports a 2025 estimate of 13,626 residents, down 1.3% from the 2020 base, and 7,437 housing units. Nearly four homes in five (78.9%) are owner-occupied, and the survey's median home value is $150,900, and median household income is $59,351. Mean travel time to work is 37.5 minutes, the longest among the three counties in that table, and 2025 saw only 23 building permits. With about 33 people per square mile, the Engineer's survey and split steps are worth planning for if you are selling part of a larger tract.

More questions about Morgan County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Where is the Morgan County Recorder located?

It is in the Riecker Building, 155 East Main Street, Room 160, McConnelsville, OH 43756. The phone is 740-962-4051.

Who do I see first when I sell land in Morgan County?

Start with the County Engineer at 740-962-3171, then the Auditor, then the Recorder. The Auditor's staff will deliver your documents to the other offices in order.

What is the conveyance fee in Morgan County?

The Auditor prints $3.00 per $1,000 of sale price, plus a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee and a $100.00 split fee for every split. Payment is by cash or a check to the Morgan County Auditor.

Is a gift of a house taxable in Morgan County?

It can be. Only the relationships listed on the DTE 100EX exemption form qualify as exempt, so read each choice on that form or ask the Auditor at 740-962-4475.

How much will Morgan County charge to record my deed?

Call the Recorder at 740-962-4051 and ask for the current sheet. The state schedule behind it is $34 for two pages, $8 for each more, and a county may add up to $5 per instrument for preservation.

Which office in Morrow County puts a deed on record?

Morrow County deeds and mortgages are recorded at the county recorder's office inside the courthouse at 48 E. High St., Mt. Gilead, OH 43338. The recorder's page lists 419-947-3060 and a weekday counter open from 8 until 4.

Mount Gilead holds the courthouse and is the biggest village in the county, so most sellers who live in Cardington, Marengo, Edison or the townships make the same trip. Anyone who prefers not to drive can file through an electronic recording company instead (see below).

What kinds of documents does the Morrow County recorder accept?

The office's documents-filed list is broad. For a home sale or an inherited house, these are the entries you are most likely to need:

  • Deeds, including warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgages, along with releases, assignments, assumptions and subordinations.
  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.
  • Trusts, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Liens of several kinds, such as mechanic's liens, notices of commencement and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominium filings, annexations and zoning resolutions also appear on the list, which tells you the same office holds the map side of the county's land records.

Can a Morrow County deed be filed electronically?

Yes. The recorder's page says e-recording has been open for every document type since September 8, 2025, and it names four vendors to call for help: CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm. Title companies and closing attorneys usually already hold an account with one of them, so a seller rarely needs to sign up personally.

Record searching moved to a different system in the same period. The records search page sends visitors to RecordHub, where you must create a login before you can look anything up. The county says the account costs nothing and that the login requirement was added to protect the records from cyberattacks.

What happens at the auditor's office before the recorder sees the deed?

Under section 319.20, the county auditor moves the parcel into the new owner's name and endorses the deed. Before that, the incoming owner or an agent for that owner files a statement of value as described in section 319.202, electronically or in three paper copies.

The statement carries two questions that matter to a Morrow seller. Has the property received a tax reduction for owner-occupied homes? And was the land ever enrolled in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program? If the answer to the second is yes, the statement must note that the land can face a recoupment charge when it stops qualifying.

The Morrow County Auditor's own conveyance fee page prints $4.00 per thousand for both real estate and manufactured homes. The grantor pays it, together with the 50 cent transfer fee that section 319.54(G)(2) sets for each parcel entered.

What does Ohio charge to record a document?

The recorder has no room to set its own prices for the basic filing. Section 317.32 prescribes a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee, and the office may tack on an optional preservation surcharge capped at five dollars, which the county keeps for general use. Payment is due when the paper is handed in, though electronic filers may settle afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method.

Recording charges printed in Ohio Revised Code 317.32
ItemBase feeHousing trust fund fee
First two pages of an instrument$17$17
Each added page (legal-size sheet or fraction, caption page included)$4$4
Certified copy, per page$1$1
Recorder's seal on a certification50 cents50 cents
Marginal reference, each$2$2

A long deed with several exhibits therefore costs more than a two-page one. Ask the title agent for a page count before closing so the check is the right size.

Which Morrow County transfers owe no conveyance fee?

The state statute names many transfers that skip the auditor's fee. The ones that come up most often in family and estate sales are these:

  • A deed that only corrects or confirms one already recorded.
  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or from a mother or father to a son or daughter.
  • A transfer among the heirs or devisees of one decedent where no money changes hands.
  • A deed into a trust whose maker kept an unlimited power to revoke it, and the deed back out.
  • Any transfer with no money or other valuable consideration that is not a gift.
  • A transfer made only to secure or release a debt.

When an exemption applies, the filing states the reason for it. Anyone unsure whether a family deed qualifies should phone the auditor before the paperwork goes to the recorder.

Who has to sign a Morrow County deed, and how is it witnessed?

Ohio's section 5301.01 requires the grantor to sign the deed and to acknowledge the signature before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. In practice most sellers use a notary at the title company or a bank.

If a mortgage is being paid off from the sale, the lender's release has its own clock. Under section 5301.36, the mortgagee must record the release within ninety days of satisfaction. Check the recorder's index a few weeks after closing to confirm it appears.

How can a Morrow County owner watch for fraudulent filings?

The recorder's office offers a free fraud alert service called Property Check. A subscriber is told when a document is filed against a named property, which helps catch a forged deed or a bogus lien early. It suits anyone whose house sits empty or came through an estate, since nobody is opening the mail there.

Alerts do not replace a periodic look at the record. A quick RecordHub search under your own name every so often costs only the time it takes to log in.

How does the Morrow County housing stock look on paper?

Morrow County sits in central Ohio across roughly 406 square miles and was organized in 1848 from parts of four neighboring counties. It borders Crawford, Richland, Knox, Delaware and Marion counties and belongs to the Columbus metro area. The villages are Cardington, Chesterville, Edison, Fulton, Marengo, Mount Gilead and Sparta, and a slice of the city of Galion reaches in from the north. Ohio's center of population fell near Marengo in 2010, and the Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course draws visitors near Steam Corners.

The Census QuickFacts page for Morrow County reports a 2025 estimate of 36,305 residents living among 14,981 housing units. Owners occupy 81.2 percent of homes, with a $222,300 median value reported for the five survey years ending 2024, and workers average a 32.8 minute trip to their jobs. The county is mostly owner-held, and a long commute suggests many residents work in other counties.

What should be in the packet before a Morrow County closing?

A clean filing starts with a deed that names the grantor exactly as the prior recorded deed does. The auditor's transfer step uses a reference to the earlier recorded instrument, so a mismatch in spelling or a missing prior-deed citation can hold things up. Bring the full legal description, the grantee's mailing address and the signed statement of value.

Also confirm whether the parcel was ever in the farm-use program. The Morrow County Auditor's page says an application for that program carries a one-time $25 fee, has a filing cutoff on the first Monday of March, and that land removed from the program owes a recoupment charge equal to the savings of three years. A seller who sold off a few acres of a farm should ask the auditor how a split affects that charge.

Finally, ask the closing agent who will hand in the paperwork and by which route. A paper deed goes through the courthouse offices in a set order, while an e-recorded deed goes through the vendor's system. Knowing the route tells you when to expect the recorded copy.

More questions about Morrow County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Which number reaches the Morrow County recorder?

Dial 419-947-3060. The counter is inside the courthouse at 48 E. High St. in Mt. Gilead, and its posted weekday hours end at four in the afternoon.

Does Morrow County accept deeds filed online?

Yes, through electronic recording vendors. The recorder's page names CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm and says e-recording has covered all documents since September 8, 2025.

What is the Morrow County conveyance fee?

The county auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand. The grantor pays it at the auditor's office, along with a 50 cent per parcel transfer fee set by state law.

Do I need an account to search Morrow County land records online?

Yes. The records search now runs through RecordHub, and the county asks users to create a free login. The county explains that the step protects the records from cyberattacks.

Is a deed between family members free of the conveyance fee?

Some are. State law exempts gifts between spouses and between a parent and child, and transfers among heirs of one decedent for no money. The filing must state the exemption, so check with the auditor first.

Muskingum County by the numbers

Where is the Muskingum County Recorder's Office?

The Muskingum County Recorder works from 401 Main Street, Zanesville, OH 43701, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 2333, Zanesville, OH 43702. The county recorder page gives (740) 455-7107 and a weekday window from half past eight until half past four, closed on legal holidays.

The same page says the office's holdings reach back to 1803, the year before the county itself was organized in 1804. Surveyors, genealogists, attorneys and title examiners all use them.

How far back do the online Muskingum County indexes go?

Not every record type was indexed from the same year, so a search that returns nothing may only mean you are looking before the index begins. The recorder's page prints a start year for each category, and a Historical Indexes tab covers earlier material.

Online index start years printed on the Muskingum County Recorder's page
Record typeIndex begins

For anything older than those years, use the Historical Indexes tab, and look at the training sheet in the office's Forms section for instructions.

What documents does the Muskingum County Recorder file?

The documents-filed list on the recorder's page covers almost everything tied to land. The entries a seller or heir meets most often are below.

  • Warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgages and every companion paper: releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and waivers of priority.
  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.
  • Trusts, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Mechanic's liens, notices of commencement and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominiums, street name changes, zoning resolutions and name changes sit on the same list.

What does the county do before a Muskingum County deed reaches the recorder?

The auditor's transfer page lays out the path. A document can be handed in at the counter, mailed, or sent through eRecording software. If the legal description uses metes and bounds, or covers something other than a full lot in a subdivision, it first goes to the County Engineer's Office on the third floor of the courthouse for approval. After that it goes to the Auditor's Office for the transfer, and only then to the recorder.

A full subdivision lot can skip the engineer and go straight to the auditor. The auditor's FAQ adds that every deed and related document must be notarized by a notary registered with the Ohio Secretary of State.

What are the Muskingum County conveyance and transfer fees?

The Muskingum County Auditor prints a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel. State law sets a floor and a ceiling for this charge. Section 319.54(G)(3) requires $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater, and section 322.02 lets commissioners add an optional tax of up to thirty cents per hundred.

The grantor, meaning the seller, pays these amounts to the auditor when the deed is delivered, according to section 319.202. The statement of value that goes with the deed is where the seller reports any owner-occupancy tax reduction or agricultural valuation tied to the parcel.

What does Ohio charge the recorder to record a deed?

The recorder's basic filing charge comes from section 317.32: a base fee of $17 for the first two pages and a housing trust fund fee of the same amount, followed by $4 plus $4 for each page after that. A document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars may be added.

Certified copies run $1 plus $1 a page, and a seal on a certification adds 50 cents plus 50 cents. The statute allows e-filers to pay after presentation by electronic funds transfer or a comparable method. The recorder can tell you which surcharge figure Muskingum County applies, so ask before you write the check.

Which transfers in Muskingum County are exempt from the conveyance fee?

Section 319.54(G)(3) excludes a long list. Sellers and heirs usually care about the following ones.

  • Gifts between spouses or between a parent and child.
  • Deeds that confirm or correct an earlier recorded deed.
  • Transfers by court order that are not the result of a sale ordered by the court.
  • Moves among heirs of the same decedent when nothing is paid.
  • Transfers into and out of a revocable trust.
  • Interests valued at $100 or less.

The statement of value must state the reason for any exemption claimed.

How can a Muskingum County owner guard against a forged deed?

Two free alert tools exist. The recorder offers Property Check, a fraud alert system that warns you about filings made on your behalf. The auditor's FAQ explains that you can also call (740) 455-7109, option 1, to have your phone number attached to your parcels so you hear when one appears on a deed to be transferred.

Anyone who suspects the ownership record has been changed should phone the auditor at that same number. The auditor says it will investigate the property record and coordinate with the proper authorities if needed.

What is the county around Zanesville like for a home seller?

Muskingum County is in east-central Ohio and is nearly split in two by the Muskingum River. Zanesville is the county seat and largest city. At 673 square miles it ranks fourth in Ohio by land area, and its 2020 population was 86,410. Neighbors include Coshocton, Guernsey, Noble, Morgan, Perry and Licking counties. Higher education is local: Muskingum University, Zane State College and an Ohio University branch campus in Zanesville.

On the Census QuickFacts table, Muskingum County lists 38,597 housing units for 2025 and a 68.2 percent owner-occupied rate. The median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $182,200, and median household income is $60,780. About one occupied home in three is rented, so many sellers here are landlords with tenants in place.

What happens to a Muskingum County deed after it is recorded?

Once the recorder indexes the deed, it appears in the online records, which the office says are refreshed each weekday. Documents are posted to the website within a reasonable time after filing, so a deed recorded this morning may not show up in a search until later in the week.

Two follow-up steps are worth doing. First, look up the parcel in the auditor's property search to confirm that the owner name and tax mailing address changed. The treasurer's FAQ says a billing address change needs a written, signed form, so a buyer who wants bills at a new address should send one. Second, when a mortgage was paid off at closing, search the mortgage index for the lender's release, since the lender has ninety days to record it under section 5301.36.

The recorder's page also carries a fair housing notice. Any deed provision that restricts the sale, rental or use of a dwelling because of race or color is invalid under federal law and cannot be enforced, which matters when you read very old deeds from the county's long record.

More questions about Muskingum County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What are the Muskingum County Recorder's hours?

Weekdays from half past eight to half past four, except legal holidays. The phone line is (740) 455-7107.

Where do I send a deed in Muskingum County?

Bring or mail it to the Auditor's Office first for the transfer, then it goes to the recorder at 401 Main Street, Zanesville. Metes and bounds descriptions need County Engineer approval before the auditor accepts them.

What is the conveyance fee in Muskingum County?

The auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus $0.50 per parcel. The seller pays it at the auditor's office.

Can I search Muskingum County deeds online?

Yes, but the deed index starts in 1977. Older records are in the Historical Indexes tab on the recorder's site, which has its own training sheet.

Does the county offer a fraud alert for my property?

Yes. The recorder runs a free service called Property Check, and the auditor will add your phone number to your parcels if you call (740) 455-7109 and choose option 1.

Who handles real estate records in Paulding County?

Paulding County's recorder files and preserves the land documents for the county, such as deeds, mortgages and easements. Its desk is inside the courthouse at 115 N. Williams Street, Paulding, the village that also serves as county seat.

On the recorder's website the records search stays available all day and night, and the office says it is free of direct charges. Drafting is outside its job: if a deed still has to be written, ask the attorney or title agent on your sale.

The county is lightly settled. Census estimates for July 2025 show 18,727 people on roughly 416 square miles of land, about 45 per square mile.

How does a deed get recorded in Paulding County?

Usually the closing agent takes care of it, and the seller never touches the deed again. Anyone doing it personally has two stops: the auditor transfers the parcel on the tax list, and then the recorder files the instrument.

Three electronic recording vendors are listed on the recorder's site: CSC, ePN and Simplifile. The listing states that eRecording submissions are taken on weekdays between 8:00 am and 3:00 pm.

Look over the deed before anyone signs it:

  • The signature has to be acknowledged before an officer named in Revised Code 5301.01, and that officer certifies the acknowledgment.
  • It should name the new owner's mailing address for tax bills and cite the prior recorded instrument, both of which the auditor uses under section 319.20.
  • Its layout should follow the state's margin and type rules, or a surcharge is added.

What does the Paulding County recorder charge?

Ohio's recorder association lists the statewide base as $34.00 for a deed or mortgage's opening two pages, then $8.00 for every page following. On top of that, a county can tack on a preservation surcharge as high as $5.00 per document, and counties choose their own amount. Phone the recorder for the exact total before writing the check.

Typical Ohio recording charges (Ohio Recorders Association fee page; Revised Code 317.32)
ChargeAmount

The extra $20 reaches documents prepared after June 30, 2009 that miss the standards. Those call for type of at least 10 points, black or blue ink only, a 3 inch blank band at the top of the first page, and 1 inch margins at the sides and bottom.

What should a Paulding County seller review before signing?

A few minutes of review can head off a rejected filing.

  • Match the seller's name to the way it appears on the last recorded deed. If it differs, explain the difference in the deed or an affidavit.
  • Collect the lender's payoff letter. A recorded release normally follows the payoff.
  • Have the buyer's complete tax mailing address in hand for the auditor's tax list.
  • When only a piece of a tract is being sold, ask the auditor and engineer whether the new description needs sign-off, since each Ohio county adopts its own conveyance standards.
  • Prepare a check for the precise conveyance fee. Paulding's auditor warns that any other amount stalls the transfer.

Closing attorneys and title agents normally cover all of these. Even in a fast cash sale the same items apply, so settle them well ahead of closing day.

What fees does the Paulding County auditor collect on a sale?

Before the deed reaches the recorder, the auditor takes two charges. The auditor's website lists the conveyance fee at $4.00 per thousand of the purchase price and a transfer fee of $.50 per parcel.

The auditor also cautions that a check has to equal the conveyance fee exactly, or the conveyance is held up. A conveyance calculator sits under the Tools menu on that site, so run your own price through it.

Section 319.202(D) puts the cost on the seller. The standard sale goes with form DTE 100, and anyone claiming an exemption uses DTE 100 (EX). Ask the auditor about extra steps when the sale includes mineral rights or a manufactured home.

What do Census figures say about Paulding County housing?

Paulding County leans heavily toward homeownership. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates give these numbers for the county.

  • Share of homes lived in by their owners: 80.1%.
  • Typical value of an owner's home: $140,800.
  • Typical gross rent: $812 monthly.
  • Households: 7,624, at 2.45 people each.
  • Housing units counted on July 1, 2025: 8,597.
  • Permits for new buildings in 2025: 28.

Twenty-eight permits across eleven villages and the farm townships is a small count, and the Census reports 90.6% of residents living at the same address a year earlier.

How big is the Paulding County economy?

Employers numbered 309 in 2023 and together had 4,033 jobs, 2.6% fewer than in 2022. About 62.6% of residents 16 and older are in the labor force, and a trip to work averages 24.0 minutes.

Business receipts in 2022 were roughly $56.0 million in transportation and warehousing, $50.4 million in health care and social assistance, and $137.3 million in retail. Household income in 2020 to 2024 had a midpoint of $67,731, and 10.4% of people live below the poverty line.

A home value of $140,800 sits well under Perry County's $191,100 and Pickaway County's $256,800 in the same Census table.

Which communities make up Paulding County?

Eleven villages dot the county: Antwerp, Broughton, Cecil, Grover Hill, Haviland, Latty, Melrose, Oakwood, Paulding, Payne and Scott. Students attend Antwerp Local, Paulding Exempted Village or Wayne Trace Local schools, and Vantage Career Center draws from the area.

Wikipedia calls the terrain extremely flat: the whole county sits in the former Great Black Swamp, and section roads run at one-mile spacing. U.S. Routes 127, 24 and 30 cross it, along with the Auglaize and Maumee rivers.

If a farm parcel is divided, the auditor will not transfer the new piece until its description has been reviewed. Check first with the auditor and the county engineer.

How can you look up a deed or mortgage release in Paulding County?

Start with the records search on the recorder's website, which connects to an Ava portal. That site also offers a property fraud alert and a notary fraud alert sign-up that send a notice when a document goes on record under a name you register.

A repaid mortgage appears as a recorded release. If you cannot recall whether a past loan was released, check before you list, because an open mortgage in the records turns up at closing.

Title companies and investors order the search regardless, so having the old deed and any release at hand saves time.

Heirs sometimes find a recorded document they do not recognize, such as an old easement or a lease. Copy its volume and page or instrument number from the search results so the title agent can read the whole instrument, then ask the recorder's office if the index entry is unclear.

More questions about Paulding County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Where does Paulding County file its land records?

At the recorder's office inside the courthouse at 115 N. Williams Street, Paulding, Ohio. The recorder's website also hosts the records search.

The auditor's site gives it as $4.00 per thousand of the purchase price, with a $.50 transfer fee for each parcel. The calculator on the auditor's site does the math for your price.

Will the recorder draft my deed?

No, the recorder only records. An attorney or title company has to prepare the document.

Why was I charged an extra $20 on a deed?

Revised Code 317.114 sets that non-standard document charge for papers that break the margin, ink or type size rules. Check the layout against the standards before you sign.

Where do you find the Perry County recorder?

Look for the recorder at 212 S. Main Street, New Lexington, where the doors are open weekdays from 8:00 am to 4:00 pm and the number is (740) 342-2494. The Perry County Auditor shares that address and those hours.

The county's page frames the office as the place that keeps land records in an organized, accessible form: who owns what, how title moved, and which mortgages exist. Staff will not run a title search for you or advise you on legal questions. They will let you sit down and search the public records yourself.

Payment is by cash or check. Cards are not taken, so settle that before you send paperwork.

The recorder's fax line is (740) 342-5539, and the auditor can be reached at (740) 342-2074. If you are sorting out several documents for one sale, calling both offices on the same day saves a second trip.

What are the Perry County recording charges?

The recorder's FAQ spells out the price: $34.00 buys the first two pages and each page beyond costs $8.00. If the document ignores the margin rules, $20.00 is added, and a document that needs a cross-reference picks up $4.00.

State law in Revised Code 317.32 allows counties to add a preservation surcharge up to $5. The Perry page lists none, so ask the office whether one applies to your filing.

What does the Perry County auditor collect on a sale?

Ahead of recording, the auditor moves the parcel into the buyer's name on the tax list. The buyer or the buyer's representative files a statement of value, and the seller owes the conveyance fee.

Statute 319.54(G)(3) sets the state portion at one dollar, or ten cents per hundred dollars of value (rounded up for any fraction), whichever is greater. Section 322.02 lets a county commissioners' board levy a transfer tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars on top, so what you owe at the table depends on Perry County's own resolutions.

The auditor's site hosts a Conveyance Fee Calculator that builds in the per-parcel transfer fee: key in the number of parcels and the price. State conveyance forms sit on the Forms page of the same site.

How can you search Perry County land records?

An online index named Adaptable Visual Access returns the volume and page for each recorded item. Images of the documents are not posted there, so call or write to the office to order a copy and learn the fee and payment options.

The office also sets owners up with a free fraud alert through its software vendor. A subscriber is told within 24 business hours when anything is recorded under their name. Because the office has to record any paper that meets the filing rules, the alert warns you but cannot block a filing.

Veterans can have a DD214 recorded by bringing the original or a certified copy and photo ID, and the office hands out veteran ID cards too.

What else does the Perry County recorder file?

Revised Code 317.08 sends a long list of instruments into the official records. The following matter most to someone selling a house:

  • Mortgages and their modifications.
  • Land installment contracts that run beyond a year, plus leases.
  • Powers of attorney, used when an agent signs for the seller.
  • Mechanic's liens, federal tax liens and similar recorded claims.
  • Purchase options, accepted only when they give an expiration day and year.

Paper goes on record in the sequence it arrives. An owner's transfer on death affidavit is filed like a deed, at the deed price, and counts only if recorded before death.

What should a Perry County seller fix before recording?

Most trouble traces to small slips. Run through this list before signing:

  • An officer listed in section 5301.01, such as a notary, witnesses your signature and certifies the acknowledgment.
  • The new owner's mailing address and a cite to the preceding recorded deed appear on the face of the deed, as section 319.20 expects.
  • Margins follow the layout rules, which avoids the $20.00 add-on.
  • You hold the lender's payoff figure. Once paid, the lender sends a release for recording, and the recorder can hand you a copy.
  • You can pay by check or cash.

When a spouse has died and a name has to come off the deed, remember the recorder records but does not draft. An attorney writes the instrument.

How does Perry County housing look in the Census data?

An estimated 35,918 people lived in Perry County in July 2025, 1.4% above the April 2020 estimates base, on about 408 square miles of land. The Census Bureau reports 15,173 housing units and 13,452 households.

  • Homes occupied by owners: 76.4%.
  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $191,100.
  • Gross rent at the midpoint: $777 monthly.
  • Average trip to work: 33.2 minutes.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 39.
  • Residents below the poverty line: 13.7%.

That 33.2 minute average is the longest of the three counties in the Census table, and Wikipedia lists Perry County in the Columbus metropolitan area.

On the income side, the same table shows household income at the midpoint of $67,460 and per capita income of $32,288 for 2020 to 2024. Employers numbered 455 in 2023, and employment of 4,478 grew 5.0% over 2022. Retail sales in 2022 came to $6,963 per resident, and 16.2% of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

How does the Perry County auditor value property?

According to the auditor, Ohio demands a full reappraisal of the county every six years, with a state percentage adjustment in the third year of each cycle. Roughly 31,000 parcels were on the books for 2024, sorted into residential, agricultural, commercial and industrial classes.

The auditor's home page also reports that House Bill 479 gives a one-time fixed reduction to current Standard and Enhanced Homestead Exemption recipients, for tax year 2026 or tax year 2027 on manufactured and mobile homes. If you are selling in the middle of a tax year, ask how that reduction carries over.

When storm or flood damage lowers what a house is worth, phone the auditor at (740) 342-2074 and ask how a damaged-property adjustment works.

What communities are in Perry County?

The state formed Perry County on March 1, 1818 out of parts of Fairfield, Washington and Muskingum counties. New Lexington serves as county seat and is the largest city. Villages include Corning, Crooksville, Glenford, Hemlock, Junction City, New Straitsville, Rendville, Roseville (partly here), Shawnee, Somerset and Thornville.

A section of Wayne National Forest falls within the county. Licking, Muskingum, Morgan, Athens, Hocking and Fairfield counties ring it.

More questions about Perry County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Are credit cards accepted at the Perry County recorder?

No. The office takes cash and checks only, according to its own page.

Are Perry County deeds viewable online?

Only the index is online, giving volume and page numbers. The document images are not posted, so contact the recorder to order a copy.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Perry County?

The recorder quotes $34.00 for the first two pages plus $8.00 for each added page. Documents with bad margins pick up $20.00, and ones needing a reference pick up $4.00.

Where is the Perry County conveyance fee figured out?

On the Conveyance Fee Calculator at the auditor's website, which folds in the parcel transfer fee. The auditor's office at 212 S. Main Street can confirm the result.

Will the recorder confirm that my title is free of liens?

No. Staff do not search titles or give legal advice. Search the public records in person, or hire an attorney or title company.

A deed that needs those stamps must be carried in, and so must a transfer on death designation.

E-recording has been offered since 2017 through a third-party vendor chosen by the submitter. Files can be sent any day, and staff process them from 8:00 a.m. to 3:45 p.m. on business days. Documents with a new survey or new legal description cannot be e-recorded and must be walked through in person.

  • Bring or mail the original with a self-addressed, stamped envelope.
  • Pay by cash, check, or card, and expect a card charge of $1.00 or 3%, whichever is greater.
  • If a deed was signed electronically and printed, a separate authenticator certificate must be attached.

What are the recording and copy fees in Pickaway County?

The base price follows the state schedule in Revised Code 317.32: $34 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that, split between a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. Pickaway County adds the optional preservation surcharge. The recorder's page says that from January 1, 2025, basic recording fees include a $5.00 per document surcharge, which goes into the county general fund for preservation and digitization of records.

Pickaway County Recorder charges as posted on its recording, FAQ and records pages
ItemAmount
Basic recording, first two pages$34 under state law
Each added page$8 under state law
Per document surcharge since January 1, 2025$5.00
Copy of a record at the counter or by request$2.00 a page
Printing images downloaded from the recorder's websiteNo charge
Card payment$1.00 or 3%, whichever is greater

What does the Pickaway County auditor require before a deed is transferred?

The auditor's site states the conveyance fee as $3.00 per thousand, for real estate and manufactured homes. Under state law the seller pays it, and the auditor will not transfer an instrument without a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX form.

The county's Transfer and Conveyance Standards, adopted by the auditor and engineer under section 319.203, add more requirements:

  • The deed carries the original signature of the grantor and cannot be a fax or a copy.
  • It shows the auditor's parcel number, the site address, the prior deed reference and the grantee's tax mailing address.
  • A grantor who is not the prior grantee needs an explanation in the deed or an affidavit.
  • A new legal description needs the Engineer's Tax Map Department to stamp it "Mathematically Approved" first.
  • A split leaving a parcel of 20 acres or less needs planning commission approval.
  • A trust conveying property files an affidavit under section 5302.171 before or with the deed.

How do you search Pickaway County records online?

The recorder uses a site called CountyFusion. Indexes run from 1/1/1990 to the present by name, historical indexes cover 1810 to 1990, and most images go back to 1980. Official Records began on April 16, 1996, and earlier records sit in separate books for deeds, mortgages, leases and other types.

You need a name to search. If you only have an address, look up the owner on the auditor's website first. Images found online can be downloaded and printed for free, while older documents can be ordered by volume and page for $2.00 a page.

The office also offers a free alert, called FRAUDSLEUTH, that warns you when a document is recorded under names you enter. A sheriff's sale list is on the sheriff's website instead of the recorder's.

Does a paid-off mortgage show up at the Pickaway County recorder?

Yes, as a recorded release. The recorder explains that the lender sends a Release of Mortgage, which is linked to the original mortgage in the records, and you can get a copy free on the recording site or from the office.

Unlike a car title, the deed is not held by the bank or by the recorder while you owe on the loan. You should have received the original after closing, and the office can copy a recorded deed if yours is lost.

To change the tax mailing address, call the Pickaway County Treasurer at (740) 474-2370. Changing the name on a deed requires a new deed prepared by an attorney.

What do Census numbers show for Pickaway County?

Pickaway County has the most residents and the highest home values of the three counties in the Census comparison used for this set of pages. The 2025 population estimate is 62,978, up 7.6% from the April 2020 estimates base, with 23,832 housing units.

  • Owner-occupied rate: 74.0%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $256,800.
  • Median gross rent: $1,020.
  • Median household income: $74,040.
  • Building permits in 2025: 406.
  • Employer establishments in 2023: 856, with employment up 23.0% from 2022.

Compare the 406 permits with 28 in Paulding County and 39 in Perry County. Pickaway is where new construction is happening, and the county sits in the Columbus metropolitan area.

What is the Pickaway County landscape like for a house seller?

The county seat and only city is Circleville. Villages include Ashville, Commercial Point, Darbyville, Lockbourne, Harrisburg, New Holland, South Bloomfield, Tarlton and Williamsport. The Scioto River runs south through the middle of the county, Big Darby Creek drains the upper west side, and about 87% of the land is used for agriculture, according to Wikipedia.

Many sales here involve acreage, so the land-split and survey rules matter. The recorder's FAQ points to the Engineer's mapping department or GIS for property maps that are not in a recorded subdivision.

One note on the recorder's page: it carried an alert about a one-time cancellation window for Homeowner Benefit Agreements with MV Realty of Ohio that ended on April 29, 2026. If you ever signed such an agreement, ask the recorder what is recorded against your parcel before you list.

More questions about Pickaway County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What time must I bring a document to the Pickaway County recorder?

Before 3:30 p.m. if you want it recorded that day. Documents brought in later are reviewed but not processed until the first thing the next business day.

Can a transfer on death designation be mailed to the Pickaway County recorder?

No. The recorder's page says documents that need the Engineer Map Department and Auditor stamps cannot be mailed, and it names transfer on death designations in that group.

How much is the conveyance fee in Pickaway County?

The county auditor states it as $3.00 per thousand, for both real estate and manufactured homes.

How do I get a copy of my recorded deed?

Download it free from the recorder's online site if it was recorded since the digital image coverage began, or request a copy by phone, email, mail or in person at $2.00 a page.

Does the recorder search my title for liens?

No. The office will show you how to search its records, but it cannot tell you whether title is clear. Consider a title examiner or title company for a full exam.

How do I reach the Portage County recorder in Ravenna?

The Portage County Recorder's office page prints a main line of (330) 297-3553, a fax at (330) 297-7349, and the same number for copy requests. Copy requests can also go by email to PCREC.COPIES@PORTAGECO.COM. Call before you drive a deed over to confirm counter hours.

Ravenna is the county seat, and the auditor's forms use 449 South Meridian Street as the county's address for property work. Hand-carried or mailed, a deed goes to the auditor on that street first, because the transfer there comes before recording.

Researchers should know that staff do not run the search for you. They will point you to the indexes and help you read them, and the page invites anyone studying title or family history to use the office.

What does the Portage County recorder keep on file?

The recorder's description of the office describes a permanent record of every paper that moves or burdens land here. Each filing gets a time stamp and a document number, then goes to microfilm and image storage and into the computer index.

  • Deeds, mortgages and easements.
  • Land titles and rights-of-way.
  • Federal tax liens and unemployment liens.
  • Uniform Commercial Code filings.
  • Leases of several kinds, along with veteran discharges and records of veteran burials.

Fees collected here are split between the county general fund and the state housing trust fund. The office also reminds commissioners and township trustees each year to file zoning resolutions and maps. What a seller cares about is that mortgage and lien releases appear in these same indexes, where the buyer's title examiner will look.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Portage County?

The county's fee page defers to the state schedule and gives one warning. A paper that breaks the state marginal rule picks up an added $20.00. The dollar figures below come from the statute, R.C. 317.32.

  • Pages one and two together: $34, split evenly between base and trust fund shares.
  • Every page after that: $8, again split evenly.
  • A county-set preservation surcharge, capped at $5 and paid to the general fund.
  • Certified copies: $2 per page in total.
  • Each marginal reference in a separate instrument: $4 in total.

The surcharge can be anything up to the cap, so ask the recorder for the total on your exact document. The statute counts the caption page, and any fraction of a page counts as a page.

What does the auditor take before a Portage County deed reaches the recorder?

The auditor's side comes first. According to the auditor's transfer page, the real estate department transfers deeds and similar papers ahead of recording. Its stated conveyance charge is four dollars for each $1,000 of price, plus fifty cents for every parcel moved. The DTE 100 form, Conveyance of Real Property, travels with the deed.

Use the rate Portage County prints, not a figure quoted for another county. A county board may also adopt a transfer tax on grantors of no more than 30 cents on each $100 of value, collected by the auditor ahead of recording (R.C. 322.02). Ask the auditor whether Portage has adopted one.

The same auditor's pages also offer parcel ownership histories, valuations, sales information and tax data, which are worth printing before you meet a buyer.

Which Portage County offices does a seller contact?

Three desks handle most of a sale, and each prints something different for the public.

Portage County offices a home seller usually needs, with what each published
OfficeTask in a saleWhat it publishes

TreasurerBills and collects property taxTwo bills a year, about half in February and half in July

The treasurer's schedule matters because the deed does not settle unpaid tax. Get a payoff for the parcel from the treasurer, and have the title company say who bears the half now accruing.

Can I search Portage County land records myself?

Yes. The recorder's page links a "Find My Deed" search, and the county posts scanned lease books on its site, with books numbered 92 through 114 posted so far and more promised as scanning continues. The office warns that its indexes default to one page for some older volumes and pages, so documents shown as a single page may run longer. Call or email the office for correct page totals before you order copies.

Copies of all records are available on request. Bring a parcel number or the names on the deed, since staff will not search on your behalf. The auditor's property search gives the owner history and sales for a parcel, which narrows what to ask for.

The state's rule on documents also applies here: Ohio requires a conveyance to be prepared and signed under the Revised Code before it is accepted for record. The recorder's page says so in plain terms.

What should I have ready before I record in Portage County?

Bring a deed that was prepared and signed under the Ohio Revised Code, since the recorder's page says all documents to be recorded must be. Have the auditor's transfer done first, and keep the DTE 100 form with the paperwork.

  • The signed, acknowledged deed with the marginal rule observed.
  • Payment for the auditor's conveyance fee and the recorder's fees.
  • A parcel number, so staff and the online index can match the right record.

After acceptance the office stamps the time, numbers the document, films and scans it, and adds it to the index. After closing, request a copy of the recorded deed for your own file.

What else should a Portage County seller know about recording?

The county covers 504 square miles of Northeast Ohio and dates to an 1808 act of the General Assembly, per its about page. Wikipedia gives the 2020 population as 161,791 and puts rented homes at 31.1% of the occupied total.

  • Format the deed to Ohio's page and margin rules to avoid the $20 surcharge.
  • Record a mortgage satisfaction soon after payoff, so the buyer's title search is clean.
  • Visit the auditor for the transfer step before the recorder.

The recorder's office has also listed a Good Deeds Program, billed as a way to prepare now and avoid the probate court process later. Ask the office for current dates and locations if a family property may pass to heirs.

A house with liens, back taxes or a stalled estate can still be sold for cash, and the buyer's closing agent handles the filings.

More questions about Portage County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the Portage County recorder's phone number?

The main line is (330) 297-3553, and the fax is (330) 297-7349. Copy requests use the same phone number and also go by email to PCREC.COPIES@PORTAGECO.COM.

How much does the Portage County auditor charge to transfer a deed?

Four dollars per $1,000 of the price plus fifty cents a parcel, according to the auditor. The recorder's fee is separate, and the auditor's transfer happens first.

Is there an extra recording fee in Portage County?

Yes, in one case. A paper that breaks the state marginal rule picks up $20.00 on top of the usual charges, so check margins before you submit.

Can I look up a Portage County deed online?

Yes. The recorder's page links a Find My Deed search, and the auditor's real estate site shows ownership history and sales. The recorder warns that page counts on older volumes can be wrong, so confirm them by phone.

Does the recorder pay off my mortgage or my taxes?

No. The recorder files papers and nothing more. Payoffs run through your lender and the county treasurer, and a closing agent normally arranges both.

Preble County by the numbers

Where do I record a deed in Preble County, Ohio?

The Preble County Recorder sits on the second floor of the courthouse, 101 E. Main Street, Eaton, OH 45320, phone (937) 456-8173. The recorder's page lists weekday service until 4:30 in the afternoon, yet the courthouse front door is locked at 4:00, so get there early.

Eaton is the county seat. Wikipedia dates the county to February 15, 1808, carved from Butler and Montgomery Counties, and gives it 426 square miles and a 2020 population of 40,999. About three in four residents live in rural areas.

Wikipedia counts 16,412 households and 18,093 housing units in the county, 9.3% of them vacant, with 76.7% of occupied homes lived in by their owners. That ownership rate means most Preble County deeds pass between owner-occupants, so expect questions about the grantee's tax mailing address and marital status at the counter. Check with the office about holiday hours before you plan a trip around a closing date.

What does it cost to record a deed in Preble County?

The county's printed schedule is short. One flat price covers a deed, mortgage, affidavit, easement, land contract, lease, mechanic's lien, trust or power of attorney: $39.00 through page two, then $8.00 for every added page. A marginal notation is $4.00.

  • Certified copies are $2.00 per page, with $1.00 more for each seal.
  • A document that misses Ohio's standardization rules in R.C. 317.114 costs $20.00 more.
  • Court, tax authority, state and federal documents, plats and DD 214 discharges are exempt from that $20.00, as are papers signed before July 1, 2009.
  • Filing a military discharge, or getting a photocopy of one, is free.

The state fee statute, R.C. 317.32, makes up the two-page figure from two $17 shares plus an optional preservation charge of up to $5, which is how a county arrives at $39. Enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope if you want the recorded paper returned by mail.

How should a Preble County deed be formatted?

The county spells out its formatting rules, and following them avoids the surcharge. Use white paper, letter or legal size, with black or blue ink and type of 10 point or larger. Submit an original rather than a copy, and skip highlighting and white-out.

  • Keep three inches clear at the top of page one for the recorder, auditor and engineer stamps.
  • Keep an inch and a half clear at the top of later pages, and an inch at the sides and bottom.
  • Show who prepared the document, and type or print a name below any signature that is hard to read.
  • State the grantor's marital status, and give the grantee's tax mailing address.
  • Include a full legal description and prior recording information, approved by the engineer before recording.

The grantor signs and acknowledges the deed before a notary public. The conveyance document must also carry the stamps of the county engineer and county auditor showing the grantor complied with R.C. 319.202.

What does the Preble County auditor charge on a sale?

The recorder's page puts the auditor's conveyance fee at three dollars for each $1,000 of price, with a 50 cent transfer fee per parcel. The auditor's counter is on the second floor of the same courthouse, (937) 456-8148, and the deed is stamped there before it goes to the recorder.

A county commission may also adopt a transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100, which R.C. 322.02 assigns to the grantor and routes through the auditor. Before you total your net proceeds, ask whether Preble County has adopted one.

The county's Office of Land Use Management, at 937-456-8171 on the first floor, answers questions about property splits and building permits. A lot split matters if you are selling only part of a parcel, since the engineer must approve the legal description.

Which Preble County offices handle a home sale?

All three main offices share the courthouse, so a seller can finish most of the errands in one trip.

Preble County courthouse offices for a home sale, with phone numbers as printed on the county's own pages
OfficeUsed forPhone
RecorderRecording deeds, mortgages and releases(937) 456-8173
AuditorConveyance fee, transfer, valuation complaints(937) 456-8148
TreasurerPaying property tax(937) 456-8140

Per the county FAQ, tax payments are taken on the second floor at the treasurer's office. The sheriff's office handles sheriff's sales on Fridays at 9 a.m. in the first-floor lobby of the courthouse, which is where a foreclosure sale of a Preble County home would be held.

How do I search Preble County land records?

The recorder offers an online search index, a title fraud service and a fraud sleuth profile through its page. The county's note on its records says indexes available online start December 14, 1999, through a CountyFusion site, and the Ohio Recorders Association page for Preble County links to the same system. For older deeds, you need to visit the office or ask staff.

The same page describes the recorder's purpose as a complete, accurate and permanent record of documents that convey or burden land, used by attorneys, historians, genealogists and land title examiners. If you are tracing an old farm or a family transfer, ask for the volume and page once you find the entry in the index.

Owners who are worried about forged deeds can register for the free title fraud service the page links.

Can the Preble County Board of Revision change my value before I sell?

It can lower or raise a value, but only on a complaint filed inside the window. The auditor's Board of Revision page takes the DTE Form 1 in the first quarter after the tax year, with a cutoff of 4:30 in the afternoon on March 31 at the auditor's office. Mail counts if it is postmarked by that day.

Three people sit on the Board: the auditor, the treasurer and a commissioner or the commissioner's representative. The page cites R.C. 5715.13 through 5715.19 for its authority. Questions go to (937) 456-8197 or (937) 456-8131. A late or defective complaint may be dismissed without a hearing, so file early.

Where do other Preble County matters go besides the recorder?

A sale sometimes pulls in other offices, and the county's FAQ sorts out who handles what. Evictions and small claims are heard by the Eaton Municipal Court at 1199 Preble Drive, phone 937-456-4941. Probate Court, second floor, 937-456-8137, handles name changes and marriage licenses. The Clerk of Courts has the third floor, 937-456-8160.

Sheriff's sales run on Fridays beginning at 9 a.m. in the first-floor lobby, and the sheriff's office at 937-456-6262 has details. A seller facing one of those sales or a tenant dispute can still deal with the recorder and auditor in the usual order, but should line up the court side first.

More questions about Preble County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How much does the Preble County recorder charge for a deed?

$39.00 covers the first two pages and each added page is $8.00. A marginal notation is another $4.00, and a nonconforming paper adds $20.00.

What is the Preble County conveyance fee?

Three dollars per $1,000 of price plus fifty cents a parcel, as the recorder's page prints it, paid to the auditor ahead of recording.

What time does the Preble County recorder's office close?

Service runs to 4:30 on weekdays, but the courthouse front door locks at 4:00. Get there before 4:00, or call (937) 456-8173 if you are running late.

Can I get my DD 214 from the Preble County recorder?

Yes. Military discharge papers are kept at the recorder's office, and filing a discharge or getting a photocopy of it carries no fee.

When does the Preble County Board of Revision take complaints?

From January 1 to March 31 of the year after the tax year, with a cutoff of 4:30 in the afternoon on March 31 at the auditor's office. Mailed ones need a postmark by then.

Where is the Putnam County recorder in Ottawa?

Ottawa is the county seat. Wikipedia notes an 1820 creation date, an 1834 organization date, and a name honoring Israel Putnam. The Blanchard River, an early travel route for settlers, crosses the county.

In what sequence does a Putnam County deed get recorded?

Three stops come before the recorder sees a deed, and the county auditor's page spells them out. The order matters, because an unstamped deed is turned away.

  1. Take the legal description to the Tax Map Office, which sits in the engineer's office and answers at 419-523-6931. All legal descriptions must be pre-approved, and the document must meet the county's conveyance standards.
  2. Once the tax map staff sign the document, bring it to the auditor, who transfers it and collects the conveyance fee.
  3. Record the transferred deed with the recorder, who follows the standards and fees on its own site.

The auditor is at 245 East Main Street in Ottawa, 419-523-6686, on a weekday 8:30 to 4:30 schedule. Under Tools on its site sits a calculator that prices the transfer before you go.

What does the Putnam County auditor charge to transfer a deed?

On its transfers page the auditor lists four dollars for each thousand of price, with the price rounded up to the next hundred, and fifty cents a parcel in transfer fee. The conveyance is not processed unless the check matches the conveyance fee to the penny.

Form DTE 100 accompanies a normal sale, and DTE 100 (EX) is the version for deeds that claim an exemption. The county's forms page carries both, so you can fill them in ahead of the visit.

A separate county transfer tax is possible under R.C. 322.02, capped at 30 cents on each $100 and owed by the grantor. Whether Putnam has one in force is a question for the auditor; the calculator gives the quickest total.

How much does recording cost in Putnam County?

The recorder's FAQ points to a fee page and says the office charges a $4.00 fee for each marginal notation. The base amounts come from the statute, R.C. 317.32.

  • Pages one and two: $34 together, half base fee and half housing trust fund.
  • Later pages: $8 each, split the same way.
  • A preservation surcharge, capped at $5 an instrument, goes to the county's general fund.
  • A certified copy costs $2 a page in total.

A document that fails the county's standards costs $20 more. Those rules, under R.C. 317.114, call for 10-point type or larger, dark blue or black ink, no highlighter, and letter or legal paper. Page one needs three inches clear at the top, later pages an inch and a half, and the sides and bottom an inch. Exempt are court papers, plats, DD 214 discharges, state and federal documents, and anything signed before July 1, 2009.

Which Putnam County offices matter in a home sale?

The table sets out what each office prints for the public, drawn from the county's own sites.

Putnam County offices a seller visits, with figures as published on the recorder and auditor sites

The auditor's home page also posts a delinquent real estate list and counts 29,689 parcels as of 2023. Sellers with a house that may have fallen behind should check that list.

How can I record a Putnam County deed electronically or by mail?

The recorder's e-recording page says the service now covers deeds and other transfer documents, and names three approved vendors: Simplifile at 1.800.460.5657, CSC at 1.866.652.0111 and Erecording Partners at 1.888.325.3365. You work through one of them rather than the county directly.

The FAQ describes how fast things move. Documents recorded at the counter go back immediately, documents e-recorded are returned immediately, and documents delivered by mail are sent out the next business day. The office also requires a full legal description, including on releases and assignments, and maintains tract indexing by geography.

Paying at the counter is simple: the FAQ says checks are made payable to the Putnam County Recorder. The same page says releases and assignments need a full legal description too, so a mortgage satisfaction needs more than a parcel number. If you are mailing a paper, allow for the next-business-day return and for the time the auditor's transfer takes first.

Records search is online. The FAQ says the indexes are open to everyone, viewing images needs a free online subscriber form, and documents are indexed on the computer starting January 1, 1993. A recording notification service is also offered.

What tools does the Putnam County auditor's site offer sellers?

Its Tools menu holds these items:

  • Sales reports and delinquency reports.
  • The conveyance calculator.
  • A tax estimator.

A GIS parcel viewer sits behind the Map link, and an Info section holds the forms the state and the office provide.

The same page posts the 2025 delinquent parcels list. Search your parcel before listing, and phone the auditor if the record looks off.

What else does the Putnam County recorder do?

Beyond deeds, the office runs the county's Ohio Century Farm registrations. A farm qualifies after 100 years in one family, and the recorder will meet with a family to check eligibility. It also keeps military discharge records, which are the DD 214 files veterans need for benefits.

Putnam County is mostly rural. Wikipedia's 2020 figures: 34,451 people over 484 square miles, with 84.2% living in rural areas and owners occupying 83.8% of occupied homes. The county board of education operates nine school districts.

Long-held land is a point of pride here. A farm owned by one family for 100 years can be registered, and qualified registrants receive an heirloom certificate signed by the Governor and the Director of the Ohio Department of Agriculture. A yard sign is available for purchase. The recorder will meet with you to check eligibility, so ask before you sell a farm that might qualify.

Wikipedia counts 12,976 households and 13,824 housing units in the county, 6.1% of them vacant.

A farm, an estate home or a house with a balance owed still goes through the same paperwork, and a cash buyer can purchase it in present condition and cover these fees at the closing table.

What are the Putnam County recorder's hours?

Doors are open weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, with recording accepted from 8:30 to 4:15. The office closes on the holidays its contact page lists.

What does the Putnam County auditor charge for a deed transfer?

Four dollars per thousand of price, rounded up to the next hundred, plus fifty cents a parcel. The check has to equal the conveyance fee exactly.

Do I need approval before I bring a deed to the Putnam County recorder?

Yes. The Tax Map Office in the engineer's office must clear the legal description, and the auditor must transfer the deed before it reaches the recorder.

Does Putnam County accept e-recorded deeds?

Yes. E-recording now covers deeds and transfer documents, through the vendors the recorder lists: Simplifile, CSC and Erecording Partners.

How much is a marginal notation in Putnam County?

$4.00 for each one, per the recorder's FAQ. A nonconforming document costs $20.00 more.

Richland County by the numbers

What does the Richland County Recorder of Deeds do?

The Richland County Recorder keeps the public record of who owns land in the county and which liens and mortgages sit on it. The counter is in the county building at 50 Park Avenue East, Mansfield. It opens on weekdays at 8:00 AM, closes at 4:00 PM, and takes no new filings after 3:45 PM. Call 419-774-5602.

The county's own recorder page traces the job back to 1787, when the Northwest Territory set up a recorder in every county. Statehood came in 1803, the job became an elected one in 1829, and a four-year term was fixed in 1936. Each filing is indexed so a title examiner can trace ownership from one holder to the next. The county page adds that the recorder answers to more than 1,000 sections of state law.

For a seller in Richland County, the recorder is the last stop. Once the buyer's deed is recorded, the transfer becomes part of the public record.

What are the steps to record a Richland County deed?

Deeds pass through several county offices before they are recorded. A typical sequence looks like this.

  • Sign and acknowledge the deed. Sign the deed, then acknowledge the signature before an officer section 5301.01 allows: a notary, a judge, a court clerk, the county auditor or engineer, or a mayor.
  • Request tax map pre-approval by email to taxmap@richlandcountyoh.gov. The recorder's page says pre-approval must be included with any electronic deed transfer for real estate.
  • At the Auditor's counter, file the conveyance statement, pay the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, and get the endorsement.
  • Hand the endorsed deed and the recording fee to the Recorder ahead of the 3:45 PM cutoff.

Electronic deed transfers are accepted. Anything the Tax Map Office and the Auditor must review still has to be carried to the courthouse. Staff do not hand out legal forms and point people to an attorney for drafting help.

Why does the Richland County Tax Map Office look at my deed?

The Tax Map Office is a division of the Richland County Engineer's Office, and it keeps the property map for every deeded parcel for the auditor. Its services include checking all recorded deeds, maintaining current maps with ownership, providing copies of surveys and checking surveys done in the county. Its collection of tax maps reaches back to 1853 and includes old road record books from the early 1800s. Phone 419-774-5620. The counter keeps the same weekday schedule as the rest of the building.

Because the office checks deeds against its maps, a seller who is splitting a lot or changing a legal description should raise it with tax map staff before the closing date.

Richland County offices a deed passes through
OfficeWhat it does for a deedPhone
Tax Map OfficePre-approves the legal description and checks recorded deeds419-774-5620

County TreasurerTakes payment of conveyance fees and shows any tax owed419-774-5622
County RecorderRecords and indexes the deed419-774-5602

Source: Richland County department pages.

What does the Auditor require before a deed is recorded in Richland County?

Section 319.202 requires the buyer or a representative to submit a statement of the property's value first. Only then does the auditor endorse the deed. The statement carries two affirmations. One asks whether the seller's bill carried a reduction such as homestead or owner occupancy. The other asks about CAUV farm valuation, since land that drops out can owe recoupment under section 5713.34.

The seller, as grantor, pays the conveyance fee set in section 319.54(G)(3). A commissioner-adopted transfer tax under Chapter 322 falls on the seller as well. The ceiling for that county tax is thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, and the auditor collects it when the deed is delivered, before recording. The Richland County Treasurer's page adds that conveyance fees are paid at the treasurer's office. Ask the Auditor what applies to your sale before setting a closing date.

The statute counts value as the whole consideration, any mortgage or vendor's lien included, and forbids willful misstatement.

What does Richland County charge to record a document?

Recording fees are set by Ohio law. Ohio's schedule starts with a seventeen dollar base fee and a seventeen dollar housing trust fund fee for the first two pages, and each added page carries four dollars of each. A preservation surcharge of up to five dollars is optional for counties (section 317.32). Certified copies and photocopies carry their own per-page charges under the same section.

Because page count moves the total, confirm the amount for your own document by phone. Use 419-774-5602 before sending any payment.

How do I search Richland County land records?

A link on the recorder's page opens an online records search where deeds, mortgages and releases can be read. This is useful for a seller checking whether an old mortgage was ever released, or whether a prior owner's lien is still on file.

The auditor's property search adds parcel data, and the Land Bank at 50 Park Avenue East, lower level 1, acquires vacant and abandoned properties. Heirs who plan to sell should check that the last recorded deed names the person who holds title.

Do older Richland County deeds without witnesses still count?

Usually yes. A deed signed before February 1, 2002 without the two witnesses the earlier law asked for is still deemed properly executed under section 5301.01(B), absent fraud in obtaining the signature. Recording it with the recorder of the land's county puts later buyers and lenders on notice.

The rule protects families holding old deeds. It does not fix a missing acknowledgment on a newly signed deed, so a current deed still needs the notary or other officer named in the statute.

Who decides whether Richland County charges a transfer tax?

The board of county commissioners does. Under section 322.02, a county may levy a real property transfer tax by resolution, after two public hearings held three to ten days apart with newspaper, website or public notice sites carrying notice for two consecutive weeks. The resolution is subject to referendum unless adopted as an emergency measure by a unanimous vote. The commissioners may also send the question to voters, and then it takes effect only if a majority approves. The rate is a local choice, so a neighboring county's figure says nothing about Richland's.

What does the Richland County housing stock mean for deed work?

The Census Bureau counts 54,904 housing units and 124,893 residents for 2025, with 114 building permits issued that year. Median monthly owner costs are $1,218 where a mortgage exists and $489 where none does. Nearly nine in ten residents (87.6%) were in the same house a year earlier.

Land in Richland County stretches from Mansfield, Ontario and Shelby to villages such as Bellville, Lexington and Plymouth, and into townships named Springfield, Troy, Weller and Worthington.

More questions about Richland County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Where is the Richland County Recorder located?

It is at 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield, Ohio 44902, phone 419-774-5602. Filings stop at 3:45 PM on weekdays.

Is tax map approval needed before a Richland County deed is recorded?

Yes for electronic deed transfers. The recorder's page says tax map pre-approval must come with the deed and gives taxmap@richlandcountyoh.gov as the address to request it.

Can I record a Richland County deed online?

Partly. Electronic deed transfers are accepted, while documents needing Tax Map and Auditor review go in person. Call 419-774-5602 to confirm which route fits your document.

Which party covers the conveyance fee on a Richland County sale?

The grantor, meaning the seller. The seller, as grantor, owes it along with any county transfer tax, paid before recording.

Will the Richland County Recorder supply legal forms?

No. No. Staff say they do not supply legal forms and suggest asking an attorney.

Ross County by the numbers

Where is the Ross County Recorder's office?

You will find the office in the courthouse, 2 North Paint Street, Suite E, Chillicothe, Ohio 45601. Its number is 740-702-3000. Documents sent by mail go to PO Box 6162, Chillicothe, OH 45601, and the office email is rossrec@bright.net. The treasurer's office is next door in Suite F, so a tax balance and a recording can be handled in one trip.

The county has a long paper trail. The county dates to August 20, 1798, and its seat, Chillicothe, served as Ohio's first and third capital. Nineteenth-century surveyors described almost one hundred earthwork enclosures and five hundred mounds in the county, and Hopewell Culture National Historical Park and Adena State Memorial are among its protected sites. Modern deeds sit on top of more than two centuries of recorded transfers.

What is the price of recording a deed in Ross County?

The fee sheet, dated January 1, 2025, prices a document by its page count. A one or two page document is $39.00, a three page one is $47.00, and every added page is another $8.00. Documents that fall outside the standard format under section 317.114 carry a $20.00 surcharge, and each marginal reference adds $4.00. The office states that its recording fees are set by the Ohio Legislature.
