Source: Ross County Recorder Table of Fees. The schedule continues to 88 pages at $727.00 and then adds $8.00 for each page beyond that.

State law explains the structure. The state fee statute sets the pattern: a base fee plus an equal housing trust fund fee, with an optional preservation surcharge of up to five dollars (section 317.32). A postage-paid, self-addressed envelope is required with every filing, so include one when you mail a deed.

What other recorder charges should a Ross County seller know about?

  • A certified copy runs $5.00 for page one and $2.00 for every page after it.
  • Ordinary copies are $2.00 per printed page, and the sheet gives $7 for a two-page document and $9 for three pages.
  • Fax charges are $2.00 a page to a local or toll-free number and $4.00 a page to a toll number.
  • According to the recorder, no one needs the original recorded deed to sell or borrow, because a certified copy from the office serves equally well.

These are the office's own figures, and they apply to documents the office handles after a sale, such as copying a recorded deed for a title company or an heir.

How do I search Ross County records online, and what should I avoid?

The recorder's website says most records go back to January 1, 1974 and further, and can be viewed and downloaded free from home through the county's CountyFusion search. The office also assists people in person while they wait. Anyone can see a deed, mortgage or release this way before listing a house.

The office warns about private companies that mail letters or turn up in online searches charging $79.99 to $99.99 for copies of a deed. These companies are not government offices, and the same records are free to view at the courthouse offices. The recorder calls those offers a scam for money, and recommends skipping them. One exception applies to military discharge papers: a DD214 is not a full public record, and only the veteran, a veterans' service office or a funeral director handling burial services can get an unredacted certified copy, free of charge.

What must happen before a Ross County deed reaches the recorder?

Start with signing and acknowledgment. Section 5301.01 names who may take the acknowledgment, including a notary public, judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer or mayor. The auditor comes next. After the buyer files a value statement under section 319.202, the Ross County Auditor endorses the deed. It also asks whether the seller's taxes had been cut by a program such as homestead, and whether the land sat in the farm valuation program, which can carry a recoupment charge.

Before the deed goes across the hall, the seller pays the auditor the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax. Section 322.02 lets a county set that transfer tax as high as thirty cents per hundred dollars of value. The Ross County Auditor knows the figure that applies.

How does Ross County property tax fit into a deed closing?

Ross County collects real estate tax one year behind. Per the treasurer, taxes attach to the property and not to its owner, so a new buyer can receive a bill soon after purchase, and the closing papers normally credit the buyer with the prorated share. In 2026 the two installments fell due February 20 and August 21; the treasurer can supply 2027 dates. Get the balance in writing and hand it to the title company.

If back taxes are owed, the treasurer's Delinquent Tax Contract splits them into five equal installments, and the SMART Payments Program spreads them over 30 months or longer. A seller with a contract open should confirm what balance stays with the property. The treasurer applies a 5% late charge when payment is received within ten days and 10% after that.

What if an old family deed in Ross County lacks two witnesses?

Ohio treats most such deeds as valid. For an instrument signed before February 1, 2002 and never witnessed by two people as the earlier statute asked, section 5301.01(B) presumes it properly executed unless fraud produced the signature. Once the deed is filed with the recorder, later buyers and lenders have notice of it. Heirs in Ross County who find a mid-century deed in a drawer should still check that it was actually recorded, because the index at the recorder's office is what a title company searches.

What does the Ross County housing stock look like?

Census figures show 76,429 residents and 32,165 housing units, and owners occupy 69.6% of homes. Median home value among owners is $171,500. Owner costs are $1,304 a month with a mortgage and $487 without. Building permits numbered 59 in 2025, and 87.9% of residents had stayed put for a year.

The county holds one city, Chillicothe, villages from Adelphi to South Salem, and 16 townships. Ohio University has run a campus in Chillicothe since 1966. Seven counties border Ross (Fayette, Pickaway, Hocking, Vinton, Jackson, Pike and Highland), and a farm that straddles a county line has its deed recorded wherever each piece of land lies. The terrain is frequent wooded hills with farmland between them, so any sale of acreage should be checked with the auditor for farm valuation before the deed is signed.

More questions about Ross County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What does a short deed cost to record in Ross County?

$39.00 under the fee sheet that took effect January 1, 2025. Pages past the second add $8.00 each, and non-standard documents add $20.00.

What address takes a mailed Ross County deed?

Send it to PO Box 6162, Chillicothe, OH 45601, with payment and the postage-paid return envelope the office requires on every filing.

Can I view Ross County records without paying a service?

Yes. Most records back to January 1, 1974 can be viewed and downloaded free through the county's CountyFusion site. Copies made in the office are $2.00 per printed page on the fee sheet.

Must I hold the original deed to sell in Ross County?

No. No. A certified copy from the recorder is as good as the original for a sale or a mortgage. Page one of a certified copy is $5.00, and later pages are $2.00 each.

Which office endorses a Ross County deed before recording?

The County Auditor does, after the buyer files a statement of value. The seller settles the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax with the auditor first.

Sandusky County by the numbers

Who keeps the land records for Sandusky County, and how do I reach them?

The Sandusky County Recorder keeps them, from Room 143 of the building at 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont, ZIP 43420. The counter opens at 8:00 AM and closes at 4:30 PM, Monday to Friday. Dial (419) 334-6226 with questions. The county's own description says the first deed went on record on May 16, 1822, so the files span two centuries of Sandusky County ownership.

Staff index every instrument by name and parcel. A title examiner uses that index to trace a chain of owners and to spot any mortgage or lien still attached. For a copy of something already recorded, the county site asks you to email the recorder's staff.

Fremont is the seat of the county. Bellevue and Clyde are the county's other two cities, and the county site also links Gibsonburg and Woodville. Whichever of them your house sits in, the paper trail ends at the same Fremont counter.

What is the path a Sandusky County deed follows from signing to the record?

Think of it as two counters on one floor. The auditor works first, in Room 109, phone (419) 334-6123. The recorder works second, in Room 143, and only the recorder's stamp puts the deed into the public index.

  • A new deed is drafted with the full legal description, which you can lift from the previous deed shown in the county's online land search.
  • The grantor signs before a notary, or another official Ohio law names for this purpose.
  • The auditor receives the deed along with the state's value statement, collects its fees, and endorses the deed.
  • The recorder takes the endorsed deed, collects the recording charge, and returns the original as you direct.

Closing attorneys and title companies commonly carry the paperwork for you. If you are giving a house to a relative instead of selling it, ask the auditor which exemption form fits before you drive downtown.

Which Ohio statutes decide whether a deed is valid and protected?

Two short sections do most of the work. R.C. 5301.01 says the grantor signs and that the signature is acknowledged before a court judge or clerk, a county auditor or engineer, a notary or a mayor, who then certifies it. A deed without that certificate is not ready to file.

R.C. 5301.25 deals with priority. R.C. 5301.25 sends land instruments to the recorder of the county where the parcel sits. Until a deed is filed there, a later purchaser who paid honestly and knew nothing of it can treat the earlier deed as fraudulent. A seller here should confirm filing after closing.

The same section adds a rule for deeds that follow a survey: the surveyor's name must appear in the deed. Ask your closing agent whether yours needs that wording.

What recording charges does the state schedule set?

The base recording charges come from R.C. 317.32, where every charge is split into two equal halves. A county can layer a preservation surcharge on top, so the counter total may run higher than the statute's figures. Phone the recorder for the posted schedule first.

Fees as printed in R.C. 317.32 (codes.ohio.gov)

The surcharge, capped at five dollars, goes into the county general fund. Payment is due at presentation, though an e-recording submitter may settle by electronic funds transfer afterward.

Who bears the transfer charges when a Sandusky County house sells?

The seller does. The buyer's side files a value statement with the auditor under R.C. 319.202, and the grantor covers the state conveyance fee plus any local tax a county has adopted under Chapter 322.

The state fee in R.C. 319.54(G)(3) is whichever is larger: $1, or ten cents for every $100 of value, with any leftover part of $100 counting as a full unit. R.C. 322.02 lets commissioners adopt a further tax capped at thirty cents per hundred. This page quotes no county total, so ask the Sandusky County Auditor what combined rate applies on your recording date.

The same statute exempts many transfers. A sampling:

  • deeds that only give or release security for a debt
  • corrective deeds that fix one already recorded
  • gifts passing between spouses or from parents to children
  • transfers ordered by a court that are not themselves sales
  • conveyances among the heirs of a single decedent where no money changes hands

An exempt deed still needs a written reason, which the state's DTE 100(EX) form captures.

Does the Sandusky County Recorder accept electronic filings?

It does. A filer signs up with one of four approved providers named on the county's vendor sheet: ePN, CSC eRecording, Simplifile or Hopdox. Lenders, attorneys and title offices typically hold an account with at least one.

Without a title office you can still file by hand. The county's public search link on the recorder page is a useful first stop, since it lets you copy your own legal description and check what is already of record against the parcel.

What do federal figures say about housing in Sandusky County?

The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 58,655 residents, 0.4 percent under the 2020 base, across 408.25 square miles of dry land. The housing count is 26,530 units holding 24,686 households.

  • Home ownership: 73.4 percent of units are owner-occupied
  • Typical owned home: valued at $160,700
  • Typical rent: $783 a month
  • Typical household income: $62,295
  • Average commute: 20.7 minutes

Because about three in four homes have their owner living inside, most competing listings are owner-occupied houses. The Sandusky River cuts northeast through the county toward Sandusky Bay on Lake Erie, so a parcel near the water deserves a flood-zone check from your title office.

How do Sandusky County property taxes tie into closing?

The county treasurer's site says bills fall due on the third Friday of February and the second Friday of July. Under House Bill 186, the treasurer set August 7, 2026 as the second-half date for the 2025 bills payable in 2026. That date is behind us.

Your closing agent requests the owed amount from the treasurer and holds it back from your proceeds. When a half-year is still open, get the treasurer's payoff number before you commit to a contract. The treasurer's site also links to sheriff sale listings and the county land bank, worth a look if the house passed through a tax foreclosure.

More questions about Sandusky County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Which office records Sandusky County deeds?

The Sandusky County Recorder, Room 143 at 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont. It is at 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont, and the phone is (419) 334-6226.

Which counter comes first, auditor or recorder?

Yes. The auditor reviews the value statement, takes its fees, and endorses the deed. The recorder accepts the instrument after that step, so plan your visits in that order.

What is the statutory cost of filing a deed here?

For the first two pages R.C. 317.32 pairs a $17 recording fee with an equal $17 for the state housing trust fund; every page after that carries a $4 and $4 pair. Counties can tack on up to $5 more, so ask the recorder what the full charge is.

Can a deed be recorded electronically in Sandusky County?

Yes, through ePN, CSC eRecording, Simplifile or Hopdox, the four providers on the county's vendor sheet. Title offices and attorneys usually file this way.

What risk comes with leaving a deed unrecorded?

An unrecorded deed loses ground to a later buyer who pays in good faith and has no notice of it, because R.C. 5301.25 labels the earlier instrument fraudulent as to that buyer.

Portsmouth is the county seat, and the auditor and treasurer also list offices at that same 7th Street address.

You can file in person or by mail. The recorder asks mail filers to enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope. Without one, the office charges postage to send the original back.

How do I pay the recorder, and what format must the document follow?

The recorder takes cash or a check, and nothing else. Make the check payable to "Scioto County Recorder", because checks written to a second or third party are refused. The office also notes that Scioto County has adopted the $5.00 record preservation fee on top of its other recording charges.

The recorder lists layout rules that a deed must meet before it will be accepted:

  • Legible type of size ten or larger, in blue or black ink only
  • Letter or legal size sheets (8 1/2 by 11, or 8 1/2 by 14)
  • No highlighted text
  • One inch margins at the sides and bottom
  • Three blank inches above the text on page one, and an inch and a half above it on every later page

A deed that misses these rules can be turned away, which delays your closing. Have the attorney or title agency preparing the deed check them before signing.

In what order does a Scioto County deed travel?

The recorder's checklist reads like this: write the deed on a fresh form rather than copying the old one, borrow the legal description from the last recorded deed, have a notary witness the signing, take the transfer to the Scioto County Auditor, and bring the deed back to the recorder once that office is done.

The auditor bills a transfer charge of its own, apart from the recorder's. That counter is Room 103 (740.355.8264) and stays open until 4:30 pm.

Two related points from the recorder's FAQ matter to sellers. After a payoff, the lender files a release of mortgage as its own document, and no new deed appears. And mobile home titles are not kept at the recorder, because they are registered with the county auditor.

What does the Scioto County Auditor charge for a transfer?

The auditor's transfer charges come from R.C. 319.54(G), and Chapter 322 allows an added county transfer tax. The county's full recording fee list is a separate sheet, so request it from the recorder before sending payment. The table covers only the auditor's statutory items.

Auditor fees as printed in R.C. 319.54(G), Ohio Revised Code
ItemFee as printed
Transfer or entry of a lot or parcel of landFifty cents for each transfer or entry, paid by the person requiring it
Receiving the statement of value (conveyance fee)One dollar, or ten cents for each one hundred dollars or fraction, whichever is greater
Deed of land sold for taxesFive dollars, paid by the purchaser

Section 319.54(G)(3) excuses certain deeds from the conveyance fee: those given only as security for a debt, corrective deeds, and no-money transfers between heirs are examples. An excused deed travels with a short statement of the reason.

What can the Scioto County Recorder not do for me?

The office does not draft documents and does not give legal advice. Its FAQ says plainly that a fill-in-the-blank form still requires choices that count as legal advice.

  • It cannot say whether you hold good and clear title. Title examiners search the recorder's index and other county offices to decide that.
  • It does not remove or release liens. A federal tax lien is recorded there, but only the issuing agency can release it.
  • Searching is left to you or a title professional, even though the records are public.
  • Birth and death certificates come from the county health department, and divorce and marriage records come from the clerk of courts and probate court.

Let the title company run the lien search. Property tax liens are the treasurer's business, so raise those with that office.

What other documents does the Scioto County Recorder handle?

Beyond deeds, the office records mortgages, mortgage releases, plats and financing statements under the Uniform Commercial Code that relate to real estate. Surveys are not usually filed there, so ask your lender or title company for one. If your home is in a subdivision, a plat map can be found by searching the subdivision name, and it shows lot lines and streets without any buildings.

Certified copies carry the office's stamp, so a printout from home cannot be certified. Come to the counter or request them by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope. A document that cites an earlier recorded one through a marginal notation costs an extra charge per reference.

How do I search Scioto County property records or guard against deed fraud?

The recorder's website offers a public records search and, as a trial, a newer mobile-friendly portal that opens recorded documents on a phone. Parcels can also be found on a GIS map kept by the county engineer, searchable by owner name, address or parcel number.

The site also offers Property Fraud Alert, a free service that monitors your name and flags new filings. The office admits it cannot block fraud and describes the tool as an early warning. Notaries get a similar free service that watches for their name or commission number.

What does the Census Bureau show for Scioto County homes?

The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate for Scioto County is 71,365 people, a 3.6 percent decline from the 2020 base, living on 610.15 square miles of land. It counts 33,078 housing units and 28,864 households.

  • Owner-occupied rate: 68.4 percent
  • Typical value of a home its owner lives in: $137,900
  • Median gross rent: $742
  • Median household income: $50,609
  • Persons in poverty: 19.1 percent

The county sits on the Ohio River where the Scioto River enters it, and Portsmouth is its only city. New Boston, Otway, Rarden and South Webster are villages. Much of the western half is forest, including Shawnee State Forest and Park. Health care and Shawnee State University anchor the local economy.

Where do property tax dates fit into the sale?

State law splits the annual real estate bill into two installments, the later one falling on June 20 unless extended. For 2026 the Scioto treasurer pushed the later installment to August 20 because of House Bill 186; that date is past. Your closing agent requests a tax payoff from the treasurer, whose office is at 602 7th Street, Room 102.

For assessment dates, appeals and relief programs, see the Scioto County property tax guide on this site.

More questions about Scioto County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When can I visit the Scioto County Recorder?

Weekdays from 8:00 am, with the last service at 4:00 pm, in Room 110 at 602 7th St., Portsmouth. Call (740) 355-8304 to check.

How do I pay to record a deed in Scioto County?

Pay by cash or by a check made out to "Scioto County Recorder". Checks payable to anyone else are not accepted. The county has also adopted a $5.00 record preservation fee.

Is a notary required on a Scioto County deed?

Yes. The recorder says every transfer is signed before a notary. Ohio law also allows a judge, a clerk of court, the county auditor, the county engineer or a mayor to take the acknowledgment.

Does the recorder issue a new deed when I pay off my mortgage?

No. A new deed is issued only when the property is transferred. When the loan is satisfied, your lender files a release of mortgage as a separate recorded document.

Can the recorder tell me whether my title is clear?

No. The office is not allowed to give opinions on title. A professional title examiner or abstractor reviews the recorder's index along with records at other county offices.

Seneca County by the numbers

Where is the Seneca County Recorder, and what does the office do?

The Seneca County Recorder works out of the county building at 109 S. Washington Street in Tiffin, the same building that houses the Auditor and the Treasurer. A county news release lists the Recorder's line as 419-447-4434. The office files deeds and mortgages in the order they arrive and marks each with the exact time of presentation, a duty found in ORC 317.13.

Seneca County lies in northwestern Ohio and covers 553 square miles, nearly 80 percent of it farmland, according to Wikipedia. The Sandusky River cuts through the county and Tiffin grew up on both banks. The county seat shares the map with Fostoria and Bellevue, which each lie partly inside the county line, plus a ring of villages and townships. Expect a deed here to describe anything from a Tiffin bungalow to a few acres on a county road.

Population has slipped from 61,901 in 1980 to 55,069 in 2020, so many sellers are heirs or owners of houses that need work. Whatever the condition, the sale ends the same way: a deed stamped at the Auditor and then filed with the Recorder.

Which office gets the deed first in Seneca County?

The Auditor does. Its transfer page says every transfer document has to be presented there before it can be recorded, under ORC 319.203. The Auditor sits in Suite 2206 of the same building, answers at 419-447-0692, and keeps weekday hours.

What the Auditor's page tells you to bring and pay:

  • A conveyance fee printed as $4.00 per thousand dollars conveyed.
  • A transfer fee of fifty cents for each parcel named in the deed.
  • A check made out to the Seneca County Auditor for the correct total. Blank checks have been refused since January 2022, and a wrong amount returns the paperwork unrecorded.
  • The state's DTE 100 form, or DTE 100 (EX) if the transfer qualifies for an exemption. Both are on the Auditor's forms page next to an online fee calculator.

The base figure comes from ORC 319.54(G)(3), which sets the state-level charge. Section 322.02 separately allows a board of county commissioners to levy a transfer tax up to thirty cents per hundred. Seneca County publishes one combined local rate, so quote the Auditor's page, not the statutes, when you budget for closing.

How do the land and weather around Tiffin shape a Seneca County sale?

Seneca County is nearly flat. Wikipedia describes terrain that slopes gently from about 290 meters above sea level in the southeast toward the edge of the old Great Black Swamp in the northwest, with almost all of it draining to the Sandusky River. Winters bring lake-effect snow and hard wind chill, and summers run hot and humid.

That mix matters when a house changes hands. Buyers and their inspectors in a flat farm county tend to look hard at roofs, gutters, drainage and basements, and a house that has sat vacant through a Tiffin winter can show it. Sellers who would rather skip repairs often choose an as-is cash sale, and the deed process described here is the same either way.

Settlement came late. The county was barely inhabited by European Americans before the 1830s, and in 1889 about 900 Luxembourgers arrived and built substantial churches and schools.

What must a deed contain before the Seneca County offices accept it?

State law asks for a grantor's signature acknowledged before an official such as a notary, judge, clerk of a court of record, county auditor, county engineer or mayor, as ORC 5301.01 lists them. That one rule covers deeds, mortgages, land contracts and leases.

Seneca County adds its own demands. The legal description must name the township or the city or village, the county and the state, and carry the right parcel numbers. The Tax Map Office reviews every description, and the Auditor's page says the wording should match the prior deed or the new survey exactly. The county directory lists the tax map line as 419-448-5719.

Splits are the slow part. A survey is generally needed, and the approving body depends on location: the Seneca Regional Planning Commission outside municipalities, the city engineer inside a city, village council inside a village. The Auditor's site also warns that after January 1, 2027, splits, resurveys and combinations will appear in property tax records only from tax year 2028. Anyone selling a piece of a larger parcel should start the survey early.

What does recording a deed cost in Seneca County?

The Recorder's fee follows ORC 317.32. For a standard instrument the statute pairs a base fee and a housing trust fund fee, and it allows a county to add a preservation surcharge. Shelby County, across the state, raised its published fee by $5 in 2025 for that reason, so totals differ from county to county. Phone the Seneca County Recorder to learn the current total, because a short payment can bring the deed back.

Seneca County and statutory charges tied to a deed
ChargeAmountWhere it is printed
Conveyance fee$4.00 per thousand dollars conveyedSeneca County Auditor, real estate transfer page
Transfer fee$.50 per parcelSeneca County Auditor, real estate transfer page
First two pages recorded$17 base and $17 housing trust fundORC 317.32(A)(1)(a)
Each page after two$4 base and $4 housing trust fundORC 317.32(A)(1)(a)
Preservation surchargeUp to $5, if the county adopts itORC 317.32(A)(1)(b)

Can Seneca County deeds be searched or filed online?

By June 30, 2026, ORC 317.13 required every recorder to offer electronic recording of real property conveyances and to publish electronic indexes and images for instruments recorded from January 1, 1980 forward, free of any access fee. That date is behind us, so ask the Seneca County Recorder which e-recording vendor the office uses.

The Auditor's site is the easiest place to start a search. It reaches any parcel by name, address or map and shows the appraisal and payment history. It also publishes a real estate sales report, and sellers can read recent Seneca County sale prices there. The Auditor lists five public computers in the building: two in its own office, two with the Treasurer and one at the Recorder.

How do Seneca County property taxes and relief programs affect a sale?

The Auditor values the county's roughly 35,539 parcels and the Treasurer bills and collects. A closing agent asks the Treasurer for the payoff on any half still open, and a seller can look up the payment history on the Auditor's site first.

  • Value complaints go to a three-member Board of Revision. The county brochure requires original notarized signatures and a filing between January 1 and March 31.
  • A further appeal after the Board rules goes to the state Board of Tax Appeals or the local common pleas court within 30 days of the notice.
  • The homestead exemption for older or disabled owners is filed with the Auditor by December 31. For 2026 bills the Auditor said new applicants needed $40,000 or less in Ohio adjusted gross household income, and disabled veterans have no income test.

The Auditor's home page also mentions a veterans' exemption created by House Bill 59 and codified at ORC 5709.17. Ask the Auditor whether a property qualifies before a sale closes.

More questions about Seneca County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Do I record a Seneca County deed with the Auditor or the Recorder?

Both, in that order. The Auditor processes the conveyance fee forms and stamps the deed, then the Recorder files it. The Auditor's page states that transfer documents must be presented there before recording.

What if my Seneca County deed has the wrong fee on the check?

The paperwork is sent back unrecorded. The Auditor's page says incorrect fees and blank checks cause rejection. Call 419-447-0692 for the amount before you write the check.

Can the Recorder turn down a deed?

Yes, in two situations. ORC 317.13 lets the recorder refuse an instrument the Revised Code does not require or authorize to be recorded, or one the recorder reasonably believes is materially false or fraudulent. The filer can ask the common pleas court for an order.

Is an attorney needed to transfer a house in Seneca County?

Nothing on the county pages makes one mandatory. Still, the Tax Map Office checks every legal description, and a mismatch holds up the sale, so many owners ask a title company or attorney to prepare the deed.

Until when can I contest a Seneca County valuation?

Through March 31 of the year after the tax year in question. Use the Board of Revision complaint form with notarized original signatures. The Auditor at 419-447-0692 can say which tax year applies to your parcel.

Shelby County by the numbers

Where do I take a deed to be recorded in Shelby County, Ohio?

Take it to the Shelby County Recorder on the second floor of the county annex at 129 E. Court Street in Sidney. Phone 937-498-7270 or fax 937-498-7272 to reach staff. The counter takes new recordings a quarter hour before the staff stops other business: Monday to Thursday that means a 4:15 p.m. cutoff against a 4:30 p.m. close, and on Fridays 11:45 a.m. against noon. Plan to arrive well ahead of those times.

The Recorder's page calls the office the steward of the county's real estate records and says they reach back to the county's start, when the land was still part of Miami County. The online index covers July 1, 1989 forward. Older research means a trip to the office, and staff will help, though they do not do genealogy searches for outsiders.

Sidney is the only city in the county, and the rest of Shelby County is villages, townships and farmland. A deed here may describe a Sidney street lot, a village house in a place with German roots, or acreage along the Great Miami River.

What does Shelby County charge to record a deed?

Under the county's 2025 schedule, a deed costs $39 for its first two pages, with $8 for every added page. The schedule explains that most recording fees climbed $5 on January 1, 2025, after Senate Bill 94 added a document preservation surcharge, which ORC 317.32 limits to five dollars.

Shelby County Recorder charges on the 2025 schedule
ServiceCharge
Deed, mortgage, lease and most filings$39 covers the first two pages
Each added page or attachment$8
Marginal notation$4 each
Non-standardization fee, per document$20
Plat, 11 by 17 inches$40
Plat, 24 by 36 inches$86
UCC financing statement$12 plus $4 per name indexed

Count the pages before you write the check, because the total moves with each added sheet and each attachment.

What do Shelby County recorder staff look for in a deed?

The Recorder's fee page lists the rules plainly:

  • Every document needs a legal description, and it must read as it does on the prior deed. A description with missing parts is rejected.
  • Mail filings need a self-addressed stamped envelope. Without postage for the return, the office holds the document.
  • Marginal notations require the volume and page of the earlier record, and each one adds $4.
  • An affidavit has to say who the current owner of the property is.

The grantor's signature must be acknowledged by an authorized officer, usually a notary, under ORC 5301.01. An unacknowledged deed is not ready for the counter.

The county page also posts a public notice on old deed language. Any clause that limits the sale, rental or use of a dwelling by race, color, sex, religion, national origin, handicap or familial status is invalid under federal fair housing law and cannot be enforced, even if it sits in a decades-old recorded deed.

Who collects the Shelby County conveyance fee?

The Shelby County Auditor does, before the Recorder files anything. The Auditor's transfer fee page prints the real estate transfer fee as $4 per $1,000 of sale price plus $.50 per parcel.

The rate rests on ORC 319.54(G)(3) and the county option in ORC 322.02. The county option falls on the grantor, which makes the seller the usual payer when the deed is delivered.

A few transfers are listed as exempt, among them family gifts, corrective deeds and deeds where no money changes hands. Ask the Auditor before assuming a deal qualifies.

What is the land like in Shelby County?

Shelby County sits in western Ohio and covers 411 square miles, with 408 of them land. Wikipedia describes low rolling hills, almost all of it farmed or built up. The Great Miami River enters from Logan County near the middle and leaves into Miami County. The highest ground, 1,149 feet, lies in the southeast corner where Champaign and Miami counties meet it.

The 2020 census counted 48,230 residents, with about 43 percent in urban areas and a median age of 40.2. The county is named for Isaac Shelby, Kentucky's first governor, and borders Auglaize, Logan, Champaign, Miami, Darke and Mercer counties, so a parcel near the line can sit close to a neighboring recorder's records. The county's first seat of government was Hardin, named for a pioneer killed there in 1792, before Sidney took over. When the county was cut down in 1848, Minster and New Bremen moved into the new Auglaize County. Many Shelby County towns trace to German immigrants, and the Miami and Erie Canal, which reached the county in 1841, gave those newcomers early work.

For a seller, the geography means plenty of rural parcels. A farmhouse on a few acres may need a survey or a split approved before it can be deeded separately, so ask the Auditor's office early about description rules.

What is the order of steps from signing to a recorded Shelby County deed?

There are four steps, in this order. The grantor signs before a notary. The deed goes to the Shelby County Auditor with the transfer fee, which the Auditor's page prices at $4 per $1,000 of price plus $.50 per parcel. The deed then goes to the Recorder, with the recording fee and a stamped return envelope if it travels by mail. Last, the Recorder indexes it, and the new owner's name appears in the county's records.

A title company normally carries a deed through those steps at a closing. A family member handling a transfer alone can do the same in person or by mail. Both offices are county offices in Sidney, so ask each for its current hours before you go, and remember that the Recorder stops taking recordings 15 minutes before it closes.

Once the filing posts, the online index from July 1, 1989 forward lets anyone confirm it, so a seller can confirm the deed went on record.

How do Shelby County property tax records and relief programs work?

The Auditor's real estate section covers valuation and tax rates, revaluation information, owner occupancy and homestead tax reductions, delinquent payment plans and razed or damaged structures. A seller can search a parcel there to see the value on record before listing.

  • A value dispute begins as a Board of Revision complaint. ORC 5715.19 allows filing with the auditor until March 31 of the next year, or until the first-half collection closes if that falls later.
  • The Ohio Department of Taxation lists the 2026 homestead reduction for seniors and disabled owners at $29,700 of value, with the application filed in the same year by December 31.
  • Back taxes can sometimes be paid through a delinquent payment plan, which the Auditor's menu lists. Ask there for terms.

At closing the title agent requests the tax payoff from the county. Because Ohio bills real estate in two halves, the amount owed depends on when in the year the sale closes.

More questions about Shelby County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What are the Shelby County Recorder's hours for recording a deed?

New recordings are accepted until 4:15 p.m. Monday to Thursday and until 11:45 a.m. Friday. Other office business continues 15 minutes longer each day, per the Recorder's page.

How much is the Shelby County recording fee for a two-page deed?

$39 on the 2025 schedule, which covers the first two pages. Pages beyond that cost $8 each, a non-standard document adds $20, and each marginal notation adds $4.

Will the Recorder hold my deed if I mail it?

Yes, if you leave out the return envelope. The county asks that mailed documents come with a stamped, self-addressed envelope, and without one the office holds the paper instead of mailing it back.

What is the Shelby County conveyance fee?

The Auditor's page prints the real estate transfer fee as $4 per $1,000 of sale price plus fifty cents for each parcel. It is paid at the Auditor's office, ahead of recording.

Can I search Shelby County deeds from home?

Partly. The Recorder's website carries an index from July 1, 1989 forward. Earlier books stay at the office, where staff help visitors search but do not take genealogy requests.

Stark County by the numbers

Where is the Stark County Recorder, and what can I find there?

The Stark County Recorder is on the first floor of the County Office Building at 110 Central Plaza South, Suite 170, Canton, OH 44702. Its posted window is 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays, with no weekend hours. It keeps the permanent record of deeds, mortgages and easements for all land in the county, and the office says those records are searchable on its website around the clock at no direct cost to users.

Stark County is the eighth most populous county in Ohio, with 374,853 residents counted in 2020. Canton is the county seat, and the other cities are Alliance, Canal Fulton, Louisville, Massillon and North Canton. The county covers 581 square miles in northeastern Ohio and was created in 1808.

Not every record sits here. The Recorder's page sends birth and death requests to the Stark County Health Department at 330-493-9904, marriage licenses to the Probate Court at 330-451-7755 and divorce records to the Family Court at 330-451-7415.

What does the Stark County Recorder charge?

The Recorder's fee page opens by saying the office does not set its prices: the Ohio Revised Code does, in section 317.32. The printed schedule lists $34 for a deed's first two pages and $8 for each more, with $4 for each cross reference. The statute also lets counties tack on a small preservation charge, and a county in western Ohio now lists $39 for the same service, so call the Canton office to confirm the figure before you mail a check.

Stark County Recorder price list as published
Document or servicePrinted charge
Deed or mortgage, first two pages$34.00

Payment can be cash, check, money order or a card, and cards carry a 2.75 percent convenience fee. Checks go to the Stark County Recorder, and altered checks are refused. A page-count chart on the fee page tabulates totals up to 90 pages.

What must the Stark County Auditor stamp before a deed is recorded?

The Auditor's real estate transfer department must endorse the deed first. The Auditor's page says a deed cannot be recorded until it carries the Auditor's stamp showing the conveyance form was filed correctly under Revised Code 319.202. The transfer line is 330-451-7333, with a second number at 330-451-7322.

  • Form DTE 100 states the value on a taxable sale, and DTE 100 (EX) states why a transfer is exempt.
  • Property already receiving the homestead or owner-occupied reduction adds its own statement of conveyance.
  • Stark's printed charge is $.004 of the price rounded up to the next hundred dollars, plus fifty cents per tax parcel.
  • Payment at that counter is by check or cash only.

The Auditor recommends that an attorney prepare the deed, though it allows owners to draft their own. Both options still need the items below.

What belongs on a Stark County deed?

The Auditor's transfer page lists what a deed has to carry:

  • The grantor's marital status, which supports the release of dower rights.
  • The grantee's name and the tax parcel numbers.
  • A current legal description that follows the county's conveyance standards.
  • A reference to the prior deed instrument.
  • The signature of the grantor and of the grantor's spouse if married, whether or not the spouse is on the title.
  • A completed notary clause with the notary's signature.

Deed types the Auditor names include administrator's, commissioner's, executor's, fiduciary, limited and special warranty, quit claim, sheriff's, survivorship, trustee and general warranty deeds. A sheriff's deed needs a description approval form, and a probate transfer arrives as a certificate of transfer or a judgment entry. A transfer on death designation affidavit, unlike most affidavits, does not require a certified death certificate.

When does Stark County require a visit to the tax map office?

The Auditor's page names combinations and splits as the cases that require a visit to the tax map office before the transfer. The same page offers a New Legal Description Application, a Tax Combine and Un-Combine Request and a Condominium Requirements checklist, and a sheriff's deed needs its own description approval form.

A seller of part of a lot or a corner of a farm should therefore call the Auditor's maps line at 330-451-7341 before a closing is scheduled, because a deed cannot be recorded until the Auditor has stamped it. The page also says the office no longer asks for a stamped copy of the previous deed, but the new document must cite it.

Which liens and special filings does the Stark County Recorder accept?

Besides deeds and mortgages, the fee page prices a list of filings that can touch a house sale. Title searchers look for these, and a seller with an unpaid lien should expect a payoff request at closing.

  • Federal tax liens and Department of Justice liens, each with a separate release filing.
  • Abstracts of judgment, which the fee page prices at five dollars.
  • State employment and workers' compensation liens, where the filing itself carries no fee.
  • UCC filings, priced per document and per name indexed.
  • Plats, priced by the square inch on the printed sizes of 11 by 17 up to 24 by 36.

Cross references at $4.00 each link a new document to an earlier recorded one.

Can I record or look up Stark County deeds online?

The Recorder says documents may be recorded electronically, with an E-Recording link on its website, and that the site lets anyone search the records free. Ohio law pushed this along: ORC 317.13 required every recorder to offer e-recording of conveyances and to put indexes and images online for instruments recorded since 1980 by June 30, 2026.

Copies cost nothing online. In the office, a self-serve copy is ten cents a page, and a staff-assisted copy is $2.00 a page. To get a certified copy by mail, send the Recorder a written request, the fee and a stamped self-addressed envelope.

Which Stark County school districts and towns appear in deed searches?

Seventeen public school districts serve Stark County, according to Wikipedia: Alliance, Canton City, Canton Local, Fairless, Jackson, Lake, Louisville, Marlington, Massillon, Minerva, North Canton, Northwest, Osnaburg, Perry, Plain, Sandy Valley and Tuslaw. The district name often appears on tax bills and sales listings, so buyers who search deeds by address see it early.

The 2020 census found 85.2 percent of residents living in urban areas and a median age of 42.2, and the county forms the Canton-Massillon metropolitan area within the larger Cleveland-Akron-Canton region. Stark County also borders eight counties: Portage, Mahoning, Columbiana, Carroll, Tuscarawas, Holmes, Wayne and Summit.

More questions about Stark County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the Stark County Recorder's address?

Suite 170 at 110 Central Plaza South, Canton, OH 44702, on the first floor of the County Office Building. Posted hours run 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays.

Is the Stark County recording fee really $34?

That is the amount on the county's published fee page for a deed's first two pages, with $8 for each added page. State law allows a surcharge of up to $5 per document, so ask the office to confirm the total before mailing.

Do I need the Auditor's stamp before recording in Stark County?

Yes. According to the Auditor's transfer page, recording waits for the Auditor's stamp, which shows the conveyance form was completed correctly. The Auditor accepts only a check or cash for the conveyance fee.

Can the Stark County Recorder take credit cards?

Yes, with a 2.75 percent convenience fee added. Cash, checks and money orders are also accepted, and checks should name the Stark County Recorder.

How do I get a certified copy of a recorded deed in Stark County?

Ask in person or mail a written request, the fee and a stamped self-addressed envelope. The published price is $2.00 a page for staff-made copies plus $1.00 to certify each document.

Who records deeds in Summit County

  • Summit County Fiscal Office - Recorder Division records deeds and mortgages.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Basic recording fee shown on page: $34.00 for first 2 pages, $8.00 each additional page; $20.00 non-compliant; $4.00 cross reference; conveyance fee $4.00 per $1000 rounded up to next $100; lot fee 50 cents. (Page shows pre-SB 94 $34 figure; other Ohio counties post $39 effective April 1, 2025.)
  • Document search available online; no e-recording page opened.

Fees

Selling in Summit County?

Summit County by the numbers

What does the Summit County Recorder Division do?

It records and preserves documents that touch real estate in Summit County. The Recorder Division sits inside the Fiscal Office, so the same elected Fiscal Officer who bills property tax also oversees recording. Deeds, mortgages and liens make up the core, and the division also keeps partnership papers, zoning amendments, military discharges, living wills and medical powers of attorney.

Anyone may view the records, with military discharges the one exception. Online search covers documents from 1988 forward, and an Index Book Archive Viewer reaches records from 1840 to 1988. The division says outright that it performs no title or property searches, which leaves that task to the buyer's title company. Staff post a turnaround of three to five working days.

Renovation of the county's Ohio Building in Akron sent Fiscal Office divisions to temporary quarters. Write recorder@summitoh.net or phone before you deliver paper to a counter.

How does a Summit County deed get from signature to the record?

A deed passes through the Fiscal Office's transfer desk first and the recording desk second. The sequence below follows the Fiscal Office's property transfer page and its recording guide.

  1. The grantor signs, and the signing is acknowledged before a notary or another listed official under R.C. 5301.01.
  2. Bring the deed and the conveyance fee statement, DTE Form 100, or the exemption statement, DTE Form 100 (EX), to the Property Transfer Department. It approves the legal description and the conveyance.
  3. Deliver by 3:30 in the afternoon if you want the transfer completed on the same business day.
  4. Take the approved deed to the Recorder Division, with recording fees on their own check.

The guide wants legible pages, typed names under every signature, the complete legal description on first recordings, citations to earlier recorded documents, a return address with a phone number, numbered exhibits and a stamped return envelope.

Several e-recording vendors work with the office: Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network.

What are the recording fees for a deed in Summit County?

Summit County recording and transfer fees as posted on the Fiscal Office fee page
ChargePosted amount
Standard recording$34.00 up to two pages, then $8.00 for each page beyond
Non-compliant filing$20.00 each
Cross-reference entry$4.00 apiece
Conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000 of price, with the price stepped up to the next $100
Lot fee50 cents for every lot named in the description, on exempt and non-exempt transfers alike
Certified copy$1.00 added per document

The base schedule is in R.C. 317.32. Read together, the statute splits the first two pages into a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fee, adds $4 and $4 for every later page, and allows a county to tack on a preservation surcharge of as much as $5. Summit's page lists $34 and $8 and shows no surcharge line, so confirm the exact total with the Recording Division first.

The division's FAQ prices a mailed copy of a deed at $4, with $1 more to certify it. The functions page lists $2 per page for copies. Military discharges go on record free.

Who pays the conveyance fee, and does Summit add a transfer tax?

The seller pays it. R.C. 319.202 has the grantee submit a value statement while the grantor covers the fee. For a sale, value means the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage balances and vendor's liens included. Gifts are measured by estimated open-market price, and knowingly misstating value is prohibited.

Ohio also lets counties adopt a real property transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02. Summit's fee page shows the conveyance fee and the lot fee, nothing more. Ask the Property Transfer Department whether any further charge reaches your deed.

A rental house carries one extra step: the auditor's endorsement tells the buyer to file rental information under R.C. 5323.02.

Which liens and releases can appear on a Summit County record?

Mortgages and liens that bear on title are filed with this division, which means a title search can surface them. The fee page sets prices for several types:

  • IRS lien: $5.00. IRS release: $3.00.
  • Workers' compensation lien and its release: no fee.
  • Unemployment lien: no fee. Its release: $4.00.
  • Plats: $0.05 per square inch, with posted sizes running from $40.00 for 11 by 17 inches to $86.40 for 24 by 36 inches.
  • Township zoning regulations: $50.00. Township zoning amendments: $20.00.

Uniform Commercial Code filings carry their own fees, and the page sends callers to 330-643-8143.

Ask your title company for the recording reference of anything it finds. The recording guide asks submitters to cite earlier documents by number, by book and page, or by recording date.

How does a recorded deed connect to the Summit County tax bill?

The deed decides whose name lands on the next bill, and the county handles the two jobs in the same office. A few details from the Fiscal Office pages matter around closing:

  • Bills show the legal owner's name, and a bill covers the prior year because Ohio collects real estate tax one year in arrears.
  • A change to the mailing address on a tax bill must come in writing from the taxpayer to the Fiscal Officer. Recording a deed does not replace that request.
  • The owner-occupancy reduction ends when the property transfers, so a buyer who will live there applies on their own.
  • The conveyance statement asks the seller whether the home currently receives a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction.

Have the title company check the tax balance with the Treasurer division ahead of recording, so any open amount gets paid at closing. The Summit tax certificate lien page says a lien sale is avoided by paying in full or entering a payment plan with the Delinquent Tax Department.

How do I fix a name or get a copy of a Summit County deed?

A recorded deed cannot be edited. The FAQ says a new deed must be prepared and recorded to change a name, and that only the person asking for the change or an attorney may prepare it. The new deed then goes back through the Property Transfer Department for the legal description and transfer before recording.

If you cannot find your own deed, request a copy by mail. Birth and death certificates are not kept here. Summit County Public Health issues them. The Veterans Service Commission helps with a lost DD 214 that was never recorded.

The office also mentions that a tax bill's mailing address changes only by written request from the taxpayer to the Fiscal Officer, which is separate from anything on the deed.

What should a seller know about Summit County itself?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table lists 538,376 residents for 2025, 250,438 housing units and a median household income of $71,622. Roughly two of every three homes are owned by their occupants (67.5 percent), the 2020 to 2024 median value of those homes is $208,700, and renters pay a median $1,026 a month.

Akron is the seat, and Wikipedia notes that the Fiscal Officer exercises the duties of auditor, treasurer and recorder. In a sale, the legal description check, the conveyance statement and the recording therefore all run through one county office.

More questions about Summit County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How long does recording take in Summit County?

The Recorder Division posts three to five working days. The Property Transfer Department can finish the transfer step the same business day when forms arrive by 3:30 p.m.

Is e-recording offered for Summit County deeds?

Yes. The Fiscal Office works with Simplifile, Corporation Service Company and eRecording Partners Network, and title companies commonly file that way.

Will the Recorder run a title search for me?

No. The division says it performs no title or property searches. Your title company or attorney handles that.

Who can prepare a replacement deed to change a name?

Only the person requesting the change or an attorney. The new deed is recorded after the Property Transfer Department approves it.

Which Summit County records cannot be viewed online?

Military discharges. Recorded documents from 1988 forward show on the website, and older index books from 1840 to 1988 open in the archive viewer.

What we confirmed on the official page

Trumbull County by the numbers

Where does a deed get recorded in Trumbull County, Ohio?

Deeds for land anywhere in Trumbull County are recorded at the Recorder's Office, 160 High Street NW, Warren, Ohio 44481. Doors are open weekdays, 8:30 a.m. through 4:30 p.m. New filings stop at 4:00 p.m. while the staff close out the day.

The recorder's own description of the job is to record, file and index papers that touch real estate, including deeds, mortgages, easements, leases, powers of attorney, plats and mechanic's liens. The index follows owner names rather than street addresses, so searching one person lists every parcel held. The county has images and data online for every record except military discharges, reaching back to 1795, the year of the first recordings in the county.

A seller does not usually deal with the recorder directly. Usually the title company walks the deed through the tax map office and auditor, then files it here. Knowing the sequence helps when a closing date is tight.

What does the Trumbull County Recorder charge to record a deed?

Fees went up April 1, 2025: the recorder now takes $39 for the opening two pages of most documents and $8 for each later page. Senate Bill 94 supplied the extra $5, a preservation surcharge layered over the base fees in Ohio Revised Code 317.32. A sample chart on the fee page reads like this:

Trumbull County Recorder fees printed on the county fee schedule
ItemFee
1 or 2 pages$39
3 pages$47
5 pages$63
10 pages$103
Marginal reference on a separate instrument$4 each
Document that misses layout standards$20 extra

Source: Trumbull County Recorder fee schedule.

Other charges from the same schedule and the recorder's FAQ:

  • Certified copy: $2 a page, plus $1 for the seal.
  • Copies made with staff help: $2 a page.
  • Plat recording: $0.10 per square inch, minimum $40.
  • Military records: no fee.
  • Cards: a 2.60 percent convenience fee applies to debit and credit payments.

Cash, checks, money orders and e-checks are also accepted. By mail, an underpayment or overpayment sends the package back unrecorded, and the office will not mail cash back, so send a check or money order.

What formatting mistakes add $20 to a Trumbull County filing?

Any document that falls short of the state formatting standard is recorded with a $20 surcharge, and the same charge applies automatically to e-filed documents that miss the mark. The recorder posts the checklist on its requirements page.

  • Ten-point type or bigger, on letter or legal paper.
  • Blue or black ink, no highlighter.
  • Three blank inches at the head of page one, which county staff use for their stamps.
  • An inch and a half of space across the top of later pages, and one inch along the edges.
  • Notary seals that print cleanly and do not overlap the embossed seal.
  • A readable printed name beneath any hard-to-read signature, and a line near the end naming who prepared the instrument.

The checklist skips plats, discharge papers, government-issued records, anything from a court or taxing authority, and papers signed before mid-2009.

How does a deed move through the Trumbull County offices?

A deed cannot go straight to the recorder. The county auditor's conveyance page says a deed filing must carry the required forms and a legible copy of the last deed of record, and it goes first to the Tax Map Office, then to the Auditor, and last to the Recorder. The auditor's conveyance room is upstairs in the Administration Building, phone 330-675-2420. Questions about legal descriptions go to the tax map department at 330-675-2473.

  • The Tax Map Office reviews the legal description and parcel split, if any.
  • The Auditor collects the conveyance fee and stamps the deed. Its posted price is $4.00 for every thousand dollars of value conveyed plus $0.50 per parcel, and an exempt conveyance pays just the parcel charge.
  • The Recorder files and indexes the deed after that.

Two checks are needed: one to the Auditor for conveyance fees, a second to the Recorder for recording. Mailed transfers are accepted at the 160 High Street NW address with a stamped return envelope, and the Auditor posts conveyance standards written with the county engineer. Counties may add a transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100 of value under section 322.02. Ask the staff in the conveyance room whether Trumbull County charges one on your deed.

The recorder tries to send originals back within 24 business hours, and most filings go out the same day. Deeds that must pass through other offices first can take longer. The office also takes eRecording through four partner vendors and accepts most documents, transfer documents included.

What will the Trumbull County Recorder not do for a seller?

Recorder staff may not run title searches under state law, so nobody there can certify that a parcel is clear. Employees also cannot draft or notarize a deed, choose a form or advise on one, and the office sells no blank forms. Attorneys and title companies handle those jobs.

The FAQ offers a few points worth knowing before listing a house:

  • A deed is binding even when unrecorded, but recording protects the new owner, because the public record would otherwise still show the former owner holding title and able to borrow against it.
  • A recorded deed cannot be edited. To add or remove a name, record a fresh deed. Errors in a recorded deed are a matter for an attorney.
  • A deed covers the land, so building a house later does not produce a new deed.
  • Re-recording is allowed only when the document itself states the reason, and costs the standard fee plus $4.

Torrens (registered land) filings were taken through June 1996 and are no longer accepted.

How are mortgage releases and liens handled in Trumbull County?

A mortgage is released when the lender records a satisfaction. The lender must start it. Some lenders mail the release to the borrower, who can carry the original to the recorder along with the fee and a stamped return envelope. After a payoff, ask the lender how the release will be filed, then check with the recorder that it landed.

Only the party that filed a lien can remove it, and the recorder does not report liens to credit bureaus or notify them when one is released. Mechanic's liens can be checked in the recorder's search, but judgment and other liens may sit with the Clerk of Courts or at the state level, which is why the recorder suggests hiring a title examiner. Deed restrictions and oil and gas interests also need an examiner's review.

What should a Trumbull County home seller know about the area?

Warren is both seat and largest city of Trumbull County, which fills a square block of Ohio's far northeast corner. It was organized on July 10, 1800 and named for the Connecticut governor Jonathan Trumbull, because the land came out of the Connecticut Western Reserve. At 637 square miles it is described by Wikipedia as roughly square, the only square county in Ohio. Cities include Cortland, Girard, Hubbard, Niles and Warren, with villages such as Lordstown and Newton Falls. Interstate 80 and US 422 cross the county.

The Census Bureau reports these figures:

  • Estimated population in 2025: 198,972, compared with 201,977 in the 2020 count.
  • Typical owned home, valued at $141,800 in the 2020 to 2024 survey.
  • Homeowners make up 71.3 percent of 86,550 households.
  • Median gross rent: $797 a month.
  • Median household income: $56,435.
  • Share of residents age 65 or older: 24.3 percent.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 112.

Before you list, gather your last recorded deed and any lien releases, which saves a second trip through the county offices.

More questions about Trumbull County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the Trumbull County fee for filing a deed?

A deed of one or two pages is $39 at the Warren office, and every page beyond that adds $8. A reference to an earlier recorded paper adds $4, and a deed that ignores the layout checklist picks up a $20 surcharge. The auditor's conveyance fee is a separate check.

Does Trumbull County record deeds by mail?

Yes, mailing works. The package needs a deed already cleared by the tax map office and the Auditor, a check for the precise sum, and a return envelope with postage. Wrong amounts come back unrecorded.

Can the Trumbull County Recorder do a title search for me?

No. State law prohibits the office from doing real estate title searches. Title companies and attorneys search the records and back the result with title insurance. You can search the county's online index yourself.

How long does Trumbull County take to return a recorded deed?

Most documents go out the same day. The recorder aims to return originals within 24 business hours, and deeds that must clear other offices first may take a little longer. Originals go back to whoever submitted them.

Is a deed valid if I never record it in Trumbull County?

A deed binds the parties even when unrecorded, but the recorder advises recording it. Until it is on record, the public index still shows the former owner, who could take out a mortgage or have a judgment attach to the property.

Tuscarawas County by the numbers

Who records a deed in Tuscarawas County, Ohio?

The Tuscarawas County Recorder holds the land records for every parcel in the county, which has New Philadelphia as its seat. The office's duties page says it makes a permanent record of each document that conveys or encumbers land, files it in archival form and keeps it open to the public. Fees collected go into the county general fund.

Indexing is the reason sellers should care. The index lets a title searcher string the filings into a chain of title, showing past owners and any debt that still rides with the land. A buyer's title agent will run that search before closing, so a clean record speeds a sale.

The county also holds registered land, called Torrens land, and the recorder handles those certificates of title. Most house sales involve ordinary deeds, but a parcel with an older registered certificate needs extra attention from the title company.

What does the Tuscarawas County Recorder charge?

The county posts the charge in a single line at the top of its recorder page, with the per-page rate and the notation rate side by side. The statute behind those numbers is Ohio Revised Code 317.32, where each fee splits into a base amount and a housing trust fund amount, with an optional preservation surcharge on top.

Tuscarawas County Recorder fees as listed on the county recorder page
ChargeAmount
First two pages of a document$39
Each additional page$8
Each marginal notation$4
Non-conforming document$20 extra

Source: Tuscarawas County Recorder.

Certified copies, plats and other services carry their own statutory rates, so ask the office what applies.

What kinds of documents does the Tuscarawas County Recorder file?

The recorder's page groups its filings by type. For someone selling a house, these categories matter most:

  • Deeds of every kind: warranty, survivorship, quit claim and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgage papers: releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and waivers of priority.
  • Land contracts, easements and leases, along with certificates of transfer and affidavits.
  • Plats and condominium drawings.
  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement, plus federal, personal-property and workers' compensation liens.
  • Military discharges, powers of attorney and trust records.

The page closes with a fair housing notice: under federal law, a deed provision restricting the sale, rental or use of a dwelling on protected grounds is void and unenforceable.

How do you get a Tuscarawas County deed approved before recording?

A deed in this county is checked by the auditor's side of the courthouse before the recorder sees it. Start at the auditor's office in the Courthouse Annex, 125 E. High Avenue, New Philadelphia, where posted hours are weekdays from 8:00 to 4:30. The auditor's page has a Deed Conveyance and Transfers section with a step-by-step procedure, a conveyance requirements form and a separate procedure for mineral deeds.

  • The GIS and Map Office reviews the deed against the tax maps. It accepts deeds for pre-approval by email at the address on the auditor's GIS page, with the surface Conveyance Form, the Mineral Conveyance Form, or both.
  • The auditor's office completes the transfer and collects the conveyance and transfer fees.
  • The Recorder's fees are paid when the deed is filed.

Conveyance fees and the per-parcel transfer charge are set by the auditor, so ask the auditor's deed transfer staff for the current rates before you write the check. A county may also adopt a transfer tax under section 322.02, limited to 30 cents on each $100 of value. The buyer files the value statement required by section 319.202, while the conveyance fee falls on the seller.

Can you record electronically in Tuscarawas County?

Yes. Since January 20, 2026 the recorder has accepted all document types by eRecording. Conveyance documents have an extra step: the submitter uploads the pre-approval forms and supporting papers first, starting with the document type, and only then sends the conveyance itself.

The county lists five approved eRecording providers: CSC, Hopdox, Indecomm Global Services, ERecording Partners Network and Simplifile. Closing agents normally hold the accounts, so a seller typically leaves the electronic filing to the title company or attorney.

Records can be searched through the county's cloud search, and the recorder posts instructions for registering an account and setting up a property alert. Ask the office how an alert works before relying on it to watch your parcel. The page also links two search tools: a cloud search site with quick and advanced modes, and a separate county index site, so a seller can compare what each shows for the parcel.

What are the county's size and history for a seller to know?

Tuscarawas County sits in northeastern Ohio with an area of about 571 square miles. According to Wikipedia, it was formed from Muskingum County in 1808, and New Philadelphia, founded the same year, is the seat and largest city. Dover and Uhrichsville are the other two cities. The Moravian mission of Schoenbrunn was founded near New Philadelphia in 1772, and the Ohio and Erie Canal came through in 1829 and 1830.

The county also has a visible Amish and Mennonite community, counted at 3,496 people or 3.7 percent of the 2020 population. For a rural parcel, ask the title company to check easements and any recorded survey.

What can a seller get from the Tuscarawas County GIS and Map Office?

The GIS and Map Office keeps the county tax parcel maps and sells printed copies. Its page lists a first county road map free and $1 for each additional one, a plat book of all 22 townships for $25, and tax maps priced by size:

  • 8.5 by 11 inches: $0.50 without a photo, $1 with one.
  • 11 by 17 inches: $1 without a photo, $2 with one.
  • 18 by 24 inches: $2 without a photo, $4 with one.
  • 24 by 36 inches: $4 without a photo, $6 with one.
  • 36 by 48 inches: $6 without a photo, $8 with one.

Surveys are stored by location and old tax map page. The office says surveys from 2014 on are online through the parcel viewer, and older ones still sit in drawers in the map office, with scanning going on as time allows. If a buyer asks for a survey of your lot, start there before paying for a new one.

The $20 non-conforming charge on the recorder's page refers to the state formatting standard in section 317.114, which sets type size, margins and ink color. Have the closing attorney confirm the deed meets it before filing.

What do Census figures show for Tuscarawas County homes?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page lists the following, for the 2020 to 2024 survey period unless noted.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $185,400.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 68.9 percent, among 38,492 households.
  • Median gross rent: $908 a month.
  • Median household income: $65,044.
  • Residents age 65 or older: 22.2 percent.
  • July 2025 population estimate: 92,373, which is 1.0 percent under the 2020 base.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 69.

Before pricing the house, ask the auditor for the parcel's county value and the title company for the last recorded deed.

More questions about Tuscarawas County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What does recording a Tuscarawas County deed cost?

Expect $39 for pages one and two and $8 for every page beyond them. A marginal notation adds $4, and a deed that fails the formatting standard adds $20. Whatever the auditor charges for the conveyance is billed on its own.

Do I need pre-approval before recording a Tuscarawas County deed?

Yes. Deeds are approved by the GIS and Map Office and the auditor before the recorder files them. The map office takes deeds by email for pre-approval, and mineral conveyances use their own form and procedure.

Can I record a deed electronically in Tuscarawas County?

Yes. The recorder accepts every document type through eRecording as of January 20, 2026. Conveyance documents must upload the pre-approval forms and supporting papers before the deed is submitted.

Where is the Tuscarawas County Auditor's deed desk?

The Auditor's office is in the Courthouse Annex at 125 E. High Avenue in New Philadelphia, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and its website has a Deed Conveyance and Transfers page.

Does the Tuscarawas County Recorder handle registered land?

Yes. The office lists certificates of title to registered (Torrens) land among its filings. If a parcel carries one, tell your title company early so it can examine the registered record.

Selling in Union County?
