Union County by the numbers

Where is the Union County Recorder's Office in Marysville?

The Union County Recorder works from the County Office Building at 233 West Sixth Street, Marysville, Ohio 43040. Hours run Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with the front desk at 937-645-3032. Its own page calls it the official land records office for real estate in the county.

Indexing is the core task. Each document is indexed so a searcher can trace a chain of title and see any debt that still attaches to the land. Images and indexes are online from 1995 forward, and the office has recently added grantor and grantee deed indexes from 1875 to 1994, mortgage indexes from 1944 to 1994 and miscellaneous indexes from 1960 to 1994. For older papers that are not digitized, staff can send copies by email, fax or mail.

The auditor and treasurer share the building, so a deed, a tax question and a filing can often be handled in one trip.

What does the Union County Recorder charge in fees?

Fees rose by $5 on January 1, 2025, after Senate Bill 94 allowed a document preservation surcharge under Ohio Revised Code 317.32. The county's chart groups deeds, mortgages, affidavits, easements, leases, land contracts and powers of attorney under one rate: $39 up front, then $8 a page.

Union County Recorder fees from the county fee schedule
ServiceFee
Deed, mortgage or similar document, first two pages$39
Each added page$8
Marginal reference on a separate instrument$4 each, on top of the recording fee
Copy, per page$2
Certified copy$1 per document added to the copy fee
Document that is not conforming$20
Veterans' discharge papersNo fee

Source: Union County Recorder fee schedule.

The county's one-to-ten page chart prints $39 for one or two pages, $47 for three, $63 for five and $103 for ten. Plats and condominium drawings run $0.10 per square inch, on sheets sized 18 by 24 inches. Zoning resolutions are $50 and zoning amendments $20.

How does a Union County deed get to the recorder?

By mail, the recorder will file a conveyance only if the Auditor's stamp is already on it. That sets the order here: Auditor first, Recorder second.

  • The buyer or a representative submits the value statement that section 319.202 requires, on the state's DTE 100 form. An exempt transfer uses the exemption statement, DTE 100EX.
  • The Auditor collects the conveyance fee, posted at $4 per $1,000 of value.
  • The Auditor stamps the deed, and the Recorder files it.

The Auditor, Engineer and Recorder adopted a shared set of Real Estate Conveyance Standards on May 1, 2014, after public hearings in February and March of that year. Those standards are what all three offices apply to a deed, so have the attorney or title company check a draft against them. Separately, section 322.02 lets a county adopt a transfer tax, so confirm with the Auditor what applies.

The fee schedule also warns that a document showing a Social Security number will be refused unless an affidavit is attached (section 317.082), so scan the draft before it goes in.

What layout rules apply to papers filed in Union County?

The county's fee schedule treats a document that misses the state standard in section 317.114 as non-conforming and adds $20. It spells out four points:

  • Print no smaller than 10 point.
  • Three inches left blank at the top of page one.
  • A 1 inch margin on each side and the bottom of every page.
  • One and a half inches of space above the text on later pages.

Have the closing agent check a draft against those four points, since the surcharge applies to each filing that misses them.

Can Union County records be filed or watched online?

Yes, in part. As of July 15, 2024 the office accepts eRecorded filings that are not conveyances. The announcement covers non-conveyance filings, so ask the office how a deed should be submitted.

Residents can also sign up for a free fraud alert service. The recorder describes it as a notification service meant to help combat real estate fraud, and the Recorder page links to the sign-up details.

What should you bring to the Union County Recorder?

A short checklist keeps a filing from being turned away at the counter at 233 West Sixth Street.

  • The original signed deed, already stamped by the Auditor if it conveys land.
  • A check or other payment for the recording fee on the county chart, which depends on page count.
  • A draft that has been scanned for Social Security numbers.
  • The marginal references, if the paper releases or assigns an earlier recorded mortgage.

Staff can explain how the records are arranged, though a title search is a job for an attorney or title company. Call 937-645-3032 before you drive over if a paper is unusual.

Which liens and releases show up in Union County records?

The fee schedule doubles as a list of the lien types that can attach to a property, which is useful when a title search turns something up. Federal tax liens and federal court judgment abstracts cost $5 to file, and a release of either costs $3. Several state liens are filed with no fee, including workers' compensation liens, Ohio EPA liens, franchise tax liens, personal property tax liens and unemployment compensation liens. A release, partial release or discharge of a franchise tax, personal property tax, tangible or intangible tax, or unemployment compensation lien costs $4.

Fixture-type UCC filings tied to land run $12, plus $4 per indexed name. Marginal references, the $4 charge that links a release or assignment to the original recorded mortgage, are billed on top of the normal recording fee. If you paid off a mortgage, check that the lender actually filed the release. An unreleased mortgage keeps appearing in the title search.

What is Union County like for a house seller?

Union County covers 437 square miles in central Ohio, with Marysville as county seat and largest city. Wikipedia reports that the county took shape in 1820 from pieces of Franklin, Delaware, Madison and Logan counties, hence the name, and that the courthouse still in use was dedicated January 27, 1883. Part of Dublin and part of Plain City lie inside the county, and Richwood, Milford Center, Magnetic Springs and Unionville Center are villages. US 33 runs through Marysville, and Honda's Marysville Auto Plant and Scotts Miracle-Gro are among the large employers.

School districts named for the county include Marysville Exempted Village, Fairbanks, North Union, Triad, Jonathan Alder, Buckeye Valley, Elgin, Benjamin Logan and Dublin City.

The Census Bureau shows a fast-growing market:

  • Population estimate for 2025: 73,446, up 17.0 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Typical owned home value, 2020 to 2024: $344,900.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 79.2 percent among 24,232 households.
  • Median gross rent: $1,247 a month.
  • Median household income: $112,322.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 968.

For a home in a platted subdivision, have the title company pull the plat and recorded restrictions together with the deed.

More questions about Union County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the fee to record a deed in Union County, Ohio?

Two pages of deed cost $39, and each page past two adds $8. Every marginal reference is another $4, and a deed that fails the formatting standard is hit with $20. The Auditor's conveyance fee is a different payment.

Does the Union County Recorder accept deeds by mail?

Only when the Auditor's conveyance stamp is already affixed. The fee schedule spells this out, so take the deed to the Auditor first and mail the stamped original with the right payment.

What are the Union County Recorder's office hours?

Staff take walk-ins Monday to Friday between 7:30 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., at 233 West Sixth Street in Marysville. Call 937-645-3032 with questions.

Can I eRecord a deed in Union County?

The recorder began accepting eRecorded non-conveyance filings on July 15, 2024. For a deed, ask the office how to submit, since the Auditor's conveyance stamp has to be on it first.

What does the Union County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

On its conveyance standards page, the county shows a conveyance fee of $4 for each thousand dollars of value. Ask the Auditor's office about any per-parcel charge and any local transfer tax.

Where does a Vinton County deed get recorded?

At the courthouse in McArthur, 100 East Main Street, OH 45651. The recorder answers at 740-596-4314 from 8:30 am to 4:00 pm on weekdays, according to the county's directory of offices.

Besides deeds and mortgages, the counter takes oil and gas leases, military discharge papers, and tax, unemployment and workers compensation liens. Staff help where they can, yet they do not run searches, assist with wording or sell blank forms. Anyone who needs a deed written should line up a title company or lawyer before the trip.

What is it like to sell a house in Vinton County?

Vinton County lies in the Hocking Hills region of southeastern Ohio. It was carved out in 1850 from parts of Ross, Gallia, Jackson, Hocking and Athens counties, spans 414 square miles and has about 13,000 people. McArthur, the seat since 1815, sits at the crossing of State Route 93 and U.S. 50.

The county has no cities and, by its own account, only one traffic light. Four villages hold the population centers, and each council meets monthly (McArthur on the third Wednesday, Hamden and Wilkesville on the second Wednesday, Zaleski on the first Tuesday): McArthur (1,701 in the 2010 census), Hamden (879), Zaleski (278) and Wilkesville (149). Twelve townships cover the rest of the map: Brown, Clinton, Eagle, Elk, Harrison, Jackson, Knox, Madison, Richland, Swan, Vinton and Wilkesville. Over eighty percent of the land is wooded, and state parks, forests and part of the Wayne National Forest bring in hikers, boaters and hunters.

The school district runs Vinton County High School on U.S. 50 and the middle school on Locker Plant Road, both in McArthur, with elementary schools in Hamden (South) and Allensville (West). The county's utility list names the McArthur Water Department and several water companies, along with AEP, Buckeye Rural Electric and Columbia Gas. For owners fixing up a house before a sale, the Development Department at 740-596-3529 says income-eligible residents can ask about loans or grants for emergency repairs, septic systems or potable water.

How do you look up a recorded deed in Vinton County?

The office holds deed books and indexes from 1850 through December 31, 1985. From January 1, 1986 on, the index is searchable on the county's Ava site, with names and index data but no images.

For new filings the recorder's page says the office is fully online for transfer documents and lists ePN (888-325-3365) and CSC (866-652-0111) as e-recording routes. Property owners can also enroll in a free fraud alert at propertyfraudalert.com or 1-800-728-3858, which pings them when something is filed against their parcel.

What does it cost to record in Vinton County?

Ohio's section 317.32 prices the opening two pages of an instrument at $34, split into two $17 halves, and each extra page at $8, split $4 and $4. Counties may layer on a preservation charge, though the statute caps it at $5. The Vinton County recorder has posted a revised fee schedule and guidelines effective January 1, 2025 through the Ohio Recorders Association, so confirm the total with the office before sending a check.

  • Zoning resolutions: $25 plus $25.
  • Zoning amendments: $10 plus $10.
  • A certified copy: $1 plus $1 per page, and the seal costs 50 cents plus 50 cents.

Which Vinton County offices does a sale touch?

Every office a seller needs sits at the same address, so one morning can cover a long list. The table uses the numbers printed on county pages.

Vinton County courthouse offices in a home sale (county directory and auditor and treasurer pages)
OfficeRole in a salePhone
EngineerApproves deed and land contract descriptions, keeps tax maps740-790-7014
AuditorStatement of value, conveyance fee, transfers on the tax list740-790-7007
RecorderRecords the deed or mortgage740-596-4314
TreasurerCollects property tax, confirms what is owed740-790-7045
Clerk of CourtsCourt filings, titles and passports740-596-3001

The county engineer, according to the county's directory, approves every deed and land contract description. Splitting a rural tract is common in this county, so that stop comes first, and the auditor's endorsement comes before the recorder will accept the deed.

What does the Vinton County auditor charge on a sale?

On its conveyance fee page the auditor publishes a single rate of $4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price, for houses and manufactured homes both. The grantor settles it when the deed is handed to the auditor. State law, in 319.54 and 322.02, allows a $1 per $1,000 fee plus an optional county tax of up to thirty cents per hundred dollars.

The same office keeps the valuation side of the file. Its triennial update page explains that state law expects values to land between 90 and 110 percent of market, measured against sales from the preceding three years, and the letter on that page warned owners to expect a notable jump in value after the last update. Owners who think a value is too high can bring a complaint to the Board of Revision, where the auditor serves as secretary beside the treasurer and the president of the commissioners. Complaints must reach the auditor on or before March 31 each year.

The homestead page describes a credit that shields up to $26,200 of market value from local taxes for qualifying seniors and permanently disabled owners, and for 2025 payable in 2026 it required new applicants to have adjusted income under $40,000.

Which Vinton County transfers owe no conveyance fee?

The statute carves out many cases, and a filing in one of them gives the reason instead of a price. These cases are the likeliest in a family sale:

  • A gift between spouses or from a parent to a child.
  • A deed that fixes an error in an earlier recorded deed.
  • A trust deed the maker can revoke.
  • Property split among heirs for no payment.
  • A transfer to a nonprofit charity without payment.
  • An easement valued at $1,000 or less.

How are Vinton County property taxes handled around a closing?

The treasurer's page warns of a 5 percent penalty on second-half bills left unpaid past the closing date and 10 percent ten days after, citing ORC 323.121. Second-half 2026 real estate and manufactured home tax was due July 30. Accepted payment types are check, money order, cash and credit card, with 2.75 percent added on cards. A labeled drop box stands in the alley behind the courthouse and the former sheriff's office, and cash does not belong in it.

The 2026 rate sheet for tax year 2025 divides the county into 18 taxing districts. Its residential and agricultural column shows 34.280207 for Brown-Vinton, 43.440994 for the Hamden corporation, 43.551322 for Zaleski and 48.162418 for the McArthur corporation, expressed per thousand dollars of valuation. Village parcels carry a higher total than township parcels.

If a bill has not arrived, call the treasurer at 740-790-7045, because a title company needs the true balance before closing.

More questions about Vinton County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the phone number for the Vinton County recorder?

The number is 740-596-4314. Weekday counter hours are 8:30 am to 4:00 pm, in the courthouse at 100 East Main Street, McArthur.

Can a deed be e-recorded in Vinton County?

Yes. The recorder says it accepts transfer documents electronically and names ePN and CSC as e-recording partners. Paper still goes to the courthouse counter.

How much is the Vinton County conveyance fee?

The auditor's page says $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price. It covers both house and manufactured home sales, and the seller pays at the auditor's office ahead of recording.

Will the Vinton County recorder help draft a deed?

No. The recorder's page says staff do not search records, help prepare a document or provide recording forms. A title company or attorney should handle the drafting.

How do I get an alert if a document is filed on my Vinton County property?

Enroll in the free fraud alert, either online at propertyfraudalert.com or by phone at 1-800-728-3858. The recorder's page says the service comes with its current recording provider.

Warren County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Warren County, Ohio?

Warren County deeds go to the recorder at 406 Justice Drive, Lebanon, OH 45036, the same Justice Drive campus that houses the auditor. The office phone is 513-695-1382 or 513-695-1383, and the fax line is 513-695-2949.

Checks are made payable to the Warren County Recorder. The counter wants the precise amount and sends back any short payment without recording it, and it suggests that frequent filers open an escrow account so an over or under payment does not hold up a same-day recording. Typical turnaround on a filing is 24 hours.

What kind of county is Warren County for a home seller?

Warren County sits in southwestern Ohio and is part of the Cincinnati metropolitan area. Lebanon is the seat and Mason is the most populous city. The county was created on May 1, 1803 out of Hamilton County, covers about 407 square miles, and is shaped like a rough square roughly twenty miles on a side.

The 2020 census counted 242,337 residents, with 77.2 percent of occupied homes owner-occupied among 93,276 housing units. The Little Miami River zigzags through the county, the Great Miami touches its northwest corner, and Caesar Creek Lake sits in Massie Township. Ten school districts serve the county: Carlisle, Clinton-Massie, Franklin, Kings, Lebanon, Little Miami, Loveland, Mason, Springboro and Wayne, along with the Warren County Career Center. The county's list of local governments names sixteen municipalities, including Lebanon, Mason, Springboro, Franklin, Monroe, Carlisle, Waynesville and Loveland, along with eleven townships.

County government is concentrated in Lebanon. The second courthouse went up in 1835 at East and Silver Streets and was renovated in 1998 for county offices, while the Justice Center, the jail, the sheriff and the juvenile and probate court sit on Justice Drive. A 100,000 square foot administration building opened there in 2001.

What does the Warren County recorder charge to record?

The recorder's fee page carries a schedule dated October 17, 2019, which tracks the amounts set in Revised Code 317.32.

Selected Warren County recording fees (Warren County Recorder fee schedule)
ItemFee
First two pages$34.00
Each additional page$8.00
Copies made by staff$2.00
Subdivision plat, 24 by 36 inches$86.40 per page
Federal lien$5.00
Federal release$3.00
Zoning resolution$50.00
Zoning amendment$20.00
Financing statement (real estate only)$12.00
Each name indexed on a financing statement$4.00

The recorder's notice says the office does not charge the optional $5 digital preservation fee. If a filer sends the extra $5 anyway, the office keeps it instead of rejecting the paper for incorrect fees. Marginal notations for indexing earlier instruments also carry no charge. Members of the public who copy documents themselves pay 25 cents per page.

How do you search Warren County land records online?

Most documents have been online since April 20, 2016, and the recorder reports that all deeds are indexed and viewable back to 1797. The search runs through a land records page that works best with the parcel number. The 10-digit parcel number appears in the upper left corner of an address or name search on the auditor's property site.

To save a copy, scroll to the bottom of the open document, click the print icon and use the PDF that opens. The recorder's page adds that more than 5 million documents have been recorded in the county, and staff will help by phone at 513-695-1382.

  • E-recording works for every document type except plats.
  • Every land record must include a legal description.
  • A transfer document that needs to be re-recorded must be redone with new notarized signatures, a rule shared by the recorder and the auditor.
  • A free property fraud alert sends an email, text or phone message when a document is filed on a parcel you own. People without a computer can sign up by calling the office.

What does the Warren County auditor require before a deed reaches the recorder?

Ohio makes the auditor transfer the deed first, and the Warren County auditor's transfer page lists what must be in order. Missing any item sends the deed back.

  • A properly completed Statement of Value and Receipt (DTE Form 100), or a Statement of Reason for Exemption (DTE Form 100 EX), plus the fees payable to the Warren County Auditor.
  • A grantor name that matches the way the grantor took title in the prior deed.
  • A reference to the previous deed of record, written on the new deed.
  • Approval and initials from the map department before the deed is presented to the auditor.
  • Form DTE 102 when the parcel is, or last year was, in the CAUV farm program.
  • The grantor's signature, notarized.

Fees listed on that page: $1.00 per thousand dollars of price as the mandatory state conveyance fee, $2.00 per thousand as the county's transfer tax, for a combined $3.00 per thousand, with leftover pennies bumped up to the next dime, plus $0.50 per parcel for the transfer itself. The county commissioners adopted the $2.00 levy, which the page labels permissive.

Which Warren County transfers are exempt from the conveyance fee?

An exempt transfer uses form 100 EX, where the grantee checks one reason from a lettered list on the back. Reasons (b), (g) and (m) need a notarized affidavit explaining the facts, since the auditor wants to know why no money changed hands.

Under section 319.54 the exempt categories include:

  • Transfers to or from governments and their agencies.
  • Deeds that exist only to secure or release a debt.
  • Confirmation and correction deeds.
  • Gifts between spouses and between parents and children.
  • Sales for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • Deeds that put property into, or take it out of, a trust the maker can revoke.
  • Transfers among heirs when no consideration is paid.

What does the Warren County recorder do after closing?

The recorder's job is to index each document so a title examiner can trace the chain of ownership and see any debt against the parcel. Recording right after closing puts the new deed in that chain, and the recorder's own description of its work says the permanent record is what makes it possible to buy land with a clear title.

The auditor's list above also requires the grantor's signature on every Ohio deed, with a notary's certificate. Warren County treats the signature and acknowledgment as a precondition and will not take the deed without them.

What does the Warren County recorder keep, and what is handled elsewhere?

The recorder answers the questions on its FAQ page plainly: the county uses tract (geographical) indexing, has no registered land (Torrens) system, does not sell blank forms, and records military discharge papers (DD214). A mailed filing has to include return postage or a prepaid envelope.

People often arrive at this office for papers it does not hold. Vital records and court files sit with other departments, and the recorder's page gives these numbers:

  • Birth and death records: 513-695-1220.
  • Marriage licenses: 513-695-1183.
  • Divorce records: 513-695-1120.

Who collects Warren County property tax on a home being sold?

The county treasurer, whose office hours run Monday through Friday from 7:30 am to 4:30 pm. Online payment goes through the county's myWarrenCountyOhio portal, and the pay-by-phone number is 513-496-2931. The treasurer's page showed February 25, 2026 and August 12, 2026 as the 2025 tax year deadlines, the later one extended after the inflation cap credit in House Bill 186 held up the second-half bills.

A seller who has not paid, or whose mortgage servicer pays from escrow, should confirm the balance before closing day so the payoff and the deed fees can be settled together.

More questions about Warren County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How do I reach the Warren County recorder?

Call 513-695-1382 or 513-695-1383, or write to 406 Justice Drive, Lebanon, OH 45036. The recorder's page lists fax at 513-695-2949 and says documents typically turn around in about a day.

What is the Warren County fee to record a deed?

Its schedule lists $34.00 for the opening two pages and $8.00 per page beyond that. The schedule carries an October 17, 2019 date, and the office says it does not collect the optional $5 preservation fee.

Does Warren County accept e-recording?

Yes, for every document type except plats. The recorder's page links to the e-recording details, and paper filings still go to the counter at 406 Justice Drive with exact fees.

What happens if my check for Warren County recording is the wrong amount?

The document comes back unrecorded. The recorder requires exact fees and returns shortages without recording, and it recommends an escrow account for filers who want over or under payments handled the same day.

How much is the Warren County transfer fee on a house sale?

The auditor's page prints $1.00 per thousand dollars as the mandatory conveyance fee plus $2.00 per thousand in county transfer tax, a combined $3.00 per thousand, and $0.50 per parcel to transfer it. The grantor pays these to the auditor before recording.

Washington County by the numbers

Where is the Washington County recorder's office?

The Washington County recorder works from the courthouse at 205 Putnam Street, Marietta, OH 45750. Call 740-373-6623, extension 2223 or 2225, or fax 740-373-9643. Counter hours are 8:00 am to 4:30 pm, Monday to Friday, with legal holidays excluded.

Every document that conveys or burdens land in the county goes into the recorder's permanent archive, and the filing fees go to the county's general fund. A deed for any Washington County parcel, whether the owner lives in Marietta or in Belpre, Beverly or Waterford, ends up at this counter or in its e-recording queue.

What is Washington County like for a home seller?

Washington County is the oldest county in Ohio, proclaimed on July 27, 1788 with settlement at Marietta beginning on April 7 of that year. Its 640 square miles rank fifth among Ohio counties by land area, and the Ohio River forms the southern and eastern line. The Muskingum River, the Little Muskingum, Duck Creek and the Little Hocking River all run to the Ohio from inside the county.

Marietta serves as seat and largest city. Marietta College, Washington State College of Ohio and the county career center are all there. The present courthouse dates from 1901. Settlement began when a New England group, the Ohio Company, bought land on the Ohio and Muskingum Rivers, and Fort Harmar at the confluence shaped that choice. Early outposts included Belpre downriver and Beverly up the Muskingum.

Census 2020 shows 27,987 homes and apartments in the county, about three of every four occupied homes lived in by their owners, and a majority of residents outside urban areas. River-valley houses in older neighborhoods and rural parcels outside town call for different paperwork, which is why the courthouse offices below matter.

Which Washington County office does what in a sale?

The auditor and recorder share the courthouse at 205 Putnam Street and the 740-373-6623 main line, which lets a seller finish two stops in one visit. The extensions below come from the auditor's website and the recorder's page.

Washington County courthouse extensions for deed-related tasks (county auditor and recorder pages)
TaskOfficeExtension
Real estate transfersAuditor2124
Property appraisal valueAuditor2141
Report new construction or demolitionAuditor2141
Homestead exemptionsAuditor2123
Tax mapAuditor2161
Recording a deed or mortgageRecorder2223 or 2225

The auditor's site also posts sales reports, and the auditor's counter keeps the same weekday hours as the recorder, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

How does the Washington County recorder take documents?

Paper goes to the counter, and electronic filing runs through approved vendors. The recorder's page names Corporation Service Company at 866-652-0111 and eRecording Partners Network at 888-325-3365. Simplifile is also listed, with a note that it cannot be used for deeds.

The county's FAQ gives a document turnaround of three days. It also spells out how payment errors are handled: filings that arrive under the correct fee are returned, and filings over by $5.00 or more are usually returned too, while an overage under $5.00 is sent back in cash. Mailing the exact amount avoids the delay.

For searching, the recorder's page links to an online records search and a second cloud-based search. The FAQ also lists uslandrecords.com as a no-charge search link.

What fees does Ohio set for recording in Washington County?

Ohio's section 317.32 builds each charge from two equal halves. The opening two pages cost $17 and $17, later pages cost $4 and $4 apiece, and a preservation surcharge is allowed up to $5. Ask the recorder which surcharge figure Washington County applies, since the statute sets only the cap.

  • A certified copy is $1 plus $1 a page, with the seal at 50 cents plus 50 cents.
  • Plats and maps are charged by the square inch, with a $20 plus $20 minimum.
  • Declarations under the living will and health care power of attorney statutes run $17 to $20 plus the same range again.
  • County land reutilization corporations are exempt from recorder fees.

What does the Washington County auditor charge on a transfer?

The auditor's FAQ states the Washington County conveyance fee as $.40 per $100 of value. That rate fits the statute's two layers, ten cents per hundred under section 319.54 and up to thirty cents more where commissioners adopted a tax under section 322.02. The auditor's website also has a conveyance calculator, and extension 2124 handles real estate transfers.

Transfers that fall into an exempt class pay nothing, though the paperwork still names the class. The cases that arise most in family sales:

  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or from a parent to a child.
  • A deed that corrects an earlier one.
  • A transfer made only as security for a loan.
  • A distribution among heirs where no money is paid.
  • A deed placing the house in a trust the owner can revoke.

The auditor's homestead page lists DTE Form 101, a Statement of Conveyance of Homestead Property, for sales of a home that carries the homestead reduction.

How does Washington County value and bill a home for tax?

By the auditor's account, every parcel is revalued at market once in six years, and the Ohio Tax Commissioner typically orders a statistical adjustment three years later using actual county sales. Property appraisal questions go to extension 2141, and the website has a tax estimator and a delinquency report.

Disputes over value go to the county Board of Revision, which the auditor's FAQ describes as a county commissioner, the treasurer and the auditor sitting together. The complaint form is due by March 31, and the hearings usually fall in April and May. Bring an appraisal report or current sales of similar houses in your neighborhood.

The auditor's pages describe the relief programs that follow a house from seller to buyer in practice:

  • Homestead for seniors 65 and over and permanently and totally disabled owners, using form DTE 105A. The exemptions page says it shields $25,000 of market value, and disabled veterans can shield $50,000.
  • The owner occupancy reduction of 2 1/2 percent for the home you own and live in, applied for between January 1 and December 31 at no cost.
  • CAUV farm value for at least 10 acres of crops, animals or commercial timber, with a one-time $25 filing fee and a yearly renewal. Missing a renewal costs the savings and brings a payback of the previous three years.

The treasurer, at the same courthouse, collects real estate and manufactured home tax. Call 740-373-6623 and choose option 3 and then 2, any weekday from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. Manufactured and mobile homes must be registered with the auditor within 30 days of placement in the county, and moving one takes a $5 permit.

More questions about Washington County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the Washington County recorder's phone number?

Call 740-373-6623 and ask for extension 2223 or 2225. Visit the courthouse at 205 Putnam Street in Marietta between 8:00 am and 4:30 pm on weekdays.

Can a deed be e-recorded in Washington County?

Yes, through Corporation Service Company or eRecording Partners Network. The recorder's page adds that Simplifile cannot be used to record deeds.

How long does recording take in Washington County?

The county FAQ gives three days. Having the auditor's endorsement and the exact fee on the deed keeps the filing from being returned.

What happens if I send the wrong fee to the Washington County recorder?

A short payment is returned. A payment over by $5.00 or more is usually returned as well, and an overage under $5.00 comes back in cash, according to the recorder's FAQ.

Which Washington County office handles a real estate transfer before recording?

The auditor, at extension 2124 off 740-373-6623. The auditor takes the statement of value and the conveyance fee, endorses the deed, and passes it along to the recorder.

Which office in Wooster files a Wayne County deed?

Look for the Recorder behind the Administration Building's first-floor doors, 428 West Liberty Street, Wooster, OH 44691, or phone 330-287-5460. The county site describes the post as keeper of legal documents, chiefly real estate papers: deeds, mortgages, liens. Subdivision plats are also filed there.

The Auditor, Treasurer, Board of Revision and Map Office occupy the same building. Wooster serves a county of roughly 555 square miles. Lawmakers drew the county in 1808, and it began operating in 1812. The Census Bureau lists 116,758 residents for July 2025.

Which stops come before the Recorder in Wayne County?

A short route is posted on the Auditor's real estate page, and a deed that skips a stop tends to come back unrecorded.

  • Draft the deed, then present it at the Map Office.
  • Carry it to the Auditor, where the conveyance and transfer charges are paid.
  • Last, file at the Recorder's counter.

The state's value statement sits behind the Auditor's stop. R.C. 319.202 requires a declaration of value from the grantee before endorsement. An exempt transfer states its reason in place of a value, using the exemption form DTE 100(EX) from the Auditor's library.

What is the Wayne County conveyance charge at the Auditor?

The Auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand dollars of price and $0.50 per parcel, applied after the price is bumped up to the next $100. The Auditor's Tools menu includes a Conveyance Fee Calculator for the arithmetic.

Unpaid taxes can stall a closing. Phone the Treasurer at 330-287-5450 for a payoff, and see the delinquent list online. The Auditor, 330-287-5430, answers conveyance questions from 8:00 am on weekdays.

What does the Wayne County Recorder charge to record?

The table reproduces the Auditor's list, which follows R.C. 317.32, in which each of the base and housing trust fund shares is $17 for pages one and two and $4 for every page after. A county may also layer on a preservation surcharge capped at $5; ask the Recorder if the total below has one.

Recording charges as the Wayne County Auditor prints them
ItemCharge
First two pages$34.00

That $20.00 line is aimed at papers that break the layout rules of R.C. 317.114, so check margins and ink with the Recorder before you sign.

What does the Census Bureau say about Wayne County households?

QuickFacts reports 44,365 households sharing 47,538 housing units, with 2.53 people in each household, and owners hold 76.6 percent of the homes.

  • Middle owner-held home value: $222,100.
  • Middle rent: $881 a month.
  • Middle household income: $73,574.
  • Share who stayed at the same address for a year: 90.2 percent.
  • Building permits during 2025: 232.

The Auditor's home page counts roughly 59,000 parcels, so most recorded deeds touch only a small slice of them in any year.

What should arrive at the Recorder's counter with a Wayne County deed?

Take the endorsed original, parcel numbers and a check. Because the Treasurer's FAQ says some name changes require a new deed, compare the owner's name on the Auditor's parcel record with the deed.

  • Land records at the Recorder are indexed by document type and parties.
  • A mortgage release is its own recording, with a marginal reference charge under the statute.
  • The Auditor's parcel search and GIS parcel viewer show earlier owners, acreage and last sale before the deed is written.

What does the value statement cover on a Wayne County sale?

The statute counts the full price paid or owed, mortgage and vendor's lien amounts included. A gift is valued at its likely open market price. Willfully misstating value is prohibited.

Two more questions ride along. One covers owner-occupied credit and homestead reductions. The other covers agricultural use valuation and any recoupment charge. A yes to either means both parties confirm the amount has been accounted for.

How does a tax due date interact with a Wayne County closing?

Installment bills are issued in January or February and again in June or July. The Treasurer's last days for 2026 were February 26 and July 30; a 10 percent penalty follows, and half is returned if the balance clears within 10 days.

If a deed records in the same week a bill comes due, put in writing who pays. Bank payments faced earlier cutoffs (February 2 and July 13 in 2026). Partial payments are accepted and all go toward the upcoming bill.

Which four Wayne County phone lines does a seller need?

  • Recorder, 330-287-5460.
  • Auditor, 330-287-5430.
  • Treasurer, 330-287-5450.
  • Board of Revision, 330-287-5433.

Call ahead with your parcel number in hand. The first handles recording, the second conveyance and parcel records, the third balances and payments, and the fourth valuation complaints. All answer from the same Wooster address.

Does a Wayne County sale let the new owner file a fresh value complaint?

Usually, yes. R.C. 5715.19 generally bars a second complaint on one parcel inside an interim period. Exceptions follow an arm's length sale, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement or a 15 percent occupancy change after the earlier lien date. A sale can therefore reopen the door for a parcel the seller already contested.

Filing opens each January 1, and for tax year 2026 the Auditor lists January 1 to March 31, 2027. Signatures must be notarized, which Auditor staff can usually do in person. The second half bill is held until the Board rules, and the first half stays payable on time.

What do Wayne County taxes look like after the deed is recorded?

Assessed value is 35 percent of market value, multiplied by the district rate and trimmed by a reduction factor. The owner-occupied credit has its own application, form DTE 105C, in the Auditor's library.

Rates differ by district, and the Treasurer's website charts them all.

Which online tools can a Wayne County seller use before recording?

  • Auditor: a parcel search and map, a conveyance calculator, a tax estimator, a levy estimator, sales reports and a delinquency report, plus downloadable forms.
  • Treasurer: payment through Autoagent online or at 1-844-615-1900, and monthly or semi-annual ACH direct debit for parcels that owe current taxes.
  • Recorder: the county's page lists the office address and phone, so a call to 330-287-5460 settles questions about what a particular paper needs.

Run the sales report and tax estimator first. They show what nearby parcels sold for and what the levies on your district would produce, which helps when you write the value into the statement.

How has Wayne County grown, according to the Census Bureau?

The county counted 114,520 people in 2010 and 116,894 in 2020, and its July 2025 estimate of 116,758 sits slightly below the 2020 base. Land area is 554.79 square miles and density was 210.7 people per square mile in 2020, up from 206.4 in 2010. Median age was 39.0 at the 2020 count, with 24.0 percent of residents under 18 and 18.6 percent 65 or older.

More questions about Wayne County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Where in Wooster do I file a Wayne County deed?

With the Recorder, 330-287-5460, in the Administration Building. Get the Auditor's endorsement first.

What recording fees does the Auditor's page list for Wayne County?

The printed list is $34.00 for two pages, $8.00 per added page, $4.00 per marginal notation, $2.00 per copy and a $20.00 standardization fee. A preservation surcharge of up to $5 is optional under state law.

The Auditor prints $4.00 per $1,000 of price and $0.50 per parcel. The grantor owes the conveyance charge.

Is the Auditor's stop before or after the Recorder in Wayne County?

Before. The sequence is Map Office, Auditor, then Recorder.

Who gives a tax payoff on a Wayne County parcel?

The Treasurer, at 330-287-5450. Its website also shows a delinquent list.

Staff keep a lasting record of every paper that transfers or encumbers land here, and indexing lets a searcher follow who held title and which debts attach. The county sits on the Ohio line with two other states: Hillsdale County, Michigan is to the north, and DeKalb and Steuben counties of Indiana are to the west. Fulton, Henry and Defiance counties complete the Ohio side. Bryan is the seat and the biggest city.

How much is recording a deed in Williams County?

Senate Bill 94 let counties add a $5.00 preservation surcharge under R.C. 317.32, and Williams County's Recorder applied it starting January 1, 2025. Reference fees and the standardization guidelines still apply on top.

Amounts taken from the Williams County Recorder's pages
ItemAmount

Certified copies follow the Ohio Revised Code schedule that the Recorder's fees page reproduces.

What layout does Ohio expect on a deed filed in Williams County?

R.C. 317.114 gives every recorder the same standard so that recording stamps have room on the page. A deed that falls short is still recorded, with $20 more collected. Here is what Williams County's Recorder asks for.

  • Dark blue or black ink only, and no highlighter.
  • A font of 10 points or larger.
  • One inch of white space left, right and bottom.
  • Page one keeps 3 inches clear at the top, later pages 1.5 inches.
  • Paper from letter size (8.5 by 11) to legal length (8.5 by 14).

Four categories escape the rules: documents signed before July 1, 2009, papers from a court or taxing authority, state and federal forms with DD214 discharges, and plats.

Which stamps does a Williams County deed need first?

A conveyance can arrive by mail only after the Engineer and the Auditor have stamped it, a rule that covers deeds, land contracts, easements and affidavits. The County Engineer reviews the legal description, the Auditor then names the conveyance charge, and for many documents the Treasurer first confirms that taxes on the parcel are paid.

  • Engineer: clears the legal description.
  • Treasurer: validates payment of taxes.
  • Auditor, 419-636-5639: states the charge.
  • Recorder: records and indexes the stamped deed.

The conveyance fee posted by the Auditor is $4 per $1,000 of price, with a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel or deed. R.C. 319.202 assigns that fee to the grantor and requires the grantee's value statement. New conveyance standards started on January 1, 2026, and a link to them is on the Auditor's page.

What does Williams County look like in Census numbers?

The July 2025 estimate is 36,549 people, a 1.5 percent drop from the April 2020 base. QuickFacts counts 15,476 households in 16,659 housing units, and 76.3 percent of homes have owner occupants.

  • Value of the middle owner-held home: $150,000.
  • Middle owner outlay: $1,163 a month with a loan, $462 with none.
  • Middle gross rent: $791.
  • Middle household income: $61,048 (2024 dollars).
  • Residents past 65: 22.8 percent.
  • Permits pulled in 2025: 44.

Density is 88.2 residents per square mile across about 421 square miles of land. Census designated places include Alvordton, Kunkle, Lake Seneca, Nettle Lake and Pulaski.

How does someone obtain a copy of a Williams County deed?

Walk in, and the counter copy of a public record, a deed among them, is $0.25 per page, with staff glad to help find it. Written requests run $2.00 per page and need the volume and page from the Ohio Land Records index, a check or money order, and a stamped envelope addressed to you. Phone and email requests are not filled.

That online index covers filings from October 25, 1999 forward and shows new entries within a day of recording. It names the owner, document type and property description without displaying the document itself. Certified copies exist, though in person a plain copy costs the same $0.25 per page, so request a certified one only when a lender or court insists on it.

Plats are searchable through the County Engineer's site. The Ohio Recorders' Association also lists every county recorder along with the regulations and fees found in the Revised Code, which is handy for comparing what neighboring counties collect.

The Recorder has flagged a mailer called a "Deed Processing Notice" from a South Dakota company that asks homeowners for $83 to send a deed copy. Deeds are public records, so a friend can collect one for you at the courthouse.

What do Williams County's population and work patterns suggest about its housing market?

Population peaked at 39,188 in the 2000 census, then slipped to 37,642 in 2010 and 37,102 in 2020. In the Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures, 61.0 percent of people aged 16 and up are in the civilian labor force and the average commute takes 19.8 minutes. The county had 802 employer establishments and 16,283 jobs in 2023, per the same source.

  • High school graduates among adults 25 and older: 91.8 percent.
  • Bachelor's degree or higher: 13.7 percent.
  • Households with broadband: 85.5 percent.
  • Veterans: 1,784.
  • Persons in poverty: 10.3 percent.

When was Williams County formed, and who oversees it?

Lawmakers created the county on April 1, 1820 and it was organized on February 2, 1824, with a name that honors David Williams, one of John Andre's captors in the Revolutionary War. Three commissioners oversee county departments. In total area it is the 53rd largest Ohio county, and its airport lies about two nautical miles east of downtown Bryan.

The Recorder holds documentation back to the start of land ownership in the county, though the online index begins in 1999, so older deeds need a trip to the courthouse.

Which other Williams County offices touch a house sale?

The county's Useful Links page maps the neighbors of the Recorder.

  • Probate Court: estates, guardianships and trusts, relevant when a house passes through an estate before sale.
  • Planning Commission handles zoning questions about lots and uses.
  • Records Center is the county repository for both public and confidential county records.
  • Clerk of Courts takes passports, divorce records and common pleas cases.
  • Property Fraud Alert: guidance posted for owners who worry about forged filings.

The Auditor, Engineer and Treasurer sit alongside these offices on the same courthouse square, and the Recorder is the last stop for a deed.

More questions about Williams County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What time does the Williams County Recorder stop taking deeds?

At 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the office closes. The counter is upstairs in the Bryan courthouse and opens at 8:30 a.m. on weekdays.

What will recording one Williams County deed cost?

Expect $39.00 for a deed of up to two pages, then $8.00 for every page beyond that, since the January 1, 2025 change. Reference fees of $4.00 may be added, and sloppy formatting brings a $20.00 penalty.

How is the Williams County conveyance fee figured?

The Auditor posts $4 per $1,000 of the purchase price, with $0.50 for each parcel or deed as the transfer fee. Ask the Auditor for the total on your price.

Does the Williams County Recorder accept deeds by mail?

Only when the Engineer and the Auditor have stamped the document beforehand. The same goes for land contracts, easements and affidavits.

What is the cheapest way to get my Williams County deed copy?

Stop by the Recorder's counter, where copies are a quarter a page. A mailed request costs $2.00 per page and must give the volume and page, with payment and a self addressed envelope.

Perrysburg was the first seat of government and Bowling Green took over in 1870; ground was broken for today's courthouse on November 28, 1893. Three county offices touch every sale. The Recorder keeps the permanent record. The Auditor changes the name on the tax rolls. The Treasurer, at 419-354-9130, is the contact for money owed on the parcel.

What makes a Wood County deed ready to record?

Start with the grantor's signature and a certificate from a notary or other authorized officer (Revised Code 5301.01). Then file with the county that contains the parcel. Under Revised Code 5301.25, an unfiled deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who paid in good faith.

The Recorder's website carries document standards and a note on marginal references. A marginal reference ties a new paper to an older one through an instrument number or a volume and page. A release names the mortgage it ends. Citing the prior deed inside a deed costs nothing extra, but citing a land contract or a terminated life estate gets indexed and priced as a reference. Before mailing a deed, run down this list:

  • The signature and notary block are complete.
  • The legal description matches the previous recorded deed or a newer survey.
  • The Auditor's endorsement appears on the front.
  • The payment covers each page, including the caption page.

What will Wood County charge me to record?

Every recording charge in Revised Code 317.32 comes in matched halves, a base fee and a housing trust fund fee of the same size. Each half is $17 for the first two pages and $4 for each page after that. A county may layer a preservation surcharge of up to $5 on top. The Wood County Recorder's site includes an estimator that totals the fees for your paperwork.

Page size is eight and a half by fourteen inches, and a fraction of a page is billed as a page, so a long exhibit adds cost. The table lists the items a home seller meets most often.

Statutory recording charges, with the Wood County copy rate
ChargePrinted amount
Pages one and twoTwo halves of $17 each
Each added pageTwo halves of $4 each
County preservation surchargeCapped at $5
Reference entered by a separate instrumentTwo halves of $2 each, per reference
Copy of a recorded page in Wood County$2.00 each

Sources: Ohio Revised Code 317.32 and the Wood County Recorder contact page.

Why does the Auditor see a Wood County deed before the Recorder does?

Call the Auditor at 419-354-9150 to arrange the transfer. The buyer files a value statement, the Auditor writes the fee on the deed, and the stamped deed moves on to the Recorder. Revised Code 319.54 prices the fee as one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is more, and the seller carries it. The Auditor shares the Recorder's floor in the County Office Building, so a deed can travel from one counter to the other without leaving the building.

Commissioners may add a transfer tax capped at thirty cents per hundred dollars (Revised Code 322.02). Whether Wood County has done so is a question for the Auditor, and the answer belongs in your closing estimate.

How do I search Wood County records or order a copy?

The Recorder's site offers three search paths. Adaptable Visual Access shows the index from 1980 forward and trails the real filing date by roughly a day. A Laredo Anywhere account shows document images, but the office designed it for high volume professional users and asks for an account request form. AmeriScan's Documents-On-Demand shows the old physical book indexes.

A June 30, 2026 deadline in Revised Code 317.13 told every county recorder to post indexes and images of instruments from 1980 onward and to accept conveyances electronically. Charging a fee simply to open a login is not allowed.

Copies cost $2.00 per page. The office wants an instrument number or a book and page with every request, and staff will not open a document to look for a legal description. Before you order, note that the Recorder's home page also carries tiles for public notices, recording fees, document standards, a short office history and a bulk images service. A typical order runs like this:

  • Search the index by name and write down the instrument number.
  • Decide whether you want the whole document or only certain pages. The first or last page needs no extra identification.
  • Send the number and page choice by email or phone.

What do Wood County's housing and job base mean for a seller?

The county's 2019 financial report named Bowling Green State University (3,300 employees), Magna (2,200), First Solar (1,200), Owens Community College (1,000), Wood County Hospital (875) and FedEx Ground (800) among its biggest employers.

Libraries follow the same patchwork. The Wood County District Public Library serves Bowling Green from its main building and a Walbridge branch, while Perrysburg, Rossford, North Baltimore, Pemberville and Weston each run their own, and all share the Woodlink catalog.

Which Wood County cities and school districts should a seller name?

Four whole cities lie in the county, Bowling Green, Northwood, Perrysburg and Rossford, along with the edge of Fostoria. The county touches seven others (Lucas, Ottawa, Sandusky, Seneca, Hancock, Putnam and Henry), and a parcel near a line is filed in whichever county holds the land. Fifteen school systems draw from Wood County, and a few are easy to confuse: Eastwood, Elmwood, Lake, Otsego and Patrick Henry are local districts, while Perrysburg and Rossford are exempted village districts. Buyers who care about schools will ask which one serves the address.

The county is named for the Army engineer who built Fort Meigs in the War of 1812, and it was established in 1820. The Wood County Airport lies a nautical mile northeast of downtown Bowling Green, and the Maumee River marks the diagonal northwest border.

If a paid mortgage never got a recorded release, ask the lender for one and record it with a marginal reference to the original. Then call the Treasurer to learn whether any tax remains on the parcel.

More questions about Wood County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How much is the recording fee for a Wood County deed?

A deed of two pages carries a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee, and each added page carries $4 and $4. If the county applies its preservation surcharge, add up to $5. The estimator on the Recorder's site gives the total for your document.

Does Wood County charge a transfer tax on a sale?

The Auditor's conveyance fee reaches most sales, and sellers pay it. A county transfer tax exists only where commissioners enacted one, so phone the Auditor at 419-354-9150.

Can I order my recorded deed by phone?

Yes. Look up the instrument number in the online index, then call or email it in. Each page is $2.00.

Do Wood County's online records include old deeds?

The index starts in 1980 and runs about a day behind. Older records are in book indexes served through AmeriScan.

Who loses if a signed deed is never recorded?

The buyer does. Someone who later buys in good faith can come out ahead of an unrecorded deed, so the buyer should file as soon as closing ends.

What we could not confirm

  • Wyandot tax due dates not located
  • Wyandot recording fees and e-recording
  • Wyandot delinquent/foreclosure facts

Which office takes a Wyandot County deed?

The Wyandot County Recorder works from Room 24 in the courthouse, 109 South Sandusky Avenue, Upper Sandusky, OH 43351, which also serves as the mailing address. Call 419-294-1442. Two deputy recorders work under the elected Recorder.

Wyandot is a rural county. Lawmakers carved it out on February 3, 1845 from Crawford, Marion, Hardin and Hancock counties. It spans 408 square miles of northwest Ohio and borders Seneca County to the north and Marion County to the south. Upper Sandusky is both the lone city and the seat. At the 2020 census Wyandot held 21,900 people, 9,084 households and 9,839 housing units, with vacancy at 7.7 percent. Owners occupy 73.5 percent of the occupied homes, and 69.7 percent of residents live outside urban areas.

That rural makeup shapes deeds here. Many Wyandot parcels are farm tracts or township acreage described by section, township and range, so the legal description gets more scrutiny than it would for a platted city lot.

Why does a deed stop at the Tax Map Department first?

The county's written conveyance standards say no deed will be accepted for transfer by the Auditor or for recording by the Recorder until the Engineer's Tax Map Department has reviewed and stamped it. The stamp reads Description Checked, Tax Map Office. The department has moved into the County Engineer's office at 320 N. Warpole Street.

The reviewer takes one of four paths on an ordinary sale with an unchanged description:

  • Approve the description as written and stamp the deed.
  • Suggest fixes for obvious typing errors, transposed numbers or rotated bearings, then stamp it.
  • Let a description with a clear point of beginning but minor flaws transfer one time, with a notice that a survey is required on the next non-exempt transfer.
  • Stamp a bad description Survey Required.

The standards define a bad description as one whose point of beginning cannot be identified or that contains an error causing ambiguity. Examples they list include missing dimensions or acreage, no section, township and range or municipality, and a parcel the grantor does not own. The standards invite deed writers to have a description checked ahead of closing, which leaves time for fixes.

Which Wyandot County transfers can skip a new survey?

An exempt transfer, with no money paid, can move on an older description that fails today's standards, and the deed gets the survey-required notice. The standards name survivorship, family trust moves, transfers to close family, life estates, corrective deeds, court-ordered transfers, and sheriff's and auditor's deeds.

A sale for money is a non-exempt transfer. If the house stands on an acreage tract with a vague description, plan on a survey request. New splits of an existing parcel need a survey recorded in the county survey records, a closure report, and at least three working days for inspection. New parcels need 40 feet of owned highway frontage for single family housing and 60 feet for multiple family housing. Parcels that miss the 200 foot road frontage rule in the regional planning checklist must meet those minimums. Call Wyandot County Regional Planning at 419-294-4931 before you plan a split.

What does a survey for a new Wyandot County lot have to show?

When an owner splits a house or acreage off a parent parcel, the survey checklist in the conveyance standards applies, and Wyandot Regional Planning in Room 16 of the courthouse reviews lots under its own rules. The checklist asks for these items:

  • A minimum property width of 200 feet and at least 1.50 acres, not counting highway right of way.
  • A lot length under four times its width.
  • Every structure, well and septic system drawn on the plat, with the distance to the nearest foot for any structure within 10 feet of a property line.
  • Required setbacks met.

Survey plats must be on quality bond or Mylar, at least 11 by 17 inches and in ink, so the Recorder can reproduce and microfilm them. When a parent parcel is divided into five or more smaller parcels, the splits are reviewed under major subdivision requirements, and earlier splits from the same parent count toward the five.

What do the Ohio statutes require of the deed itself?

Under Revised Code 5301.01 the grantor signs and has the signature acknowledged by an authorized officer, usually a notary. Revised Code 317.13 has the Recorder log each instrument with its date and the minute it arrived, so filing order settles priority.

The same section lets a recorder turn down a paper that the Code does not authorize or that looks fraudulent, with a court remedy for the filer. It also set a June 30, 2026 deadline for electronic recording and online indexes reaching back to 1980. Ask the Wyandot office which electronic options it offers.

Which transfers owe the Auditor's conveyance fee?

Most sales do, and the seller pays. Revised Code 319.54 states the fee as one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater, and Revised Code 319.202 has the buyer file a statement of value first. In a sale, value is the whole consideration, with any mortgage on the property counted in.

Transfers the statute excludes from the Auditor's conveyance fee
Type of transferFee under 319.54(G)(3)
Gift between spouses, or parent and childNot charged
Among heirs or devisees of one decedent, no money paidNot charged
Into a trust the grantor can revokeNot charged
To confirm or correct a recorded deedNot charged
Sale to a buyer for moneyCharged at the rate above

Source: Ohio Revised Code 319.54. The statute lists more exemptions, such as court ordered transfers that are not sales.

Revised Code 322.02 also lets a county adopt its own transfer tax. Ask the Wyandot County Auditor whether one applies.

What does recording cost at the Wyandot County Recorder?

The page-based charges in Revised Code 317.32 are the same statewide, and the Recorder can quote your total. A long metes and bounds description adds pages, so ask before you mail the deed.

Pull the previous deed before the new one is typed. The standards require any new metes and bounds description to cite the prior deed and the source of each exception, and the acreage must be shown to three decimal places. A tract may carry no more than four exceptions.

How do I research a Wyandot County parcel before listing it?

The Tax Map Department also helps the public find property, check ownership and obtain new addresses in unincorporated areas. Its county page offers downloads of tax maps, property surveys and legal descriptions, plus a current parcel data file in ZIP format that the county supplies as is, with no guarantee of accuracy. The County Auditor keeps an online tax map site as well.

The county describes this as a tax map system rather than a full GIS and has no GIS department for advanced requests. An owner with an older farm or edge-of-town house can collect three items early:

  • The parcel number and acreage the Auditor shows on the tax map.
  • The last recorded deed, with its legal description and any exceptions.
  • Any recorded survey for the tract, which settles whether a survey will be demanded on the next transfer.

Comparing the deed acreage with the tax map matters because the standards for older descriptions that are not metes and bounds tolerate a difference of only 0.2 acre on parcels under 5 acres and 5 percent on larger ones.

More questions about Wyandot County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Is a survey required for a Wyandot County house?

Sometimes. A sale with an unchanged description moves after the Tax Map stamp. A bad description earns a Survey Required stamp, and any split of a parcel needs a recorded survey.

Where is the Wyandot County Tax Map Department?

It operates from the County Engineer's office at 320 N. Warpole Street in Upper Sandusky, after moving from its earlier location.

Who covers the Auditor's fee in Wyandot County?

The seller. The statute measures it at the greater of one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value.

How do I reach the Wyandot County Recorder?

Phone 419-294-1442, or visit Room 24 of the courthouse at 109 South Sandusky Avenue.

Can a deed be turned away?

Yes, if the paper is not authorized for recording or looks fraudulent. The filer can go to court to seek an order.
